name: advancecomp
desc: Recompression utilities for .PNG, .MNG, .ZIP, and .GZ files
why: Aggressively recompresses PNG and ZIP files with better deflate; a fun look at how file containers can be squeezed further.

brief.what_it_is: AdvanceCOMP is a set of command-line recompression utilities for .ZIP archives, .PNG images, .MNG video clips and .GZ files. It takes an existing compressed file and rewrites it with a stronger deflate encoder, so the file stays valid but gets smaller. The package ships four executables: advzip (zip files), advpng (png files), advmng (mng files) and advdef (deflate streams inside png, mng and gz files).
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says it is mainly intended for recompressing a collection of emulated-game rom, snapshot and clip files.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage says it recompresses ZIP, GZ, PNG and MNG files using the Deflate 7-Zip implementation, and recompresses MNG files using Delta and Move optimization. The README gives no further detail on the mechanism.
brief.install_notes: The fetched pages give no install steps beyond the Homebrew formula name. The GitHub README says the package runs on Linux, Mac OS X, DOS, Windows and other Unix-like platforms. No runtime, account or configuration is mentioned.
brief.standout: Rather than a new compressor, it re-encodes the deflate streams inside existing containers (ZIP, PNG, GZ, MNG) with the 7-Zip deflate implementation, so the output stays a standard file. The homepage also points users to OptiPNG and pngcrush as other PNG optimizers.
brief.status: Unknown. The fetched homepage and GitHub README show no release date, last commit date or version number, so I cannot judge whether it is actively maintained. The homepage does link to a download page, a forum and a support page, which I did not fetch.
brief.caveats: The fetched pages list no command-line usage, so I could not confirm flags or invocation syntax. The homepage says the tool is mainly aimed at emulation rom and snapshot collections. The homepage names other PNG optimizers (OptiPNG, pngcrush) as alternatives, which suggests the project is not a general-purpose PNG optimizer. The Homebrew entry has no caveats.
quotes: AdvanceCOMP is a collection of recompression utilities for your .ZIP archives, .PNG snapshots, .MNG video clips and .GZ files.
It's mainly intended for recompressing your rom, snapshot and clip collection of emulated games.
Recompress ZIP, GZ, PNG and MNG files using the Deflate 7-Zip implementation.
fetch_log: https://www.advancemame.it/comp-readme.html: fetched, worked; short page with feature list and nav links, no commands
https://github.com/amadvance/advancecomp: fetched, worked; README lists the four tools with one-line descriptions, no commands or version/date

judge.reason: It is a niche recompression utility, but replacing deflate streams with a stronger encoder is routine optimization rather than a distinctive idea.

name: aespipe
desc: AES encryption or decryption for pipes
why: Old-school AES over pipes with a loop-AES lineage, a small curio that opens a window onto Linux disk encryption history.

brief.what_it_is: aespipe is a command-line filter that reads data from standard input, encrypts or decrypts it with AES, and writes the result to standard output. Its README says it can create and restore encrypted tar or cpio archives, and it can encrypt and decrypt loop-AES compatible encrypted disk images. Keys can come from a passphrase or from a gpg-encrypted key file passed with -K. The README's example usage is aespipe -d -K mykey1.gpg <archive.aes | bzip2 -d -q | tar xvpf -.
brief.why_it_exists: The README gives no explicit motivation beyond its role in the loop-AES ecosystem: it is the pipe-based AES tool that lets you encrypt archives and images that loop-AES can also mount. The author is Jari Ruusu, and the package is copyright 2002-2025.
brief.how_it_works: aespipe sits in a shell pipeline between a producer and a consumer, so tar, bzip2, dd, or mkisofs feed it data and the output goes to a file or device. Its AES code is derived from Brian Gladman's implementation, with optimized assembly for x86, amd64, arm, and aarch64, and it can use VIA padlock, Intel AES, or ARM CE hardware with a software fallback. The README also describes a bz2aespipe wrapper script that uses a seeded, iterated key setup to slow dictionary attacks.

commands_seen.context: Generates the Makefile; run first when building from source. Options include --enable-asm=amd64 and --enable-intelaes.
Builds aespipe after configure.
Runs the test suite, which uses the bundled gpgkey[123].asc key files.
Installs to /usr/local/bin by default; --bindir=/usr/bin can change this.
Example 1: writes a bzip2-compressed, encrypted tar archive using the bz2aespipe wrapper script.

commands_seen.cmd: tar cvf - files... | bzip2 | aespipe -w 10 -K mykey1.gpg >archive.aes
commands_seen.context: Example 2: writes an encrypted archive using a gpg-encrypted key file; the -w 10 flag is used with that key file.
Example 2: restores the archive, prompting for the passphrase that decrypts the key file.
Example 3: appends an encrypted ISO9660 image after the key file stored in the first 8192 bytes.

commands_seen.cmd: dd if=/dev/fd0 bs=64k | aespipe -K /etc/fskey1.gpg | dd of=/dev/fd0 bs=64k conv=notrunc
commands_seen.context: Example 4: adds loop-AES compatible encryption in place to a 1.44 MB floppy.

commands_seen.cmd: dd if=/dev/fd0 bs=64k | aespipe -d -K /etc/fskey1.gpg | dd of=/dev/fd0 bs=64k conv=notrunc
commands_seen.context: Example 4: removes that encryption from the same floppy.

brief.install_notes: The README says to build from source with ./configure, make, make tests, and make install. Assembly code needs a GNU toolchain, and if configure detects it wrongly, --disable-asm may be needed. Building on the Homebrew side is not covered in the README. The gpg-based key-file examples need gpg installed, and gpg version 1 versus 2 changes a build-time workaround, so reconfigure if you switch versions. Reading /dev/random can block until entropy is available. Mounting loop-AES images on Linux requires the loop-AES package, version 3.0a or later.
brief.standout: Instead of a password-only archive, it can use a gpg-encrypted key file made of 65 random keys and can encrypt an existing floppy or CD image in place, staying compatible with the loop-AES on-disk format. It is a small, Unix-pipeline-first tool that fits into dd, tar, and mkisofs.
brief.status: maintained, with some uncertainty. The README is dated 2025-04-29, the aespipe-latest.tar.bz2 tarball is dated 2025-09-02, and the directory index shows an updates/ folder modified 2026-09-26. The README itself has no release history, so the ChangeLog is the place to confirm.
brief.caveats: The README warns that gpg may let keys leak to swap: 'gpg appears to prevent its own keys from being leaked to swap, but does not appear to prevent data handled by it from being leaked to swap,' so gpg-encrypted key files depend on encrypted swap. Assembly support needs the GNU toolchain, and configure can misdetect it. The Homebrew formula's caveats are empty. The README file is under the GNU GPL, but I did not verify the license of the aespipe source code itself. The homepage is a bare SourceForge-style directory listing, not a project landing page.
quotes: aespipe program is AES encrypting or decrypting pipe. It reads from standard input and writes to standard output.
A random password seed and password iteration count are used to slow down dictionary attacks.
gpg appears to prevent its own keys from being leaked to swap, but does not appear to prevent data handled by it from being leaked to swap.
fetch_log: https://loop-aes.sourceforge.net/ - worked, but returned a directory index listing rather than a landing page; it links to aespipe.README, which I then fetched.
https://loop-aes.sourceforge.net/aespipe.README - worked; this is the full README, with build instructions, examples, and file list.

judge.reason: A straightforward AES pipe filter with loop-AES compatibility, but its archive and disk-image workflows do not make the underlying idea distinctive enough.

name: airspy
desc: Driver and tools for a software-defined radio
why: Driver and tools for an SDR, a real door into radio, though deprecated and hardware-dependent.

brief.what_it_is: Airspy host software: a C driver library and command-line tools for Airspy software-defined radio receivers, which are USB hardware sold separately (the homepage lists HF+, R2, Mini and SpyVerter R2 products). The Homebrew formula installs eight executables: airspy_gpio, airspy_gpiodir, airspy_info, airspy_lib_version, airspy_r820t, airspy_rx, airspy_si5351c and airspy_spiflash. The README does not document what each tool takes in or puts out, so any description beyond names is inference. The names suggest that airspy_rx streams received radio samples from the device to a file or stdout, and that airspy_info reports device details, but I could not confirm this from the pages read. The repo describes itself as 'A tiny and efficient software defined radio' and supports Linux, Windows and FreeBSD.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as host software 'for AirSpy, a project to produce a low cost, open source software radio platform.' The homepage describes the hardware as combining 'Software Architecture, DSP and RF techniques' to be 'a serious alternative to both cost sensitive and high end receivers.'
brief.how_it_works: The README does not explain the internals. It says the code is 'based on HackRF project' and that the build uses CMake with libusb, so the tools talk to the receiver over USB. The homepage says the radios integrate with the SDR# application for acquisition, analysis and demodulation.

commands_seen.cmd: sudo apt-get install build-essential cmake libusb-1.0-0-dev pkg-config
commands_seen.context: Linux (Debian/Ubuntu/Raspbian) prerequisites: compiler, CMake, libusb headers and pkg-config.
Downloads the master branch source archive for the Linux build.
Unpacks the source archive.
Enters the unpacked source directory.
Creates an out-of-tree build directory.
Changes into the build directory.
Configures the build and asks it to install udev rules so the USB device is accessible without root.
Compiles the host library and tools.
Installs the built files system-wide.
Refreshes the shared library cache after install.
FreeBSD step (run as root): adds a user to the plugdev group so they can access the device.

brief.install_notes: Hardware: an Airspy receiver plugged in over USB is needed to do anything useful with these tools. Linux: needs build-essential, cmake, libusb-1.0 dev files and pkg-config; the CMake flag -DINSTALL_UDEV_RULES=ON installs udev rules, then sudo ldconfig. FreeBSD: pkg install git cmake, then cmake .. -DLIBUSB_LIBRARIES=/usr/lib/libusb.so, make, make install, and add the user to the plugdev group. Windows: either Visual Studio 2013 or later with a libusb 1.0.20 download and pthreads-w32 2.9.1 extracted into the source tree, or MSYS2 mingw64 with pacman packages for gcc, make, pkgconf and libusb, built via CMake with MinGW Makefiles. Windows versions older than Vista need a driver installed, or Zadig can swap in WinUSB for the AirSpy USB device. No account or licence key is mentioned in the README.
brief.standout: Ordinary SDR tooling is usually bundled with a single app, but this repo is a plain C library plus a small set of named command-line tools, and the homepage pitches the hardware as a cheap alternative to high-end receivers. The README is also unusually candid about one Windows trap: Ctrl-C in airspy_rx does not stop cleanly under Cygwin or MinGW shells and can corrupt the output file.
brief.status: unknown. The README gives no release date, version number or recent commit. The two GitHub pages I fetched returned only the README, with no commit or release metadata. The scout notes call the project deprecated, but I could not confirm that from these pages. The homepage is current (copyright 2026 and a live product line), but that describes the vendor, not this repository's upkeep.
brief.caveats: Needs Airspy hardware to be of any use. Builds are fiddly: Windows requires either Visual Studio 2013 or an MSYS2 environment, and the README pulls libusb and pthreads from external URLs, one of which is an old ftp:// link. Tools must be run from a native Windows command shell, not Cygwin or MinGW, or airspy_rx may not stop cleanly and may corrupt its file. The README has no usage documentation for any of the eight tools. The FreeBSD clone command uses backslashes in the URL. The README does not state a licence, though it says the code is based on the HackRF project. The scout note says deprecated, which I could not verify from the pages.
quotes: A tiny and efficient software defined radio.
This repository contains host software (Linux/Windows) for AirSpy, a project to produce a low cost, open source software radio platform.
There is a whole world below 30 MHz.

name: aften
desc: Audio encoder which generates ATSC A/52 compressed audio streams
why: An open ATSC A/52 AC-3 audio encoder, a rare look inside a broadcast codec that most developers never touch.

brief.what_it_is: Aften is a command-line audio encoder that produces compressed audio streams in the ATSC A/52 format, also known as AC-3 or Dolby Digital. The homepage describes it as an encoder that generates these streams from the A/52 specification, and it is used in DVD-Video content. The homepage does not spell out the input format. The installed tools (wavfilter, wavinfo, wavrms) suggest WAV audio is the working material, but that is an inference from the executable names. The Homebrew package installs four executables: aften, wavfilter, wavinfo and wavrms.
brief.why_it_exists: The project began as a stand-alone command-line version of the FFmpeg AC-3 encoder and has since grown with structural changes and extra features. The name is an acronym for 'A Fifty-Two ENcoder', and it is also the Danish and Norwegian word for 'evening'.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage names the reference specification for the encoding algorithm and bitstream format as ATSC Standard A/52 (Revision A). It says Revision B adds E-AC-3 (Dolby Digital Plus), which the project lists as a future goal. The homepage does not describe the internal encoder pipeline.

commands_seen.context: Clones the current development source from the project's SourceForge git repository. The homepage gives this as the way to get the latest git version.

brief.install_notes: The homepage links a 'Building Aften with CMake' document, which suggests a CMake build from source, but I did not follow that link, so I have no build steps. The homepage also links 'Commandline help', which I did not follow either. Building from the git clone is the route the homepage gives for the latest code. The homepage gives no runtime, account or hardware requirements.
brief.standout: It is an open implementation of a broadcast and DVD audio codec that most developers never open up. The project name, its origin as an FFmpeg-derived encoder, and its Danish/Norwegian meaning for 'evening' are all unusual touches.
brief.status: Mixed evidence, so I'd call it unknown. The homepage says the current release is Aften 0.0.8 and that 'Development of Aften is very active, and there are some major changes currently in-the-works.' However, the footer reads 'website ©2007 Justin Ruggles', and the page shows no release date for 0.0.8, so the date of the latest activity is unclear.
brief.caveats: The authors state they make no claim that the software or its output is Dolby Digital compliant. Content made with it should not be labelled as containing Dolby Digital technology or carry Dolby trademarks without authorisation. E-AC-3 (Dolby Digital Plus) is not yet supported; it is a future goal. Licensing is mostly LGPL, with some portions under the Xiph.org variant of the BSD licence, and each source file states its own licence. The git clone uses the git:// protocol. The homepage's ©2007 footer and undated release make the maintenance status uncertain.
quotes: Aften is an audio encoder which generates compressed audio streams based on ATSC A/52 specification.
The Aften project started as a stand-alone commandline version of the FFmpeg AC-3 encoder.
E-AC-3 encoding is one of the future goals of the Aften project.
The authors make no claims that this software or any content created with this software is Dolby® Digital compliant.

name: airspyhf
desc: Driver and tools for a software-defined radio
why: Driver and tools for the Airspy HF+ SDR, a real door into listening to the HF radio spectrum.

brief.what_it_is: airspyhf is the user-mode host driver and tools for the Airspy HF+, a software-defined radio receiver for the HF and VHF bands. The README describes it as host software for Linux and Windows, and says macOS builds use the same CMake steps without the udev rules. The package installs five command-line programs: airspyhf_rx, airspyhf_info, airspyhf_calibrate, airspyhf_gpio and airspyhf_lib_version. The README does not describe what each program does, so their roles are inferred from their names. The input is the radio hardware over USB, and the output is the driver library plus those tools on the host machine.
brief.why_it_exists: The README gives no stated motive. The homepage frames the Airspy line as high-performance, affordable SDR receivers that work with the free SDR# software, and its HF+ page says "There is a whole world below 30 MHz."
brief.how_it_works: The README does not explain the internal mechanism. It says the Airspy HF+ driver is based on the Airspy R2 driver, which is itself based on the HackRF project. Host access to the device goes through libusb, and on Linux the install step can add udev rules that control which users can open the device.

For a stand-alone desktop, the README suggests the uaccess option. On Windows you need Visual Studio 2013 or later with libusb-1.0.20 and pthreads-win32 2.9.1 extracted into the source tree, or MinGW with CMake and libusb headers. No brew-specific notes or first-run steps were given beyond the README.

name: aldo
desc: Morse code learning tool released under GPL
why: A Morse code trainer from the GNU project, a small old-school audio tool with a genuine signal-and-sound angle.

brief.what_it_is: Aldo is a Morse code learning tool for GNU/Linux, released under the GPL. It plays Morse code through your audio output and asks you to identify it, offering four training modes: Classic (random characters), Koch method (characters added progressively), Read from file (Morse generated from a text file you write), and Callsign (random amateur radio callsigns). You type or select what you hear, and the program checks your answers. Input is audio-based training material generated from text, and output is your practice results and audible Morse.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents it as a plain Morse code learning tool. The Savannah summary describes it as a Morse tutor for practising receiving characters and callsigns by ear.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage describes the training methods but does not explain the audio or scoring internals. The Koch method plays two characters at full speed (20 wpm) and adds one more character each time you identify at least 90 percent of them. Read from file generates Morse from a text file you write.

commands_seen.context: Debian install on unstable, shown on the homepage as run by root (the homepage shows it after a root@somewhere:~# prompt).
Clones the development repository from Savannah.
Enters the cloned source directory.
Builds from git source (bootstrap, configure, make), then runs the built binary at ./src/aldo. The homepage shows this after an aldouser@somewhere:~/aldo$ prompt.

brief.install_notes: Build prerequisites listed on the homepage are gcc 3.x or later and libao. Source tarballs are on the download page, and the latest listed version is aldo-0.7.7, with the signature available. Older releases are on the old web page. Debian packages it, so on Debian unstable you can use apt-get. Building from git needs the bootstrap step before configure. No accounts, hardware, or runtime configuration are mentioned on the pages I read.
brief.standout: It is a small, old-school audio tool with a sound-first approach, and the Koch method is a well-known adaptive learning scheme for Morse. It is packaged in Debian and has a classic Unix build from source.
brief.status: Probably quiet, though the evidence is mixed. Savannah lists Development Status 5 - Production/Stable, the project was registered in February 2003, and it has 2 open bugs out of 9 total. The homepage names aldo-0.7.7 as latest but gives no release date, and I found no last-commit date. The homepage also describes itself as a Savane-hosted project with 3 active members. Treat maintenance as unknown rather than confirmed active.
brief.caveats: Mainly developed for GNU/Linux, and the Savannah page says the project is not part of the GNU Project even though it is GPL licensed (GPL v2 or later). Build requires a C compiler and libao, so there is some build setup. No Windows or macOS instructions appeared on the pages. The homepage also links to GtkMMorse as another option, which is not covered here.

Two morse characters will be played at full speed (20wpm) until you'll be able to identify at least 90 percent of them.

name: alpscore
desc: Applications and libraries for physics simulations
why: Physics simulation applications for quantum many-body models; real science you can run, though it leans toward a research library.

brief.what_it_is: ALPSCore is a C++ library collection for numerical physics simulations, mainly of condensed matter systems with strongly correlated electrons. Its README describes it as providing generic algorithms and utilities for physics problems, and the homepage calls it a set of tested, standardized components. It takes C++ code that links against it, via CMake's find_package(ALPSCore), and provides reusable building blocks such as accumulators, parameters, and HDF5 I/O for simulation programs. It does not ship standalone command-line applications: the brew entry lists no executables, and the install docs only build and test the libraries. The older ALPS application codes live at alps.comp-phys.com, per the homepage.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says the libraries aim to provide well tested, robust, standardized components for numerical simulations so that physics codes need not be rewritten, and the README says the project is meant to increase software reuse in the physics community.
brief.how_it_works: ALPSCore is built with CMake (3.16 or newer) and needs a C++14 compiler, HDF5, Boost headers, and Eigen 3.3.4 or later. Downstream projects use find_package(ALPSCore) and link against ALPSCore_LIBRARIES, optionally naming components such as accumulators and params. All ALPSCore libraries and the projects that link them must use the same C++ standard for ABI compatibility.

commands_seen.context: Gets the source from GitHub; the release tarballs are the other option.
The INSTALL.md 'simplest build' configure step, run from a build directory; it downloads and co-installs Eigen3.
Alternative configure step when Eigen3 is already installed and its headers are passed in.
Parallel build on Linux; macOS uses make -j$(sysctl -n hw.logicalcpu).
Runs the test suite. Note that some MPI tests can segfault at exit with OpenMPI 5.x on macOS even though the assertions pass.
Installs ALPSCore into the CMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX directory.
Troubleshooting step for when CMake cannot find Boost (BoostConfig.cmake, Boost 1.70 or newer).
Suggested when the MPI compiler does not match the C++ compiler and link or runtime failures appear.
Configures the Ising Monte Carlo tutorial project against an installed ALPSCore.

brief.install_notes: Packaged installs exist for MacOS via MacPorts (sudo port install alpscore, which may not be available in every MacPorts version; the README says to fall back to source if it fails). Debian and Gentoo packages are mentioned. Source build needs CMake 3.16 or newer, HDF5 1.10.2 or newer (1.14.x is fine), Boost 1.70 or newer, and Eigen 3.3.4 or newer, which the build can download. The tests need a C++17 compiler, since the bundled GoogleTest requires it; otherwise configure with -DTesting=OFF. ALPSCore builds as C++14 by default, and -DALPS_CXX_STD=c++17 (or c++20) selects another standard. HDF5 is found through the HDF5_ROOT environment variable. HPC systems with environment modules often need Boost_DIR or EIGEN3_INCLUDE_DIR set by hand. MPI is optional.
brief.standout: Unlike most physics codes, this is a reusable library layer rather than a single application: it aims at algorithms and utilities that other simulation codes can share, and it documents its build against Boost, Eigen, and HDF5 at length. Its Simons Foundation funding ties it to the Many Electron Problem collaboration.
brief.status: unknown. I did not see a release date or a last-commit date. The GitHub README has a CI/CD badge for the master branch, and the homepage links to GitHub, issues, and a wiki, so it looks active but I could not confirm recency.
brief.caveats: It is a library, not a turnkey application, so there is no executable to try from the command line. The brew entry has no executables and no caveats. Building needs Boost, HDF5, Eigen, and CMake, and ABI consistency means every linked project must use the same C++ standard. Tests need a C++17 compiler. The homepage points the legacy ALPS application codes to a separate site (alps.comp-phys.com) that I did not visit. I did not see a licence name in the fetched text; the README only points to LICENSE.TXT.
quotes: The ALPSCore project, based on the ALPS (Algorithms and Libraries for Physics Simulations) project, provides generic algorithms and utilities for physics problems. It strives to increase software reuse in the physics community.

The ALPS Core libraries aim to provide a set of well tested, robust, and standardized components for numerical simulations of condensed matter systems, in particular systems with strongly correlated electrons.
The libraries are open source and available for everyone to use in their own numerical simulations.

name: apkeep
desc: Command-line tool for downloading APK files from various sources
why: Downloads APKs from multiple app stores, opening a door into how mobile apps are sourced and inspected.

brief.what_it_is: apkeep is a command-line tool written in Rust that downloads Android APK files from several sources: the Google Play Store, APKPure, and F-Droid. You give it an app ID such as com.instagram.android, plus a source flag if you are not using Google Play, and it saves the APK to a directory you name. It can also take a CSV file of app IDs for batch downloads, list the available versions with -l, and fetch a specific version with an @version suffix. The README also describes Docker images and Termux installs on Android.

It describes per-source access: Google Play requires an email address and an AAS token obtained first (see USAGE-google-play.md), APKPure is a third-party site hosting Play Store APKs, and F-Droid downloads are checked to be signed by F-Droid maintainers, with an alert if verification fails.

name: archivemount
desc: File system for accessing archives using libarchive
why: Mounts any libarchive-readable archive as a filesystem, a neat door into how archive formats can be treated as directories.

brief.what_it_is: Archivemount is a FUSE filesystem that mounts an archive so it can be browsed like an ordinary directory. The README describes it as glue code between libarchive and FUSE. It takes a possibly compressed archive such as a .tar.gz, .zip or .iso and presents its contents as a mounted filesystem. This is the -ng fork, an upstream-derived version that fixes Debian and upstream bugs. The fork also adds a Port to OpenBSD commit.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says this is the archivemount upstream, derived from upstream tarballs, with fixed Debian and upstream bugs. It notes that the upstream author died in 2020, and this fork carries the work forward.
brief.how_it_works: Archivemount uses libarchive to read archive entries and FUSE to expose them as a filesystem. Writes are handled differently: libarchive cannot write archives, so on unmount the whole archive is recreated from the changed tree, with a .orig backup of the original kept. Because FUSE backgrounds the process, the unmount command can return before the unmount has finished, and the README says to check the process list for archivemount to see the real state.
brief.install_notes: The README lists these requirements: GNU Make, libarchive-dev, libfuse3-dev or libfuse-dev, and pkgconf. It also says you can skip pkgconf by using just the libraries and fixing up the c++ *.cpp files manually. No accounts or runtime configuration are mentioned. No install or build command lines appear in the README.
brief.standout: It treats an archive as a directory and handles writes by rebuilding the whole archive at unmount, instead of editing it in place. The README also carries a detailed tracker of which upstream and Debian bugs are libarchive bugs, which are fundamentally invalid, and which are incoherent.
brief.status: Maintained, as far as the page shows. The most recent commits on trunk are listed as 22 days ago. The page also shows a release notes entry for 1c, and the README is current about the fork's bug fixes. I did not confirm a release date.
brief.caveats: Writing is not native. Changes are applied by recreating the archive only at unmount, and if that fails the changes are lost. The README says there is no guarantee data is written correctly and warns in capitals: DO NOT TRUST THIS SOFTWARE. It says the author is not responsible for lost data. Libarchive supports many more formats for reading than for writing, so re-created archives may use a different tar or compression variant. Unmount can return before it has finished. Licensing is 0BSD and LGPL-2.0-or-later.
quotes: It can be used to mount a (possibly compressed) archive (as in .tar.gz or .zip or .iso) and use it like an ordinary filesystem.
Writing to an archive with libarchive is unfortunately not possible.
THERE IS ALSO NO GUARANTEE THAT DATA IS WRITTEN CORRECTLY. DO NOT TRUST THIS SOFTWARE!

name: arp-scan-rs
desc: ARP scan tool written in Rust for fast local network scans
why: A fast ARP scanner is a direct door into how local devices announce themselves on the link layer.

brief.what_it_is: arp-scan-rs is a command-line tool, installed as the arp-scan binary, that finds the hosts on your local network by sending ARP requests. It takes a network interface or IPv4 range as input, sends one ARP request per target address, and prints the hosts that reply, with IPv4 address, MAC address, hostname, and vendor (looked up from the IEEE OUI file). Output can be a plain table, JSON, YAML, or CSV. The README also lists scan profiles (default, fast, stealth, chaos) and options for timing, bandwidth, VLAN tagging, and raw ARP field customization.
brief.why_it_exists: The README describes it as a minimal Rust scanner that finds all hosts on a local network using the ARP protocol, inspired by the arp-scan project by Roy Hills.
brief.how_it_works: The README does not explain the mechanism in depth. It says that by default the scanner sends ARP requests to each address in the selected IPv4 range, with a 10ms gap between requests to avoid an ARP storm, and that the default destination MAC is broadcast (00:00:00:00:00:00). Replies are collected until the minimum timeout (2000ms by default) passes. Frame building uses libpnet, which the Windows build notes mention.

The MAC vendor names need the IEEE OUI CSV: it is optional, and without it the vendor column stays empty. Its default path is /usr/share/arp-scan/ieee-oui.csv, and --oui-file points elsewhere. On Windows, the README says to follow the libpnet Windows instructions and place Packet.lib in the project root, but Windows is not listed as a supported platform. The README does not say whether root or capabilities are needed to send raw frames.
brief.standout: It is a Rust port in the spirit of the original arp-scan, with a single static-friendly binary and a set of scan profiles (fast, stealth, chaos) that bundle timing and packet options. It also exposes raw ARP header fields (operation, hardware type, protocol type) and Ethernet-level MAC and VLAN overrides for experimentation.

name: ascii
desc: List ASCII idiomatic names and octal/decimal code-point forms
why: Eric Raymond's ASCII reference tool with idiomatic names is a charming old-school curiosity, though shallow.

brief.what_it_is: A command-line tool called ascii that takes a character in almost any notation (a literal character, caret form like ^A, C escape like \n, hex, decimal, octal, binary, ISO/ECMA code, teletype mnemonic, HTML entity name, or slang name) and prints every other known name and code-point form for that character. Run with no arguments it prints a small ASCII chart. Output options -d, -x, -o and -b force the output radix, and -t gives script-friendly output. It is also usable as a quick base converter for 8-bit values.
brief.why_it_exists: Eric S. Raymond wrote it in November 1990 to make it easy to translate between the many ways ASCII characters are named and written, which the homepage says is especially handy for reading cc(1)'s octal 'invalid-character' messages and for serial communications work.
brief.how_it_works: Each argument is tried against every convention the tool knows, and if an argument could mean more than one character, names for all of the candidates are printed. Unrecognized or out-of-range arguments are silently ignored. Prefixes select an interpretation: h, 0x, x or \x for hex; d, 0d or \d for decimal; 0o, o or \o for octal; 0b, b or \b for binary. The man page says comparisons are case-insensitive and dashes map to spaces.

commands_seen.context: Synopsis line from the man page. Shows the options and the optional character-alias argument; it is a usage template, not an example.
Mentioned in the man page text: with no options, ascii behaves like ascii -h, which shows the options summary and a simple ASCII table.

brief.install_notes: Installs with brew install ascii, as the Homebrew scout notes list it. The upstream project distributes a gzipped source tarball (ascii-3.32.tar.gz) and says the code is usually packaged as 'ascii' by distributions. The project repository is at https://gitlab.com/esr/ascii. I did not see any runtime, account, or configuration requirements.
brief.standout: A single small tool that cross-references nearly every naming scheme for a character in one place, including USENET-era hacker slang names, Teletype mnemonics, ISO/ECMA code positions, and HTML/SGML entity names, and can run from any notation as input.

Shell metacharacters, especially backslash, must be quoted or stringized in arguments. Unrecognized arguments are silently ignored, so typos produce no error. name: ascii2binary
desc: Converting Text to Binary and Back
why: Converts text to binary and back in odd representations, a small transform with a pleasing old-school feel.

brief.what_it_is: Two small POSIX C command-line programs that convert between textual and binary representations of numbers. ascii2binary reads whitespace-separated textual numbers from stdin and writes their binary equivalents; the type and precision are chosen with flags. binary2ascii reads binary numbers and writes text, with flags for type, size and format. Unsigned integers can come out in binary, octal, decimal or hexadecimal, signed integers only in binary or decimal, and floats only in decimal, standard or scientific notation.
brief.why_it_exists: The author describes them as useful for generating test data, inspecting binary files, and interfacing programs that produce textual output with programs that need binary input, and for reformatting numbers. The page's example is normalising variable-length hex Unicode range endpoints to a uniform 6-digit width for a table.
brief.how_it_works: Each program is a filter over stdin and stdout, so they chain with ordinary shell pipelines. Flags select the numeric type (for example -t ul, -t uc, -t f), the base or bit grouping (-b), field count (-n), width (-w) and padding, and whether output is scientific (-e). Localisation uses GNU gettext, so the -L flag can read and write numbers in other locale formats such as de_DE and en_US. The page notes that to inspect a float's raw bytes you can treat the input as unsigned characters.

commands_seen.context: Reads the text number 0x10001000 from intex.asc and writes it as a binary unsigned long to intex.bin.
Converts the binary unsigned long back to text in hexadecimal, printing 0x10001000.
Prints the bytes of the binary file as unsigned chars in binary, four per line, grouped as 00000000 00010000 00000000 00010000.
Converts the decimal float 2235.643 into a binary float file.
Reads the float back and prints it with one digit of precision in a 6-wide field, giving 0002235.6.
Prints the float in scientific notation, giving 2.236e+03.
Shows the raw bytes of the float as hex, four per line: 0x4A 0xBA 0x0B 0x45.

name: asm6809
desc: Cross assembler targeting the Motorola 6809 and Hitachi 6309
why: A cross assembler for the 6809 and 6309, a door into the rarely visited world of Motorola retro CPUs.

brief.what_it_is: asm6809 is a portable cross assembler for the Motorola 6809 and Hitachi 6309 CPUs, so you write 6809 or 6309 assembly source on a modern machine and it produces machine code for those chips. It accepts arbitrarily complex expressions with most C-style operators, forward references, macros and conditional assembly. Output formats are raw binary, DragonDOS binary, CoCo RS-DOS (DECB) binary, Motorola SREC and Intel HEX. The homepage shows no command-line examples.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage gives no explicit motivation. It presents the tool as a portable assembler for the 6809 and 6309, with the Dragon and Tandy CoCo platforms implied by the DragonDOS and RS-DOS output formats.

No runtime, account or hardware requirement is mentioned. XRoar, a Dragon/CoCo emulator, is named as a way to run the output.
brief.standout: It is a modern, portable cross assembler for a niche CPU family that covers many retro output formats, including the Dragon and CoCo disk and tape formats, so its output can run directly on period-accurate emulators like XRoar. The project also keeps packaged builds for Debian, Ubuntu and Windows.

name: asroute
desc: CLI to interpret traceroute -a output to show AS names traversed
why: Annotating traceroute hops with AS names is a neat door into how internet routing is actually organised.

brief.what_it_is: asroute is a command-line tool written in Rust that reads traceroute output and summarises the autonomous systems (AS) the path crosses. You pipe `traceroute -a` output into it, and it prints one line per hop showing the AS name and country code instead of only raw IP addresses. Hops that do not respond show as `*`, and reserved ASNs show as names such as `AS0 (Reserved)`. The README's example traces a route to bhutan.gov.bt.
brief.why_it_exists: The author wanted to see the companies and networks that carry their traffic, not individual hops, and to see how much shorter paths get when a site uses a CDN. The README says the tool was also written to scratch an itch: to try building a Rust CLI and to see how easily it can be distributed through Homebrew.
brief.how_it_works: It parses the output of `traceroute -a`, which annotates each hop with its origin ASN. It then looks up each ASN's name and country using Team Cymru's ASN-to-name service, via the cymrust Rust crate. The README does not describe the internals beyond this.

commands_seen.context: Installs the tool through Homebrew, the only installation method the README lists.
Usage example: runs traceroute with AS annotation on the Bhutan government site and pipes the output into asroute, which prints one AS name per hop.

brief.install_notes: Install with `brew install asroute`. The README gives no other install steps, runtime requirements, accounts, or configuration. The Todos list checks off brew install as done.
brief.standout: Instead of building a traceroute of its own, it post-processes the `-a` annotation that traceroute already provides and turns each hop into a named network operator. The README's own note says the tool exists mainly as a small Rust CLI and a Homebrew distribution exercise, and it points to lft as the more capable option for serious network analysis.
brief.status: unknown. The README shows no release version, date, or changelog. It lists brew install as done and has open Todos (-h usage, progress indicator, a mode that runs traceroute itself). I did not check the GitHub releases or commit history, so I cannot say whether it is maintained.

name: atasm
desc: Atari MAC/65 compatible assembler for Unix
why: An assembler for the Atari 8-bit MAC/65 dialect, an old-school environment that opens a door into retro machine code.

brief.what_it_is: ATasm is a command-line cross-assembler for the 6502 CPU, written in C. It reads 6502 assembly source and produces Atari 8-bit binary load files. It can also write .XFD or .ATR disk images, or Atari800 and Atari++ machine state files. The README says it is mostly compatible with the Mac/65 macro assembler from OSS Software, so existing Mac/65 source and macro libraries should assemble with it.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says the aim is to let Atari home-brew coders edit and build with modern editors instead of the original Mac/65 cartridge editor, which one reviewer called excruciating. It says code can be built quickly on a modern machine.
brief.install_notes: Download atasm109.zip from the SourceForge Files page (397.7 kB). The package includes all source code and a Windows binary. The README says it compiles cleanly on Linux, macOS/X, or any platform with GNU C or Clang, so on Unix you build from source. The README gives no build command, and I saw no runtime, account, or configuration steps. The Homebrew formula name is atasm.
brief.standout: It is a drop-in path for old Mac/65 code: the project's own README describes it as compatible with an existing macro assembler, and it targets Atari disk images and emulator state files directly. The Atari-specific directives and undocumented opcode support also set it apart from a generic 6502 assembler.
brief.status: Quiet. The SourceForge page and README both show last update 2021-03-21, with a README copyright notice of 1998-2021 and a 2021 modification by Peter Hinz. The project was registered 2002-06-15. It has 7 downloads per week and 2 user reviews, from 2012 and 2013. I found no later release or commit.
brief.caveats: The README says 'mostly' Mac/65 compatible, so some Mac/65 code may need changes. Licence is GPLv2. The Windows binary is included, but on Unix you have to compile it yourself. The README gives no build instructions or usage examples, and I did not find a separate docs site. The SourceForge page lists the project as 'Brought to you by' a single maintainer, schmelze.
quotes: ATasm is a 6502 command-line cross-assembler that is compatible with the original Mac/65 macroassembler released by OSS software.
Code development can now be performed using "modern" editors and compiles with lightning speed.
ATasm runs native on IBM PCs in Windows and compiles cleanly under Linux, MacOS/X or any platform with the GNU C or Clang compiler.

judge.reason: A useful Atari-specific 6502 assembler, but its compatibility and disk-image outputs don’t make it stand out from the crowded retro-assembler niche.

name: audiowaveform
desc: Generate waveform data and render waveform images from audio files
why: Turns audio into waveform data and images, a modest audio-to-visual transform that is close but not especially deep.

brief.what_it_is: audiowaveform is a C++ command-line program that reads MP3, WAV, FLAC, Ogg Vorbis or Opus audio and writes waveform data as binary .dat or JSON .json files. It can also render a PNG waveform image from a waveform data file, at a chosen time offset, zoom level, size and color scheme. Audio is first combined to mono, then the minimum and maximum sample values are computed over each group of N input samples, so each group produces one min/max pair in the output. It can also convert MP3 to WAV.
brief.why_it_exists: The README describes the output as data that 'can be used to produce a visual rendering of the audio, similar in appearance to audio editing applications.' The README also suggests generating data once and rendering many images from it, and mentions web use with Peaks.js.
brief.how_it_works: Input channels are mixed to mono, then min and max sample values are computed over every N input samples, where N is set by --zoom (default 256), giving one min/max pair per output point. The result is stored as .dat or .json, and a PNG is drawn from that data at a given zoom or pixels-per-second, with optional start and end times. The README advises building a .dat file first, because decoding long MP3 files can take significant time.

commands_seen.context: Homebrew install on macOS, per the README's Mac OSX section.
Creates a binary waveform data file from an MP3 at 256 samples per point with 8-bit resolution.
Renders a PNG from an existing .dat file at 512 samples per pixel. The README notes zoom cannot be finer than the zoom used to create the .dat.
Renders a 1000x200 PNG at 50 pixels per second, starting 5.0 seconds into the audio.

commands_seen.cmd: ffmpeg -i test.mp4 -f wav - | audiowaveform --input-format wav --output-format dat -b 8 > test.dat
commands_seen.context: Pipes ffmpeg-decoded audio from a video file into audiowaveform over stdin and stdout to produce a .dat file.
Converts a binary .dat waveform file to JSON.
Converts MP3 to WAV audio, which the README lists as a secondary use.
Build option to statically link the library dependencies, run from the build directory.
Installs the program to /usr/local/bin and man pages to /usr/local/share/man by default.
Shows the help message, which the README gives as the check that the build runs.

brief.install_notes: Homebrew works on macOS. Ubuntu users can use the PPA ppa:chris-needham/ppa. Debian .deb packages (amd64 and arm64) and RHEL/CentOS RPMs are on the Releases page. There is an AUR package for Arch, a Docker image (realies/audiowaveform, Alpine-based), and a flake.nix for Nix users. Windows binaries are on the Releases page. Building from source needs cmake 2.8.7 or later, g++ 4.6.3 or later, and Boost 1.46.0 or later, plus libmad, libid3tag, libsndfile, and gd. Unit tests use Google Test, which the README says to download and symlink by hand. The default build is Release and tests are on by default, and ENABLE_TESTS=0 turns them off.
brief.standout: It is a small, focused tool: decode once, store a compact min/max pyramid-style file, then render images or JSON from that file at any zoom without re-decoding. It is built for embedding in web players, with binary and JSON outputs and a bars style with rounded corners. The README describes it as an audio-editor-style waveform renderer, which is familiar territory, so the value is in the practical pipeline rather than new technique.
brief.status: Maintained. The Codeberg page shows a latest commit 'Fixed loadWaveformData()' dated 2026-07-29, a VERSION file and CHANGELOG at 1.11.1 dated 2026-05-17, 37 open issues, 2 open pull requests, 17 releases and 38 tags. The README was updated with flake.nix support on 2026-05-17.
brief.caveats: The README's install section still shows 1.10.2 Debian packages and a 1.10.1 Amazon Linux RPM, which lag the current 1.11.1 version. Piping into audiowaveform works only for MP3, WAV and raw input, not FLAC or Ogg Vorbis. Opus needs libsndfile 1.0.29 or later. Building from source needs several C and C++ libraries, and the Google Test download is manual. The Windows static build is a separate project (compile-static-audiowaveform). The source is hosted on Codeberg and the README points to git@codeberg.org for cloning. The page also shows a notice that Codeberg has changed its terms, which does not affect this project directly. The README does not state a license beyond 'See COPYING'; I did not open COPYING, so I cannot confirm the license name.

name: autotrace
desc: Convert bitmap to vector graphics
why: Turns bitmaps into vector outlines, a transform from pixels to geometry that is neat but a long-standing, fairly ordinary tool.

brief.what_it_is: AutoTrace is a command-line program that converts bitmap images into vector graphics. It reads raster formats such as BMP, TGA, PNM/PPM/PGM/PBM, and anything ImageMagick can read, then writes vector output in formats including PostScript, SVG, xfig, SWF, EMF, DXF, CGM, MIF, and sk, plus output through pstoedit. The homepage describes it as a free alternative to commercial tools like CorelTrace or Adobe Streamline.
brief.why_it_exists: The author says the aim is 'the development of a freely available application with a functionality similar to CorelTrace or Adobe Streamline', and hopes it will become 'better than all commercially available programs'.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage does not explain the tracing mechanism in detail. It mentions median-cut colour quantization, despeckle filtering, and centerline tracing, and says outlines are fitted with curves. The contributions list says the core fits outlines and that the current code traces each outline twice.
brief.install_notes: The homepage says AutoTrace ships as source code and some binaries, and that other platforms must compile it themselves. The steps are to download the archive from the SourceForge files page, unpack it, and run make. No runtime, account, or configuration is described. The page does not list the make command as a verbatim command line.
brief.standout: It is an early, open-source take on the pixel-to-geometry problem, and its homepage carries a long, candid list of similar projects and research references (Schneider's Phoenix curve fitting, SUSAN denoising, color quantization papers). It also served as the backend for mftrace and TeXtrace, which convert bitmap fonts to outlines.
brief.status: Quiet. The latest release on the homepage is version 0.31.1, dated 11/09/02. The homepage's 'Last modified' line is 12/12/16. The Download section says 'AutoTrace 0.31.1 (no support by me)', and the Bugs section is a bare '?!'. The homepage is an old SourceForge-era site, and the news items stop in 2004. The scout note calls it a long-standing, fairly ordinary tool.
brief.caveats: The homepage has no documentation beyond online help. Building it from source is the only route on most platforms. The contributions list says whole pictures must fit in memory, and the page calls ImageMagick input 'very slow for loading big images'. The author says he does not support the 0.31.1 release. The page includes a 2002 note about an earlier rival (ScanFont). Licence: GNU GPL, per the homepage.

AutoTrace is free software. AutoTrace is distributed under the term of GNU GPL.
Currently there is no documentation other than the online help.

name: avra
desc: Assembler for the Atmel AVR microcontroller family
why: Open AVR assembler; a close call, pairs with hardware hacking but the tool itself is a straightforward assembler.

brief.what_it_is: AVRA is a command-line assembler for Atmel AVR microcontrollers, written in C99. You give it an AVR assembly source file, such as mysource.S, and it writes an Intel HEX file named mysource.S.hex by default; the -o option changes that name. EEPROM data always goes to a separate file called program.eep.hex in Intel HEX format. It also writes a COFF file after a successful assembly so AVR Studio or another COFF-compatible debugger can simulate or emulate the program.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says AVRA is 'almost compatible with Atmel's own assembler, AVRASM32', and is designed 'to replace AVRASM32 without special changes in your current Atmel AVR Studio enviroment.' It adds features the author considered useful: extra preprocessor directives, more flexible macros, and build-time meta tags.
brief.how_it_works: AVRA reads the source in passes; the changelog mentions a second pass where variable values are kept. It adds extra directives (.define, .undef, .ifdef, .ifndef, .if, .else, .endif, .elif, .elseif, .warning) and enhanced macros that take bracketed parameters, with register pairs like r16:r17 and typed parameter suffixes such as _i and _16. Meta tags such as %DAY%, %MONTH%, %YEAR%, %HOUR% and %MINUTE% are replaced at assembly time, so a build can embed its own date or a serial number.

commands_seen.context: Build step from the README: run in the project root to build the avra executable, which is produced at src/avra.
Install step from the README, run after make to install the built avra binary.
From USAGE.md: basic usage. Compiles the source file and writes the result in Intel HEX format to mysource.S.hex.
From USAGE.md: suppresses register reassignment warnings, the only warning class the docs say can be suppressed.

brief.install_notes: Beyond brew install: build from source with make in the project root (binary at src/avra), then optionally make install. The default make OS is linux, which assumes a typical GNU toolchain; other platform files live in src/makefiles, and you override OS when calling make. The README says those other platforms are not all well tested. Building on Windows with MS Visual Studio 2019 needs additional files, pointed to by an external gist. No accounts, runtimes or hardware are mentioned.
brief.standout: AVRA is a drop-in-style replacement for Atmel's AVRASM32 that keeps its command-line conventions so it works inside AVR Studio, and it adds C-style preprocessor directives and overloaded, typed macros that accept multi-register operands like a:b. Its macro features are the main thing separating it from a plain assembler.
brief.status: quiet. The README lists the latest release as 1.4.2 (2020-07-18), and the changelog's newest entry is from that date. The README also says the project sat inactive for eight years before Virgil Dupras took it over to prepare v1.4. I did not see a last-commit date, so I cannot say more than that.
brief.caveats: Not all AVRASM32 command-line options are supported, and the -e eeprom file option is not supported; EEPROM always goes to program.eep.hex. Only Intel HEX output is supported. Forward references are not supported for .ifdef and .ifndef. The README says it is only 'almost compatible' with AVRASM32. Building outside Linux may need extra work, and the README says the non-Linux platform files are not all well tested. Windows builds need MS Visual Studio 2019 and extra files from an external gist. The README does not state a license in the parts I fetched, so check the repo before reusing the code.

name: avce00
desc: Make Arc/Info (binary) Vector Coverages appear as E00
why: Converts obscure Arc/Info binary coverages to readable E00, a neat format-translation door despite being deprecated.

brief.what_it_is: AVCE00 is an open source ANSI-C library that reads and writes Arc/Info binary vector coverages as if they were E00 text files. Input is a binary coverage; output is a stream of E00 lines through AVCE00ReadNextLine() and AVCE00WriteNextLine() in the library. For users who only want conversion, the package also ships the AVCIMPORT and AVCEXPORT programs. The executables listed in the package metadata are avcdelete, avcexport, avcimport and avctest.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames it as a way to make binary coverages readable through E00, so existing E00 translators can add binary coverage support by swapping in the library's read and write functions.
brief.how_it_works: The library presents a binary coverage through the same line-by-line interface as an E00 file. A translator that already reads and writes E00 can call AVCE00ReadNextLine() and AVCE00WriteNextLine() in place of its own read and write functions. The homepage describes this at a high level only and points to the library documentation for details.
brief.install_notes: The homepage offers a Windows zip (AVCE00-2.0.0-WIN32.ZIP) with precompiled AVCIMPORT and AVCEXPORT. The source package is avce00-2.0.0.tar.gz or .zip. The page gives no build steps, dependencies or configuration, so those would need to come from the library documentation, which I did not follow.
brief.standout: It is a format-translation library that makes a closed binary GIS format look like a plain text interchange format, so existing E00 tools gain binary coverage support without being rewritten. The homepage also says it is a single ANSI-C library rather than a larger GIS stack.
brief.status: Quiet. The latest release is version 2.0.0 from August 17, 2006, and the homepage was last updated August 21, 2006. The page does not say the project is abandoned. The scout note calls it deprecated, but the homepage itself does not say that.
brief.caveats: The Windows binaries are DOS executables that run under Windows 95, 98 and NT, so they are old. The homepage does not state a license beyond calling the library Open Source (Free). Bugs go to the maptools Bugzilla, and the author says he may not have time to answer every email. The page describes no features beyond conversion and the read/write functions.
quotes: AVCE00 is an Open Source (i.e. Free!) ANSI-C library that makes Arc/Info (binary) Vector Coverages appear as E00!
It allows you to read and write binary coverages just as if they were E00 files.
Comments, suggestions (and bug reports of course!) about this library are always welcome... please keep in mind that I may not have time to respond to all Emails (but I'll do my best).

name: bbe
desc: Sed-like editor for binary files
why: Sed-like editor for binary files, a direct tool for rewriting bytes and poking at file formats.

brief.what_it_is: bbe is a command-line editor for binary files, described by its own page as "a sed-like editor for binary files." Where sed reads input line by line, bbe reads arbitrary blocks from an input stream and applies byte-related transformations to the blocks it finds. It takes a binary file or stream as input and writes the transformed bytes out. The SourceForge page gives no usage examples, so the exact script syntax is not confirmed from what I read.
brief.why_it_exists: The page's only statement of purpose is the block-oriented contrast with sed: sed assumes line-structured text, and bbe is meant for data that has no line structure.
brief.how_it_works: According to the SourceForge description, bbe reads arbitrary blocks from an input stream and performs byte-related transformations on the blocks it finds, rather than splitting input into lines as sed does. I did not see a README or documentation describing the command language or block-matching syntax.

name: bchunk
desc: Convert CD images from .bin/.cue to .iso/.cdr
why: Splits raw CD bin and cue images into ISO tracks, a quiet look at how optical disc data is actually laid out.

brief.what_it_is: bchunk is a command-line converter for CD images. It takes a raw CD image in the .bin/.cue format (sometimes .raw/.cue), which is common for CD/VCD images distributed online, and splits it into separate track files. Data tracks come out as .iso files that hold an ISO file system, and audio tracks come out as .cdr files in native CD audio format. Since version 1.1.0 it can also write audio tracks as WAV.
brief.why_it_exists: The bin/cue format is used by popular non-Unix CD-writing software but is not supported by most other CD burning programs, so bchunk exists to make those images usable on Unix and Linux. The page describes it as a Unix/C rewrite of Bob Marietta's BinChunker, written with his help and access to his Pascal/Delphi source.
brief.how_it_works: The page gives little internal detail. It describes the output: .iso tracks can be mounted through a loop device on Linux or written to CD-R with cdrecord, and .cdr audio tracks can be written with cdrecord -audio or converted to WAV or other formats with sox. The tips section notes that a byte-order mismatch can make audio sound like loud noise, and that the -s option on bchunk swaps byte order.

name: bender
desc: Dependency management tool for hardware projects
why: Hardware dependency management is a niche corner worth a look, though it is mostly build plumbing.

brief.what_it_is: Bender is a dependency management tool for hardware design projects. It takes a package description in Bender.yml that lists HDL dependencies, which can come from Git repositories (by tag or revision) or local paths. It resolves compatible versions, records the exact result in Bender.lock, and outputs ordered source sets, include directories, defines, and target-specific file groups for downstream simulators and synthesis tools such as QuestaSim, VCS, Vivado, and Verilator.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says it is designed to fit existing hardware flows rather than impose a registry, directory layout, or simulator choice, and that it provides reproducible dependency resolution for IP reuse.
brief.how_it_works: A package is defined by three files: Bender.yml declares metadata, dependencies, sources, and targets; Bender.lock pins the resolved revisions; Bender.local holds local overrides, such as when developing a dependency in place. The usual loop is to edit Bender.yml, run bender update to resolve, bender checkout to fetch the pinned revisions, and bender script to emit tool inputs.

name: berkeley-db
desc: High performance key/value database
why: An old embedded key/value database with a long history; a strange old-school engine worth exploring for its internals.

brief.what_it_is: Berkeley DB is a family of embedded key/value database libraries, according to Oracle's homepage. Applications link the library and reach data through simple function-call APIs, with listed bindings for C, C++, Java/JNI, C#, Python and Perl. The homepage lists BTREE, HASH, QUEUE and RECNO storage methods, an SQL API made by incorporating SQLite, and a Java Direct Persistence Layer and Collections API. The Homebrew package installs 15 companion utilities (db_dump, db_load, db_verify, db_recover, db_stat and others), but the homepage does not describe them, so their roles are unverified beyond their names.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage pitches it as a way to build custom data management without the overhead traditionally associated with custom projects, using well-proven building blocks that can be configured for needs 'from the hand-held device to the data center'.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage says the products use function-call APIs for data access and management, and offer selectable storage access methods (BTREE, HASH, QUEUE, RECNO). It also lists replication for high availability as a feature. It does not explain the internals (log, locking, page cache) in the pages I read.
brief.install_notes: Nothing install-specific appeared on the homepage. name: betty

name: bgrep

name: bingrep
desc: Greps through binaries from various OSs and architectures
why: Colour-maps the structure of binaries across OSes and architectures, a visual way to see how executables are laid out.

brief.what_it_is: bingrep is a command-line tool that takes a binary executable or object file and prints its internal structure as colour-coded output. It accepts ELF (32/64-bit, plus arm, x86, openrisc), Mach-O (32/64-bit, arm, x86), Unix and BSD archives, and PE files (debug only). Other formats parse and colour, but relocations may not display correctly. The output is a set of coloured tables showing addresses, offsets, and sizes of things like symbols, program headers, and section headers. It can also dump the parsed structure in debug form, demangle symbols, and print a hextable or file offset ranges.
brief.why_it_exists: The author needed to quickly see the load address, offset, or size of a symbol, program header, section header, export, or import, and found objdump and nm too slow for that. He wanted the values colourised so he could spot them and move on. The name is admittedly poor: he uploaded it as a personal tool, named the executable bg, and then had to rename it because that clashed with the Unix bg command.
brief.how_it_works: The README does not describe the internals in detail. It says the actual loading and parsing is done by the goblin library (github.com/m4b/goblin), and bingrep is the front end that renders the parsed result as coloured tables. Search is listed as in progress and currently only works for ELF targets.

name: bigloo
desc: Scheme implementation with object system, C, and Java interfaces
why: A Scheme compiler that targets C and JVM, a less-known Lisp with a real compiler to explore.

brief.what_it_is: Bigloo is a Scheme-family programming language and compiler. You write modules in its strict-parenthetical syntax, and the compiler turns them into small, fast standalone binary executables through its C backend, or into JVM output if you choose the JVM backend. It can call C functions directly through extern declarations and interoperate with Java programs on the JVM backend. It also ships libraries for threads, object-oriented programming, and multimedia, which the homepage's music-player example uses.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says its design is governed by one rule: enabling Scheme-based programming style where C(++) is usually required. It presents itself as a practical language and environment that offers features traditional languages have but functional languages seldom support.
brief.how_it_works: The bigloo command compiles a module file into an executable, as in 'bigloo fib.scm -o fib'. The C backend generates C code, so the result is a native binary. Bigloo code can call C functions and share data with them through the module's extern declarations, such as (extern (macro printf::int (::string ::string ::long) "printf")). The homepage does not describe the internal compilation pipeline beyond this.

name: binsider

brief.what_it_is: Binsider is a terminal user interface (TUI) for analyzing ELF binaries, the executable format used on most Linux systems. You point it at a binary and it shows general file info (size, ownership, permissions, date) and linked shared libraries, the ELF layout (sections, segments, symbols, relocations), strings, and a hexdump, with an option to execute the binary and trace its system calls and signals. Input is a binary file path; output is an interactive terminal view rather than a text report. The homepage describes it as offering features similar to readelf and strace.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a way to get inside ELF binaries with one tool: static and dynamic analysis, strings, linked libraries and hexdumps, all in a user-friendly terminal interface. The project tagline is "Swiss army knife for reverse engineers."
brief.how_it_works: Static analysis parses the ELF structure and lets you navigate sections, segments, symbols and relocations. Dynamic analysis executes the binary and traces system calls, signals and execution flow, similar to strace and ltrace. String extraction works like strings(1) and is aimed at finding things like URLs or passwords; the hexdump view gives a structured look at raw bytes.

brief.what_it_is: blink1-tool is a C command-line program that drives the blink(1), a small USB RGB LED indicator made by ThingM. You pass it colour, brightness, fade, blink and pattern options, and it sends them to the light over USB HID. It can also list connected devices, read back the last colour sent, and store colour patterns in the device's flash. The same repo builds blink1-tiny-server, a small HTTP JSON API server for controlling the light, and blink1control-tool, which goes through the Blink1Control app instead of USB.
brief.why_it_exists: The blink(1) is pitched as a glanceable status light that connects cloud services, email, URLs and scripts to a visible colour, so you can see what is happening without checking a window or typing a command. The blink1-tool repo exists so that scripts, servers and headless machines can drive that light directly.
brief.how_it_works: The tool talks to the blink(1)'s built-in USB firmware through hidapi (default) or libusb, and on Linux through hidraw. Colours can be given as RGB values or hex codes, with optional gamma correction and fade time in milliseconds. Patterns can be played from the command line, or saved to the device so it runs without a host connected.

name: bnfc

brief.what_it_is: The BNF Converter (bnfc) is a command-line compiler-construction tool. It takes a Labelled BNF (LBNF) grammar file, such as Sum.cf, and generates a compiler front-end from it. name: bootterm
desc: Simple, reliable and powerful terminal to ease connection to serial ports
why: A focused serial terminal for talking to boot loaders and embedded boards; useful and low-key, though the concept is familiar.

brief.what_it_is: BootTerm, invoked as `bt`, is a command-line serial terminal aimed at single board computers and USB serial adapters whose ports appear and disappear. It takes a serial device (auto-selected, named, or waited for) and a baud rate, and gives you an interactive console on that port. Captures can go to fixed or time-stamped files, and stdin/stdout can be used to inject or download data. It is a single C binary with no dependencies beyond libc.
brief.why_it_exists: The author wanted a serial tool that is simple, reliable and powerful for the board-bring-up phase, when the serial console is the only interface. He found existing tools either badly designed or incomplete: screen's key mappings, minicom disabling scrolling, cu's unclear usage, and fragile Python one-liners that crash or spin on disconnect.
brief.how_it_works: On start, bt lists serial ports with their driver and description, and connects to the most recently registered one unless told otherwise. Internal commands are reached through an escape character (default Ctrl-]) followed by a single key, such as q to quit, b to send a break, or D, R and F to toggle the DTR and RTS pins. Wait modes (-n for a new port, -a for a named or any port) poll until a suitable port appears, which suits USB boards that reconnect after reset. Captures are append-only, and timestamps can be added in several formats.

A configurable hardware condition, such as a jumper, decides whether it stays in bootloader mode and accepts USB data, or hands control to the application already in flash. name: buildapp
desc: Creates executables with SBCL
why: Turns Common Lisp programs into standalone SBCL executables; a niche old-school Lisp tool that is a close call.

brief.what_it_is: Buildapp is a command-line tool that turns a Common Lisp program into a standalone executable. You give it a Lisp image setup as flags: files to --load, ASDF systems to --load-system, --require'd modules, and --eval'd code, plus an --entry function. It loads all of that into SBCL (or CCL), then saves the image as a runnable binary with --output. The output is a single file you run directly, such as ./hello-world. The tool is written in Common Lisp and is a small, separate utility, not a Lisp implementation.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a way to define an application environment by loading files, systems, and code, then dump an executable image with an arbitrary startup function. It is similar to cl-launch and hu.dwim.build, and it deliberately stays narrow: startup initialization, debugger management, command-line parsing, and library fetching are left to other tools.
brief.how_it_works: Buildapp parses its flags into a description of the requested build, then writes a temporary Lisp dumpfile with the matching load, eval, and require steps. It runs sbcl (or ccl) as a subprocess with no init files, loads that dumpfile, and the dumpfile ends by calling save-lisp-and-die (or ccl:save-application) to write the executable. Debugger hooks are changed so that errors quit with a special exit code instead of entering the interactive debugger, and most compile and load output goes to a log stream that --logfile can redirect to a file.

name: c3c
desc: Compiler for the C3 language
why: Compiler for the C3 language, a C successor with its own design choices; a strange-enough language to explore for an afternoon.

brief.what_it_is: C3 is a general-purpose, compiled programming language that is a near-C successor: its syntax and semantics stay close to C, with modern additions such as modules, generics via generic modules, slices, operator overloading, compile-time reflection, macros, contracts, and Result-style error handling. The Homebrew package installs the c3c compiler, which takes .c3 source files and produces native binaries (for example, `c3c compile main.c3` produces an executable named after the module). It also ships a standard library (std::io and others). The README says the compiler is verified on Windows, macOS, Linux, OpenBSD and NetBSD, and lists Wasm32 as a supported target.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames C3 as 'an evolution, not a revolution': it aims to keep C's speed and familiar syntax while modernizing everyday development, and it explicitly takes inspiration from the C2 language, iterating on top of C rather than inventing an entirely new language. Its design principles include 'Try to stay close to C - only change what's really necessary' and 'Avoid big ideas & the more is better fallacy.'
brief.how_it_works: C3 source is compiled by the c3c compiler, which uses LLVM (the build fetches it with -DC3_FETCH_LLVM=ON, or uses system LLVM). Full C ABI compatibility means C3 code can be linked into C/C++ projects without special types; the README cites vkQuake as a demo where a portion was converted to C3. In debug builds the compiler inserts runtime bounds and value checks, and the standard library provides detailed stack traces for debug builds. Generic types are made by parameterizing an entire module, for example `module stack <Type>;` then `alias IntStack = Stack {int};`.

brief.install_notes: Homebrew is not the only route: the README lists precompiled tarballs and zips for Windows, Linux, macOS (Arm64 only) and OpenBSD, plus install scripts, Scoop (`scoop install c3`), Arch, Fedora (COPR), NixOS flake, Gentoo GURU, and Docker builds. Building from source needs CMake, git, clang, and libcurl development headers; the README lists per-distro package names. The standard library must sit at ../lib/std/ or /lib/std/ relative to the compiler for hello world to build. The macOS binary is unsigned and needs the xattr step. Brew's own caveats field was empty.
brief.standout: C3 deliberately sits in the 'C with fixes' niche rather than being a new language: it keeps the C ABI and no mandatory headers, and replaces the preprocessor with semantic macros that read like functions and can use compile-time reflection over types. The language has Result-style errors with a catch syntax, and debug builds add extensive bounds checks and stack traces, which is unusual for something this close to C.

Stack traces are limited on OpenBSD. Licensing is split: the compiler source under src is LGPL 3.0, while the standard library, tests, and examples are MIT. The Linux install script edits ~/.bashrc. Building from source needs LLVM and libcurl, and the vendor-fetch feature needs libcurl. The homepage itself is a language site, not a repository, so I read the homepage and then the GitHub README at github.com/c3lang/c3c.
