name: funcoeszz
desc: Dozens of command-line mini-applications (Portuguese)
why: Dozens of obscure shell mini-utilities in Portuguese, a quirky one-of-a-kind toolbox worth an idle browse.

brief.what_it_is: Funções ZZ is a collection of about 190 small command-line utilities for UNIX-like systems (Linux, BSD, Mac OS X, Cygwin), written in shell with bash, sed, awk and grep. Each tool is a short command with a zz prefix, such as zzdolar for the dollar rate, zzcpf to validate or generate a Brazilian CPF number, zzdata for date arithmetic, zzromanos for Roman numerals, or zzrot13 for ROT13. Input comes from arguments or stdin, and output is plain text on stdout. Several tools fetch live data from the web, including exchange rates, lottery results, TV schedules and weather. The homepage says 190 tools, while the README says 'mais de 180' (more than 180).
brief.why_it_exists: The README gives no formal problem statement. The homepage describes it as a free, 100% Brazilian, mature project by Aurelio Jargas, built by volunteers 'por prazer' (for pleasure), and its tagline invites visitors to 'Curtiu? Use a versão online ou instale em sua máquina e aproveite!'
brief.how_it_works: The whole collection is shell code using bash, sed, awk, grep and regular expressions. The official release is a single generated file that loads quickly into your shell; the beta keeps each function in its own file under a zz folder, which is slower to load but tracks the newest code. You source the script from your shell profile, and each function then becomes a command you can call directly or pipe into.

commands_seen.context: Validates a CPF number; prints 'CPF válido' or says why it is invalid. With no argument it generates a random CPF.
Date arithmetic: counts the days between today and a given date (example output 13642).
Pipes the numbers 1 to 5 into zztac, which prints them in reverse order.
Looks up the tracking history of a postal parcel by its tracking code.
Given an IP address and prefix length, prints the mask, network, and broadcast address.
Solves a second-degree equation from its three coefficients and prints the roots and vertex.
Converts text to uppercase; README example output is TÁ FUNCIONANDO.
Beta install step: downloads the repository into your home folder.
Beta install step: appends the loader lines to your ~/.bashrc file.
Runs a single function from the official Docker image without installing anything locally (example output shows two DST dates).

brief.install_notes: Via Homebrew, the caveats tell you to add two lines to your shell profile: an export of ZZPATH pointing into the Homebrew opt folder, and a source of that same file. They also say a newer Bash than the macOS default is required. The README's official route is to download the single release file from funcoeszz.net/download and follow the instructions there. The beta route is git clone, then ./funcoeszz zzzz --bashrc, which writes ZZOFF, ZZPATH and ZZDIR settings into ~/.bashrc; ZZOFF lets you turn off unwanted functions. Docker is an option: docker pull funcoeszz/zz. No accounts or API keys appear in the README.
brief.standout: Brazil-specific tools sit alongside general ones: CPF and CNPJ validators, lottery results and random bets, a bicho (jogo do bicho) number lookup, Brazilian city and state lookups, and a parcel tracker. It is all plain shell with no runtime beyond bash, and there is a self-installing zzzz --bashrc command, which is an unusual touch.
brief.status: Maintained, as far as I can tell. The homepage carries a release banner announcing version 21.1 with an announcement and download link, and says the project is 21 years old. I did not see a release date or last commit date, so the exact recency is unknown. Some sample outputs on the homepage are dated 2013 to 2021, so those examples are old.
brief.caveats: Needs a newer Bash than the macOS default, per the Homebrew caveats. Documentation and most examples are in Portuguese, and many tools are Brazil-specific (lottery, CPF/CNPJ, bicho, Brazilian cities and TV), so they are of limited use elsewhere. Several tools depend on live web pages, so they will break when those sites change; I inferred this from the tool names and outputs, not from a README warning. The beta install is slower to load and more manual. The homepage and README disagree on the count (190 versus more than 180). Licensed GPL-2.0-only. Sample outputs on the homepage are dated, so do not treat them as current results.

name: gaffitter
desc: Efficiently fit files/folders to fixed size volumes (like DVDs)
why: Solves a knapsack-style packing puzzle for fitting files onto DVD-sized volumes, an obscure and charming old utility.

brief.what_it_is: GAFFitter (Genetic Algorithm File Fitter) is a command-line tool written in C++ that arranges a list of files or directories into volumes of a fixed capacity, such as CD or DVD sizes. It takes a list of items, either as arguments, on stdin, or as size-identifier pairs, and outputs the selected items grouped into numbered volumes with a summary line for each (sum, difference from target, item count). Its aim is to minimize wasted space so that fewer volumes are needed.
brief.why_it_exists: The author describes it as a way to reduce the number of volumes needed to pack items by smartly arranging the input list, since the order you feed files in determines how well they fill each disc.
brief.how_it_works: The search is a genetic algorithm, a global meta-heuristic, rather than a simple greedy fill. It has many tunable parameters (seed, generations, population size, crossover and mutation probabilities, selection pressure) and presets from -1 (fast) to -9 (best). Other modes include a Best Fit approximation (--approximate) and a plain order-preserving split (--split).

commands_seen.context: Basic usage: pack the .ogg files into 700 MiB volumes, printing each volume's contents and a summary line.
Limit the output to a maximum of one volume with a 4.37 GiB target.
Read the file list from stdin via a pipe (the - argument) and pack it into 1.4 MiB volumes.
Split the files in their original order into 10 MiB volumes, preserving order at the cost of more wasted space.
Direct input mode: pass size-identifier pairs instead of file names, and show each item's size.
Documented workaround to follow symbolic links, since GAFFitter itself does not follow them: get sizes from du and feed them in as direct input in bytes.
Example with a 2048-byte block size, stated to be equivalent to the du pipeline above apart from symlink handling.
Bundled Python helper that packs files into DVD-sized volumes and creates ISO9660 images with genisoimage or mkisofs; outputs DVD-0001.iso, etc.
Bundled helper that packs files into DVD volumes for burning with K3B.
Bundled Python helper that integrates GAFFitter with the Brasero burner; calls Brasero once per volume.

brief.install_notes: The homepage gives no installation steps beyond pointers to a Git repository, the latest version 1.0.0 download, and official Debian packages. It targets GNU/Linux and other POSIX systems. The optional gaff-iso script needs genisoimage or mkisofs, the gaff-k3b and gaff-brasero scripts need K3B or Brasero, and the Nautilus scripts need awk, sed and echo and must be placed in ~/.gnome2/nautilus-scripts/ and set executable. Nothing on the page describes a build process.
brief.standout: It is a genetic-algorithm take on the bin-packing problem, shipped as a Unix filter with a deliberately rich command-line interface. The author also bundled a set of front-end scripts for ISO creation and burning tools from the GNOME and KDE era, which gives it a distinctly period flavour.
brief.status: Appears quiet. The homepage footer says 'Last updated on Mon Aug 3 2015', and the latest version listed is 1.0.0. The page gives no release date and no commit date, so I cannot confirm more recent activity.
brief.caveats: Runs on GNU/Linux and other POSIX systems only; the author says it could be ported to non-POSIX systems but does not claim it works there. The genetic algorithm is a heuristic and the page calls the approximation mode non-optimal. --split preserves order but usually wastes more space. GAFFitter does not follow symbolic links without the du workaround. Brasero handles only one volume at a time. The license is GPL v3 or later. The bundled scripts depend on tools that may no longer be common. The page does not mention Homebrew.
quotes: Genetic Algorithm File Fitter, or just GAFFitter, is a command-line software written in C++ that arranges (via a genetic algorithm) an input list of items or files/directories into volumes of a certain capacity (target), such as CD or DVD, in a way that the total wastage is minimized.
By smartly arranging the input list, GAFFitter fits better the given items and so optimizes (reduces) the number of required volumes to pack them.
It is Free Software! (GPL)

name: gauche
desc: R7RS Scheme implementation, developed to be a handy script interpreter
why: A capable R7RS Scheme with a long history, a classic Lisp worth exploring beyond the usual interpreters.

brief.what_it_is: Gauche is an R7RS Scheme implementation aimed at scripting and real-world programming. It runs Scheme programs from the command line (the homepage shows a script that builds an SVG file and writes it to disk). The page says it ships with networking, Unicode strings, regular expressions, threads, and common algorithms and data structures built in. It also has lazy sequences, an object system with a metaobject protocol, and a package manager with over 200 libraries and extensions.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents Gauche as a Scheme for practical scripting, with quick startup time and smooth integration with the operating system, suitable for automation, build tools, and shell-like scripting.
brief.install_notes: The homepage has a 'Download Gauche' button with latest release 0.9.15 and a 'Documentation' link, but gives no install steps, dependencies, or first-run instructions. Packages are managed with the gauche-package command, which the homepage mentions in text only. The installed executables listed in the metadata are gauche-cesconv, gauche-config, gauche-install, gauche-package, and gosh.
brief.standout: Gauche combines a small, fast-starting Scheme for scripting with batteries included and a lot of language extension: integrated lazy sequences (the homepage example uses generator->lseq and lmap-accum to build an infinite Fibonacci list), and a CLOS-like object system with a metaobject protocol. The homepage example is a short Scheme program that produces an SVG spiral file.
brief.status: Maintained, by the evidence on the homepage: latest release 0.9.15 and a news item dated 2025/12/14 announcing a Gauche-gtk2 0.6.2 update. The page says it has been developed and used for over two decades. I did not see a dated commit history or the release date for 0.9.15.
brief.caveats: The homepage makes no claims about supported platforms, licensing, or build requirements, and I did not open the documentation, so those are unverified. The Documentation and extension-browser links did not give URLs in the fetched text, so I did not follow them. The homepage is a marketing-style page, so performance claims ('fast') are the project's own wording.

Gauche emphasizes quick startup time, smooth integration with the operating system, and expressive syntax, making it suitable for automation, build tools, and shell-like scripting.
Developed and used for over two decades, Gauche focuses on stability, backward compatibility, and long-term maintainability.

name: gaul
desc: Genetic Algorithm Utility Library
why: An old genetic algorithm library with example programs, a classic door into evolutionary computation.

brief.what_it_is: GAUL (Genetic Algorithm Utility Library) is an open source C programming library, released under the GNU General Public License, for building applications that use evolutionary algorithms. It provides data structures and functions for handling the data that serial and parallel evolutionary algorithms need. It also includes some non-GA stochastic optimisers for comparison or local search, such as hill-climbing, simulated annealing, and differential evolution, and much of its functionality can be reached through a simple S-Lang interface. The homepage lists the current version as devel-0.1849 with examples-0.1849. The input is a problem you encode as chromosomes and a fitness function, and the output is an evolved population.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says it is 'designed to assist in the development of code that requires evolutionary algorithms.' The stated current aims are documentation, examples and test cases for the open-source release, with wrappers for languages other than C/C++ planned.
brief.how_it_works: Per the homepage, GAUL offers Darwinian, Lamarckian or Baldwinian evolutionary schemes, steady-state and generation-based GAs, and an island model, with multiple simultaneously evolved populations. It is chromosome-datatype agnostic, with common chromosome types built in, plus most usual crossover, mutation and selection operators and hooks for user-defined operators. Parallelism is available through MPI, OpenMP 2.0, pthreads, or a forked-process model.
brief.install_notes: The homepage gives no install command. It says the main development platform is Linux with gcc, that it should be fairly easy to build on any POSIX system, and that it uses GNU maketools for portability. It reports successful use on RedHat Linux, FreeBSD, Solaris and IRIX, and says it can compile on Microsoft Windows with a few minor features disabled. MPI, OpenMP and pthreads support are optional parallel backends, and the S-Lang scripting interface is an optional layer. The brew formula's executable is gaul_diagnostics, but the homepage does not describe that program.
brief.standout: It is a long-lived, feature-dense GA library that covers many evolutionary schemes and also bundles comparison optimisers (Tabu Search, Simulated Annealing, Simplex, Differential Evolution) in one C library. It also ships a large set of example programs, which is the classic entry point the scout notes point to.
brief.status: Unclear from the homepage. The version string is devel-0.1849, the copyright runs 2000-2022, and the last press release listed is from 22 April 2005. The page has no explicit last-commit or release date, and the 'Latest Changes' link was not followed. The sourceforge development link and documentation link contain misspelled domains ('souceforge'), which suggests the site has not been carefully maintained, but that is an inference, not a stated fact.
brief.caveats: The homepage says GAUL 'is still under heavy development, and therefore is unlikely to be bug free.' Windows builds have some features disabled. Commercial modifications need separate terms from the author. The development home and documentation links on the page use the misspelled domain 'souceforge.net' and 'gaul.souceforge.net', so they may not resolve. The docs were not fetched, so no commands could be verified beyond the homepage. The homepage is a classic-looking HTML site with no code samples.
quotes: It is designed to assist in the development of code that requires evolutionary algorithms.
GAUL is still under heavy development, and therefore is unlikely to be bug free.
Trivial to extend using external code via the built-in code hooks.

name: genometools
desc: Versatile open source genome analysis software
why: Genome analysis toolkit with real bioinformatics depth, though it is a heavy specialist library.

brief.what_it_is: GenomeTools is a free, open source collection of bioinformatics tools for genome informatics, combined into a single binary named gt. It is built on a C library, libgenometools, which provides classes for efficient implementation of sequence and annotation processing software. The homepage lists bundled tools including LTRharvest, Tallymer, uniquesub, AnnotationSketch, LTRdigest, MetaGenomeThreader, GtEncseq and Readjoiner, plus tools built on the library such as GenomeThreader, ParsEval, LTRsift and FISH Oracle. The README does not spell out specific input and output formats beyond sequence and annotation data.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents it as a versatile genome analysis system that bundles many published bioinformatics tools into one place rather than separate programs. The README frames it as a collection of tools that share a common library for efficient processing of sequence and annotation data.
brief.how_it_works: Tools are exposed as subcommands of one binary, gt, which sits on top of the C library libgenometools. The library's modules provide the shared data structures for sequences and structured genome annotations, and each published tool is built on those modules.

commands_seen.context: Debian/Ubuntu install of the most recent stable version, run as root, which provides the gt executable.
Installs the library and development headers. The README says this is not needed just to use the tools.
macOS install via Homebrew on supported macOS versions.
Builds from source on a typical 64-bit Linux system; the README says this should usually suffice.
Installs a source build into the gt subdirectory of the home directory; the same options as the original make run must be repeated. Without prefix it installs system-wide and needs root.

brief.install_notes: Packages exist for Debian, Ubuntu, Homebrew on macOS and the AUR (per README badges). Building from source needs the Cairo libraries and development headers for AnnotationSketch support; without them, build with cairo=no, which drops AnnotationSketch. On 32-bit systems add 32bit=yes. Source tarballs are on GitHub releases, and the INSTALL file in the repository has full build instructions. No accounts or runtimes are mentioned.
brief.standout: It is one binary bundling many separately published research tools from the same group, including a shared sequence data structure (GtEncseq) and a drawing library (AnnotationSketch). Its method papers are cited directly on the homepage, which makes it a reference collection as well as a toolkit.
brief.status: Unknown, leaning maintained. The GitHub README has a live build-status badge and package badges for Debian, Ubuntu, Homebrew and AUR. name: genext2fs
desc: Generates an ext2 filesystem as a normal (non-root) user
why: Builds ext2 filesystem images without root, a neat door into how filesystems are laid out on disk.

brief.what_it_is: genext2fs is a command-line tool that generates an ext2 filesystem image as an ordinary non-root user. It writes the image file directly, so you do not mount it to copy files in. It can also create device nodes and set user and group IDs without being superuser. The homepage does not describe its exact inputs or flags, and no commands appear on the page.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames it as a way to build ext2 images without root, since normally that needs mounting the image or being superuser. The author's words: "It doesn't require you to mount the image file to copy files on it."
brief.install_notes: The homepage says most Linux distributions already package genext2fs. For bugfixes and newer features, it says to get the source from GitHub and build it yourself. The GitHub URL was not given as a link in the text I received, so I did not follow it. Homebrew installs the executable named genext2fs.
brief.standout: Building a filesystem image without mounting it or using root is the unusual part. It makes a small, readable window into how ext2 lays out inodes, blocks and device nodes on disk.
brief.status: Quiet. The homepage says "the project is kind of hibernating right now." I found no release date or commit history because the GitHub repository was not fetched.
brief.caveats: The homepage is very thin and gives no usage examples, supported options, or platform details. Bug reports go through an issue tracker that the homepage links to but whose address I could not read. The project is described as hibernating, so expect slow fixes. I could not confirm the GitHub source location from the homepage text alone.

name: ghex
desc: GNOME hex editor
why: A GNOME hex editor is a classic binary-exploration tool, though a fairly ordinary one.

brief.what_it_is: GHex is a simple hex editor for the GNOME desktop. It loads data from any file and lets you view and edit it either as hex or as ASCII. The project's wiki page describes it as useful for debugging object code or encodings, and notes it is also used to edit saved games, for example to add score or lives. name: glktermw
desc: Terminal-window Glk library with Unicode support
why: A Glk terminal implementation lets classic Interactive Fiction like Zork-style Infocom games run in a terminal with Unicode.

brief.what_it_is: glktermw is a Glk library for Unix terminals, built on GlkTerm 1.0.4 and modified by Alexander Beels to accept and display Unicode characters through ncursesw. Glk is an interface standard for interactive fiction. A Glk program calls the library's windowing, text input and output functions, and glktermw draws those windows in a terminal and passes keystrokes back. The homepage is the Glk specification page rather than a page for glktermw, so the package-specific details below come from the IF Archive listing and the homepage's own description of the Unicode port.
brief.why_it_exists: Glk exists so that interactive fiction interpreters and games can be written once against a standard API and then run on many platforms, each with its own Glk library. The homepage describes Glk as 'a free standard' and says that 'If you're going to run a Glk program, you need a Glk library which runs on your machine.' glktermw fills the terminal slot and adds Unicode.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage describes GlkTerm as 'implemented using the curses.h screen control library', and says the wide-char version is 'modified to use ncursesw or ncurses to display and accept all Unicode characters which the terminal supports.' The Glk spec adds that Unicode text files must be UTF-8. A Glk game is compiled or linked against the library, and the library handles the terminal.
brief.install_notes: Homepage gives no install commands. It says the library should compile on Unix systems that have curses.h, and the Unicode version needs ncursesw or ncurses. The IF Archive lists the source as glktermw-104.tar.gz, so installation is a source build from that tarball; no binary package or brew-specific steps appear in what I read. Brew reports no executables for this formula, so it installs a library, not a runnable game. You need a separate Glk program, such as a Glk-based interpreter or game, to run anything.
brief.standout: Unlike most terminal IF tools, this is a library for a shared interface standard. Any Glk-compliant game or interpreter can run on it without changes. The Unicode port is a single community patch on an older library, which makes it an unusual piece of IF plumbing.
brief.status: Quiet. The homepage says of the wide-char GlkTerm port: 'No longer supported.' The IF Archive file glktermw-104.tar.gz is dated 14-Oct-2012, which is the most recent upload I could see for it. The Glk spec itself is maintained: the homepage was last updated June 2, 2025, and the spec is at version 0.7.6.
brief.caveats: The upstream note says the wide-char GlkTerm port is no longer supported, and the base GlkTerm 1.0.4 is also unsupported and targets Glk 0.7.4 rather than the current 0.7.6. Platform is Unix-like systems with curses or ncursesw. The scout note says it runs 'Zork-style Infocom games'. The homepage does not say that. It lists Dungeon 3.2B for Glk, Nitfol and Zeal (Z-machine interpreters), and Glulx, which are Glk programs, so Infocom-style games are plausible, but the connection is an inference. Dungeon 3.2B is the Fortran lineage that Zork came from, not Zork itself. Licence terms were not visible in what I read.

name: glkterm

brief.what_it_is: GlkTerm is a C library that implements the Glk interactive fiction API for a terminal window. It uses the curses.h screen control library to draw text windows and accept keyboard input, so Glk-based interpreters and games can run in a Unix terminal. The homepage is the Glk specification page, and GlkTerm appears there as one entry in a list of Glk libraries. brief.why_it_exists: Glk is a standard interface that lets interactive fiction programs run on any platform that has a Glk library, so one game can work on many systems. GlkTerm supplies the terminal version of that interface.
brief.how_it_works: A Glk program calls the Glk API for windows, text input and output, and events. GlkTerm implements those calls on top of curses, which handles the terminal screen and keyboard. The homepage describes its scope only briefly and does not explain the internals.
brief.install_notes: No shell commands appear in the homepage or the IF Archive listing, so the install steps are not documented there. The homepage says GlkTerm is C source code that should compile on any Unix system or reasonable facsimile, provided curses.h is available. The wide-char build needs ncursesw or ncurses. Obtaining it means downloading the source tarball from the IF Archive and compiling it yourself. The Homebrew formula here is a library with no executables, so a Glk game or interpreter must be linked against it or run with a Glk-based interpreter.

name: gobo
desc: Free and portable Eiffel tools and libraries
why: Eiffel tools and libraries bring Design by Contract to the terminal, an unusual language ecosystem most developers never touch.

brief.what_it_is: Gobo Eiffel is an open-source collection of compilers, tools and libraries for the Eiffel programming language, distributed as a downloadable archive or source tarball. The README lists 19 Eiffel libraries (kernel, lexical, parse, regexp, XML, XPath, XSLT, test, thread, time and others) and 13 command-line utilities: geant, gec, gecc, gecop, gedoc, geimage, gelsp, gelex, gelint, gepp, getest, gexslt and geyacc. The utilities are optional, since the library classes can be used on their own. The README says the tools are built to run across different Eiffel compilers, and it lists gec (the Gobo Eiffel Compiler) and ISE Eiffel as supported compilers.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says one of the project's main concerns is to give the Eiffel community tools and libraries that are free and portable across Eiffel compilers, so developers can keep using their favourite compiler and still get the Gobo extras.
brief.how_it_works: The utilities are written in Eiffel and built from source with a script, using either the bundled Zig toolchain or a system C compiler as the backend. Installation means unpacking a release, pointing the GOBO environment variable at it, adding its bin directory to PATH, and running install.sh. The README also notes that Eiffel compilers use $NAME for environment variables in their ECF files, so the project uses that convention rather than Windows %NAME%.

commands_seen.context: Builds the Gobo tools such as gec and geyacc. The argument is zig if the Zig toolchain was installed, or a system C compiler such as gcc.
Optional step after copying a Zig download into the tool directory, to patch it for use with the Gobo build. The README gives it with no further explanation.

brief.install_notes: Download the release archive for your platform and architecture (Windows: gobo-windows-{x86_64,arm64}-*.7z; Linux: gobo-linux-*.tar.xz; macOS: gobo-macos-*.tar.xz; other platforms: the gobo-*.tar.gz source package or a Git checkout). Unpack it to a directory of your choice, optionally set GOBO (Windows: %GOBO%) to that directory, and add its bin directory to PATH. For the tools, run bin/install.sh with a C compiler, or install Zig first. Zig is optional: download it, place it in tool/gec/backend/c/zig with the zig executable at the root, and run the patch script. The README also points to ISE Eiffel as a supported compiler, but no ISE-specific steps are listed.
brief.standout: Most Eiffel tooling is tied to one vendor's compiler. Gobo is designed to work across several Eiffel compilers and ships its own compiler (gec) with a bundled Zig-based C backend. The project covers a whole toolchain (lexer and parser generators, linter, preprocessor, test runner, XSLT processor, language server) under the MIT license. The scout note's pitch of bringing Design by Contract to the terminal is not the README's own framing; the README describes compilers and tools for Eiffel, and the homepage mentions Design by Contract in the context of consulting.
brief.status: Maintained. The README lists gec 26.10.18 as a supported compiler version, the copyright line runs to 2026, and it advertises a nightly build with features under development. The repository has about 9,458 commits, 64 stars and 26 forks. I did not see a last-commit date on the page, so this rests on the version and copyright evidence.

Building the tools needs a C compiler or the optional Zig download, so setup is not a single brew install. The Zig patch step is given with no explanation. The utilities are only useful if you need them; the libraries can be used alone. name: gpp
desc: General-purpose preprocessor with customizable syntax
why: A general-purpose preprocessor with user-definable syntax, a strange tool for rewriting text in arbitrary grammars.

brief.what_it_is: GPP is a general-purpose preprocessor, a command-line tool that rewrites text by expanding macros. Its syntax is customizable, so it is not tied to one programming language. It has built-in macro sets for C/C++, LaTeX, HTML, XHTML, and Prolog files. It takes an input file containing text and macro calls, and writes the expanded text out. The README also says the project's own documentation is generated by GPP from a macro file (gpp.pp) in HTML, LaTeX, or troff (man page) output.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents GPP as a middle path between the C preprocessor, which is much more tied to C-family languages, and GNU m4, whose syntax the author describes as heavier and less flexible than GPP's.
brief.how_it_works: The README says GPP's syntax can be customized, which is what lets one tool serve many languages. It ships built-in macros for several formats. The READMEs do not describe the internal mechanism in more detail.

commands_seen.context: Source install from the portable tarball; the README says this should work in most cases if make and a C compiler are present.
After installing, runs GPP on its own documentation source to generate the HTML docs; the README says this is also a basic functionality test.

brief.install_notes: Source tarballs (.tar.bz2) come from GitHub releases or nothingisreal.com, and the included INSTALL file has the steps. Needs make and a C compiler. Windows is not covered by the standard steps: the README suggests Cygwin or MSYS, or else hand-editing config.h.in into src/config.h and compiling src/gpp.c with HAVE_CONFIG_H defined (and WIN_NT if the compiler does not define it). Building from the GitHub development version requires setting up GNU Autotools by hand. Binary packages exist for Debian, FreeBSD, macOS, openSUSE, Ubuntu and Fedora, but they are made by third parties, and the authors take no responsibility for them.
brief.standout: GPP lets you define the macro syntax itself, so one tool can handle C, LaTeX, HTML, Prolog, or anything else, where cpp is tied to C and m4 has a fixed, heavier syntax. Its own documentation is produced by running GPP on a macro file, which the README calls instructive.

name: gravity
desc: Embeddable programming language
why: An embeddable programming language, obscure enough to be a fun side trip into language design.

brief.what_it_is: Gravity is a dynamically typed, lightweight, embeddable programming language written in C with no external dependencies beyond the C standard library. It is class-based with Swift-like syntax, and supports procedural, object-oriented, functional, and data-driven styles, plus prototype-style use via special built-in methods. The CLI takes a .gravity source file (or inline code with -i) and runs it, or compiles it to bytecode with -c. The project also ships a library (libgravity) that host applications can embed.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says Gravity was developed from scratch for the Creo project to offer an easy way to write portable code for iOS and Android. It is written in portable C99 so it can be compiled on any platform.
brief.how_it_works: A multipass compiler with an optimizer turns source into bytecode, which runs on a stack-based VM. The source tree is split into compiler/ (lexer, parser, AST, semantic analysis, IR, optimizer, codegen), runtime/ (stack VM and built-in types), and shared/ (value representation, hash table, array, mark-and-sweep GC). Coroutines are implemented as fibers.

name: gss-ntlmssp

why: Opens a door into NTLM authentication inside GSSAPI, an old Windows auth handshake most people never see.

brief.what_it_is: gss-ntlmssp is a mechglue plugin for the GSSAPI library that implements NTLM authentication. It plugs into a GSSAPI installation so that programs using the standard GSSAPI calls can authenticate with the NTLM handshake, the older Windows challenge-response scheme. The README says it has been built and tested only against the libgssapi from MIT Kerberos, version 1.11 or later. The README does not describe a standalone command-line tool.
brief.why_it_exists: The README gives no explicit problem statement. It says the project was made much simpler by Samba's work and by Microsoft's MS-NLMP protocol documentation, which suggests the goal is NTLM support under GSSAPI, where it was not otherwise available.
brief.how_it_works: It is a mechglue plugin, so GSSAPI's mechanism-glue layer loads it as one of several authentication mechanisms behind the common GSSAPI interface. It implements the NTLM message exchange as specified in MS-NLMP. The README does not go into further detail on the mechanism.
brief.install_notes: The README gives no build or install steps; these are not in the README and the wiki home page does not include them. It requires an MIT Kerberos libgssapi of version 1.11 or newer. Releases are on the GitHub Releases page, and the wiki links to an older Pagure release page. Contribution guidance is on a contributions page linked from the wiki.
brief.standout: It brings NTLM, a Windows authentication protocol most people never see, into the GSSAPI framework through the mechglue plugin mechanism rather than as a separate library. The OID space 1.3.6.1.4.1.7165.655.1.x was donated by the Samba Project, which is an unusual detail.

name: grt
desc: Gesture Recognition Toolkit for real-time machine learning
why: A real-time gesture recognition toolkit, an obscure ML library with a genuinely curious application domain.

brief.what_it_is: GRT (Gesture Recognition Toolkit) is a cross-platform, open-source C++ machine learning library for real-time gesture recognition. It takes in any N-dimensional floating-point vector, such as samples from cameras, Kinect, Leap Motion, accelerometers, or a custom sensor, plus labeled training data from .grt or CSV files. It outputs a trained model that predicts a class label and likelihood for each new sample, and it also provides regression and clustering. Modules for preprocessing, feature extraction, classification, regression, and post-processing can be chained into a GestureRecognitionPipeline. The README also describes a companion GUI, available as a separate download.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a toolkit for real-time gesture recognition, built to work with live sensor data while also supporting conventional offline machine learning. The homepage example shows the pattern: set up a pipeline, train it on a labeled dataset, then call predict on each incoming sensor sample.
brief.how_it_works: Modules share one interface: input is an N-dimensional float vector, and each class offers train, predict, save, load, reset, and clear. A pipeline chains them with the << operator, for example a MovingAverageFilter, then an FFT, then a RandomForest classifier, and pipeline.train(trainingData) fits the whole chain. The README also notes that class label 0 is reserved as a null gesture for automatic gesture spotting, so real gestures should not use label zero.

commands_seen.context: Running the Getting Started example from the README. It takes one argument, the CSV data file to load, then splits, trains, saves, loads, and tests a KNN pipeline.

name: h2c
desc: Headers 2 curl
why: Converts HTTP/2 header dumps into curl commands, a small but odd way to look at protocol headers.

brief.what_it_is: h2c is a small converter from curl. You paste a raw HTTP/1.1 request (request line, headers, and body) into a web form, and it returns a curl command line that would send that same request. The page's example turns a POST with Host, User-Agent, Shoesize, Cookie and Content-Type headers plus a two-line JSON body into a single curl invocation. The page also describes uploading a saved request file with curl itself, and a local copy of the tool is available on GitHub.
brief.why_it_exists: The page frames it as a way to turn a captured HTTP request into a reproducible curl command. The page does not state a broader motivation beyond that.
brief.how_it_works: You submit the raw request text, either in the web form or by uploading a file with curl --data-urlencode http@file https://curl.se/h2c/. The service parses the request line and headers, then emits a curl command with --header, --cookie, --user-agent and --data-binary options, and assumes an https:// URL built from the Host header. The page says the conversion happens on the curl server, and that running h2c locally keeps requests private.

name: halibut
desc: Yet another free document preparation system
why: Sgt. Tatham's document system with its own markup language, an idiosyncratic one-off worth a look.

brief.what_it_is: Halibut is a documentation production system, a free tool for writing manuals in its own markup language. It reads one source format and produces several output formats from the same text: plain ASCII, HTML, PDF, PostScript, Unix man pages, Unix info (.info files directly), and Windows HTML Help (.CHM) and WinHelp (.HLP) files without a separate help compiler. It is primarily aimed at people producing software manuals.
brief.why_it_exists: Halibut's author, Simon Tatham, wrote it because TeX targets printed pages, TeXinfo's output was not to his taste, debiandoc-sgml lacked the indexing support he wanted, and he disliked DocBook's verbose angle-bracket syntax. It grew out of his work on NASM, where he needed documentation on the web as well as in printable and online formats.
brief.how_it_works: Source is written in a TeX-like backslash-and-braces markup, for example \i{this wrapper} to add a word to the index and \u00F6{oe} for Unicode with a fallback representation. Each output format supplies its own configuration directives, which tailor things like HTML headers, style sheets, and site links. The HTML and PDF outputs carry hyperlinks for every cross-reference, including the index and contents.

commands_seen.context: Gets the latest development sources from the git repository; --recursive is needed because the project uses git submodules.

brief.install_notes: Release source is halibut-1.3.tar.gz, which builds as portable ANSI C. The page says it needs at least a 32-bit platform. Windows users can download a prebuilt Windows executable. For development sources, use git clone with --recursive so submodules are included. Nothing on the page mentions brew-specific steps.
brief.standout: Unlike TeX-derived tools, Halibut is built to emit many output formats directly, including Windows HTML Help and WinHelp, rather than going through TeX or a post-processor. Its indexing system, with merged entries, duplicated entries, and rewritten index styles, is designed in from the start rather than bolted on.

name: hcxtools
desc: Utils for conversion of cap/pcap/pcapng WiFi dump files
why: Converts WiFi capture formats and shows how handshakes are structured, though it is tied to a security-testing niche.

brief.what_it_is: hcxtools is a small set of command-line utilities written in C for Linux. It reads WiFi capture files (cap, pcap, pcapng, and gzip-compressed versions of these) and converts the WPA handshake and PMKID data in them into hash files that Hashcat or John the Ripper can work on. The package also includes helpers that filter those hashes, compute or verify a PSK or PMK, generate weak PSK candidates, build wordlist candidates, convert hashes back into cap files, show MAC vendor information, and upload captures to the wpa-sec.stanev.org service. The README lists ten executables: hcxpcapngtool, hcxhashtool, hcxpmktool, hcxpottool, hcxpsktool, hcxeiutool, hcxwltool, hcxhash2cap, wlancap2wpasec, and whoismac.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says the main purpose is to detect weak points in one's own WiFi network by analysing hashes. Converting a dump file to a WPA-PBKDF2-PMKID+EAPOL hash lets the user check whether the WLAN key or PMK was sent unencrypted, or whether an AP or client is vulnerable to common wordlists or weak password generation.
brief.how_it_works: hcxpcapngtool parses the 802.11 frames in a capture and extracts PMKID and EAPOL handshake messages, then writes them as hashes in Hashcat mode 22000 format (and JtR formats). The README's Bitmask section explains that each EAPOL hash is built from two handshake messages: one supplies the MIC and the EAPOL frame, and the other supplies the nonce that is not already embedded in that frame. Message-pair bits and flags record which messages were used and whether the capture looks like an AP-less attack or a router with a known nonce-error pattern. The README's workflow line is hcxdumptool -> hcxpcapngtool -> hcxhashtool (additional hcxpsktool/hcxeiutool) -> hashcat or JtR.

commands_seen.context: Clones the source repository before building from git head (the README's install guide).
Changes into the cloned source directory.
Compiles all tools in parallel, using as many jobs as the machine has CPU cores.
Installs the built binaries to /usr/bin. The README says to run this as root.
Installs the built binaries to /usr/local/bin instead, as root.

brief.install_notes: Most Linux distributions package hcxtools, so the package manager is the simple route. To build from git head, you need a current distribution and these dependencies: Linux kernel 5.15 or newer (mandatory), a recent gcc (README says gcc >= 16 recommended), libopenssl 3.0 or newer with headers, librt, zlib with headers (for gzip input), libcurl 7.56 or newer with headers (used by whoismac and wlancap2wpasec), and pkg-config. Build with make, then make install, optionally with PREFIX=/usr/local. The README says the hcxpcapngtool version must match the hcxdumptool version. No accounts or hardware are needed to run the converters. The README also suggests Arch Linux for notebooks and desktops and OpenWRT for small systems like a Raspberry Pi or router. The hcxdumptool capture tool is a separate project and is not covered here.
brief.standout: Unlike most WiFi tools, which capture or crack, hcxtools stops at conversion: it turns captures into the exact hash formats that Hashcat and JtR accept, and the README says Hashcat endorses it. Its message-pair documentation explains which handshake messages were combined into each hash, which is unusual detail for a tool of this kind.
brief.status: Probably maintained, but I could not confirm a date. The README gives no release or last-commit date, and the page I fetched did not show them. It targets current toolchains (kernel 5.15 or newer, gcc 16 recommended), says the branch is 'pretty closely synced' to the Hashcat and JtR repositories, and points to Hashcat mode 22000 as the recommended format. Those are signs of active upkeep, but they are not a dated release record.
brief.caveats: Linux only. The README says Windows, macOS, Android, emulators and wrappers are unsupported. The README says it is not recommended for inexperienced users and expects knowledge of Linux, 802.11, and key derivation. Hash modes 250x and 1680x are deprecated, and the README recommends mode 22000. Dump files should not be merged, because this destroys custom-block hash values. The tools do not correct nonce errors, so packet loss can produce a wrong PTK. Output files are appended to existing files, except pcapng, pcap and cap outputs. The tools do not crack WPA PSK, WEP, or WPS, and do not decrypt traffic; the README names aircrack-ng, Reaver, Bully, and tshark for those jobs. The README frames the work as checking your own network. The wlancap2wpasec upload target is a third-party service.

Its output is one single HTML file, which HACHA can cut into smaller files. name: hidapi
desc: Library for communicating with USB and Bluetooth HID devices
why: A plumbing library, but HID device access is a real door into USB and Bluetooth peripherals if you poke at devices with it.

brief.what_it_is: HIDAPI is a C library for talking to USB and Bluetooth HID-class devices (keyboards, game controllers, custom gadgets, and similar) on Windows, Linux, FreeBSD and macOS. An application passes it a vendor ID and product ID, or a serial number, and gets back a device handle. From there it can read device strings (manufacturer, product, serial) and send or receive input, output and feature reports. It can be built as a shared library (.so, .dll or .dylib), or embedded by adding a single source file per platform plus one header. The homepage is Doxygen API reference output (version 1.9.8), and the README is the source repository's readme.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says the library is multi-platform and lets an application interface with USB and Bluetooth HID-Class devices across major operating systems. It was started by Alan Ott (signal11) and moved to libusb/hidapi on June 4th, 2019 to merge important bugfixes and continue development.
brief.how_it_works: HIDAPI has four back-ends: Windows (using hid.dll), Linux/hidraw (using the kernel's hidraw driver), libusb (using libusb-1.0 for Linux, BSD and other UNIX-like systems), and macOS (using IOHidManager). On Linux, the hidraw or libusb back-end is chosen at link time by linking libhidapi-libusb or libhidapi-hidraw. The hidraw back-end works with USB and Bluetooth devices but only with devices that have hidraw nodes, so keyboards and mice generally won't work through it. The libusb back-end talks to USB devices directly and does not support Bluetooth.

commands_seen.context: README's example for installing the HIDAPI development package on Ubuntu via APT. Other package managers may use different package names.

brief.install_notes: On Linux, unprivileged users need a udev rule file to access HID devices through hidapi; the README points to udev/69-hid.rules in the repo as an example. Building from source is covered in BUILD.md, which the homepage also links to with separate CMake and Autotools (deprecated) instructions. The optional Test GUI needs the Fox Toolkit v1.6 library, and the README gives no install instructions for it. The console app hidapitester is a separate third-party project. No accounts or runtimes are needed.

name: httpry
desc: Packet sniffer for displaying and logging HTTP traffic
why: A passive HTTP sniffer is a tidy way to watch the protocol that runs everything, though it is somewhat dated.

brief.what_it_is: httpry is a command-line tool for displaying and logging HTTP traffic. It listens on a network interface (or reads a saved capture file with -r) and parses each request and response line along with its header fields. Output goes to the console, to an output file with -o, or to syslog when run as a daemon with -d. It does not show raw HTTP bodies and does not analyze traffic itself. The distribution also includes Perl scripts for processing httpry log files.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says httpry is meant to capture, parse and/or log traffic for later analysis rather than analyze it directly, and that it is 'written to be as lightweight and flexible as possible, so that it can be easily adaptable to different applications.' Its listed uses include seeing what users on a network are browsing, checking server configuration, researching HTTP usage patterns, watching for dangerous downloaded files, and verifying HTTP policy enforcement.
brief.how_it_works: It uses libpcap to capture packets, optionally filtered by a BPF-style expression (default 'tcp port 80 or 8080'). It searches the start of each packet for HTTP request or response data and ignores packets where it finds none. Output fields are chosen with a comma-delimited format string (-f), and a rate mode (-s) shows requests per second per active host. The README says it does no reordering or reassembly of packets.

brief.what_it_is: HuExpress is a multi-platform emulator for the PC Engine, also known as the TurboGrafx-16. You give it a game file (the README lists ROM, ISO, ISQ, ZIP, and HCD formats), an optional backup RAM file, and options, and it runs the game in a window with OpenGL video and SDL sound. It is a fork of the Hu-Go! emulator by zeograd. The README is dated version 3.0.4, November 25th, 2017, and calls itself a first release with bugs expected. brief.how_it_works: The README says the emulator is based on a PC Engine emulator by Bero, with improvements from Hmmx's homepage, and that it reads its settings from huexpress.ini first and then from the command line. Developers can read and change many internal game variables through shared memory (identifier 25679), and can pause or step the CPU through the s_external_control_cpu field. The built-in cheat tool works by searching RAM for a value you type in while the game is paused (F1), then freezing or setting it (F2 and F3).

name: iir1
desc: DSP IIR realtime filter library written in C++
why: A realtime IIR filter library for DSP; the filters are fascinating, but as a library it is only a building block.

brief.what_it_is: iir1 is a C++ library of infinite impulse response (IIR) filters for Linux, Mac OS X and Windows. It implements Butterworth, RBJ and Chebyshev filters (types I and II) as lowpass, highpass, bandpass and bandstop/notch filters, and can import coefficients designed in Python with scipy. You feed it one sample at a time (float or double) with filter(x) and get the filtered sample back. The filter parameters are set with setup() using a sampling rate and analogue cutoff frequencies, or setupN() using normalised frequencies between 0 and 1/2.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a fast, realtime sample-by-sample filter for DSP work. It is a further development of Vinnie Falco's DSPFilters, which processes audio arrays; iir1 was adapted for per-sample realtime use, with the setup call no longer needing the order and the elliptic design code removed in favour of importing scipy coefficients.
brief.how_it_works: The filter order is a template argument, so the filter state is allocated at compile time and the README says it runs without any malloc or new calls. All realtime filter code is in header files, so the compiler can optimise the filter and the main program together. Invalid setup() values, or parameters that produce NaN coefficients, throw exceptions, and defining IIR1_NO_EXCEPTIONS switches that off.

Building from source needs cmake plus a C++ compiler; the README says gcc and clang have been tested, and it also says it compiles directly on a Raspberry Pi. Linking can use cmake's find_package(iir) with iir::iir or iir::iir_static, or a plain -liir flag. Windows users are told to use the static library. Demo programs and unit tests can be turned off with IIR1_BUILD_DEMO and IIR1_BUILD_TESTING. No accounts or runtime services are needed.
brief.standout: The filter order is baked in at compile time through templates, so the per-sample path has no allocation, and the whole filter is header-only so the compiler can inline it into the caller. name: ioping

brief.what_it_is: ioping is a command-line tool that measures disk I/O latency in real time. You point it at a file, directory, or block device, and it issues small read requests and prints the time each one takes, one line per request, much as ping does for network round trips. When interrupted it prints summary statistics: requests completed, IOPS, throughput, and min/avg/max/mdev latency. The README's examples show a directory on an ext4 filesystem, a raw device with random reads (-R), and a raw device with sequential reads (-RL).

brief.how_it_works: The README does not explain the internals. From the examples, it sends a series of I/O requests to the target and reports the latency of each one, then computes IOPS and throughput over the run. Options switch between random (-R) and sequential (-L) access patterns on a device.

name: kyoto-cabinet

Records are organized in a hash table or a B+ tree, and each key must be unique within a database. It has no concept of data tables or data types. It is written in C++ and offered as an API for C, Java, Python, Ruby, Perl, and Lua, and the homepage also links specifications for command line utilities.

brief.how_it_works: Records are stored in a single data file and indexed either by a hash table or a B+ tree, chosen when the database is used. Keys must be unique, and values are plain byte strings with no schema. The homepage gives no further internals.

brief.what_it_is: Lasso is a free C library that implements the Liberty Alliance standards for federated identity and single sign-on. It is built on libxml2, XMLSec and OpenSSL. It takes SAML and Liberty protocol messages in and produces or verifies them, so applications can handle identity provider and service provider roles. brief.how_it_works: Lasso is a C library with XML and cryptographic code underneath (libxml2, XMLSec, OpenSSL). Applications call it to build and process protocol messages for each supported profile. SWIG generates high-level bindings for Python, Perl, Java and PHP, with preliminary .NET assemblies. The homepage's support matrix lists which IdP and SP profiles are marked OK, including Single Sign-On (Artifact, Browser POST, LECP), Single Logout over HTTP-Redirect, HTTP-GET and SOAP, Federation Termination Notification, Name Identifier Registration, Identity Provider Introduction, Attribute Query and Authorization Decision Query.

name: lcm
desc: Libraries and tools for message passing and data marshalling
why: Lightweight Communications and Marshalling is a neat multicast message-passing system, but it is a library family rather than a visible door into anything strange.

brief.what_it_is: LCM (Lightweight Communications and Marshalling) is a set of libraries and tools for message passing and data marshalling. It provides a publish/subscribe model in which programs send and receive typed messages over UDP multicast. It also includes automatic code generation that turns message type definitions into marshalling and unmarshalling code for several languages. The README lists C, C++, Java, Lua, MATLAB, and Python (3.7 and later) as supported, with C#/.NET and Go marked unmaintained. Tools shipped alongside it include lcm-gen, lcm-logger, lcm-logplayer, lcm-logplayer-gui, and lcm-spy.
brief.why_it_exists: It is aimed at real-time systems where high bandwidth and low latency are critical. The docs say it was originally developed in 2006 for the MIT DARPA Urban Challenge team and has since been used in many robotic and autonomous systems.
brief.how_it_works: Peers communicate directly over UDP multicast, with no central broker or hub and no daemon process. Message types are described in the LCM type specification language, and the lcm-gen generator produces the type-safe marshalling code for each target language. Logging and playback tools record and replay the traffic.
brief.install_notes: The README links to separate install and build instructions pages (Installing LCM, Build Instructions from source) and to a releases page on GitHub. I did not fetch those pages, so I have no verified commands or steps. The docs also list a separate UDP Multicast Setup page, which suggests network configuration may matter for multicast traffic to work. Nothing in the pages I read mentioned special hardware or accounts.
brief.standout: It avoids the usual broker-based design: there is no central database, hub, or daemon, and peers talk to each other directly over multicast. Typed message definitions also generate matching code across several languages, and the logging and playback tools are built in.
brief.status: Maintained, per the GitHub README's Roadmap section, which says "The LCM project is active again" and that the current plan is stability and maintenance patches. I did not see a release date or last-commit date in the pages I fetched, so the recency of activity is unverified beyond that note.
brief.caveats: The README lists Go and C#/.NET as unmaintained, and says PRs are welcome for them. Platform support is listed as GNU/Linux (Ubuntu 22.04 and 24.04, Fedora 42), macOS 14 and 15, and Windows 2019 and 2022, plus other POSIX-1.2001 systems per the docs. The homepage I first requested redirects to the /lcm/ docs path. I did not check the license.

name: libcpucycles
desc: Microlibrary for counting CPU cycles
why: Microlibrary from djb's circle for measuring CPU cycles precisely, a rare glimpse into how timing is actually counted in hardware.

brief.what_it_is: libcpucycles is a small C library for counting CPU cycles. A program includes <cpucycles.h>, calls cpucycles() whenever it wants a reading, and gets back a long long. It is linked with -lcpucycles. The library picks a timer from machine-level cycle counters for many architectures (amd64, arm32, arm64, loong64, mips64, ppc32, ppc64, riscv32, riscv64, s390x, sparc64, x86) or, failing those, from OS-level mechanisms (mach_absolute_time, perf_event, CLOCK_MONOTONIC, and a microsecond gettimeofday fallback). A companion cpucycles-info program prints a summary of cycle-counter accuracy.
brief.why_it_exists: The author argues that cycle counts are the most precise timers typical software can reach, and that they are central to understanding and improving performance. Compiler intrinsics such as __rdtsc() work only on Intel/AMD and are noisier than PMC counters, and __builtin_readcyclecounter() works only with clang, so each package otherwise has to build its own portable layer. The stated goal is to provide state-of-the-art cycle counting centrally for all packages to use.
brief.how_it_works: On the first call to cpucycles(), the library benchmarks the available mechanisms and selects the one that does the best job. Subsequent calls are thread-safe and very fast. Hardware counters are preferred (PMC or TSC on amd64, PMC or VCT on arm64, and so on), with the OS-level mechanisms as fallbacks in order of accuracy.
brief.install_notes: The homepage does not describe installation, packaging, or build steps beyond the API line: include <cpucycles.h> and link with -lcpucycles. Homebrew provides the package with two executables, cpucycles-info and cpucycles-open. Nothing about hardware, accounts, or runtime configuration was visible on the page.
brief.standout: Instead of asking each package to write its own cycle-counting shim, it centralizes per-architecture counter selection and self-benchmarks at runtime to choose the best available source. That makes it a shared utility rather than a one-off timing hack.
brief.status: The homepage shows 'Latest release: 20260901' and 'version 2026.09.01 of the Intro web page'. That is the only dated evidence. I could not see a commit history, a changelog, or a repository from the homepage alone, so beyond that release line the status is unknown.

name: libdvbcsa
desc: Free implementation of the DVB Common Scrambling Algorithm
why: An open implementation of the DVB scrambling cipher, a window into how satellite and cable TV protection works.

brief.what_it_is: libdvbcsa is a C library that implements the DVB Common Scrambling Algorithm (DVB/CSA), the cipher used to scramble MPEG transport stream packets in digital satellite, cable and terrestrial TV. It provides both encryption and decryption. It takes MPEG-TS packets and a control word (key) in, and returns scrambled or descrambled packets out. It ships a single-packet implementation and a faster parallel bitslice implementation, and the homepage describes its API as five functions for the single-packet path and six for the bitslice path.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents it as a free, portable, GPL-licensed implementation of a standard cipher that is otherwise hard to get as open code. The author argues that since libdvbcsa implements a published standard, using it is legal, and that the GPL keeps it free and limits its use to free software products.
brief.how_it_works: The library offers a classic one-packet-at-a-time cipher path and a parallel bitslice path that processes several packets at once using MMX, SSE or Altivec SIMD instructions, which the homepage credits for throughput of 300 Mbps or more on recent processors. The homepage says it has been tested on 32-bit, 64-bit and 128-bit word widths and on both little-endian and big-endian machines. The homepage does not explain the internal cipher design beyond this.

Use of the SIMD paths depends on the target CPU supporting MMX, SSE or Altivec.
brief.standout: It is a small, focused library for a cipher that most people only meet inside closed set-top boxes and conditional-access systems, and the author presents it as legal because it implements a published standard. Its two-tier design, with a simple scalar path and a SIMD bitslice path, is a clear example of performance work on a cipher.

HiSlip, the newer and more efficient protocol used by next generation LXI instruments, is listed as future work and is not yet supported.

name: libmagic
desc: Implementation of the file(1) command
why: The engine behind file(1) uses a huge magic-number database that is a fun window into how file formats are identified.

brief.what_it_is: libmagic is the library behind the Unix file(1) command, which identifies what kind of data a file holds by reading its contents rather than trusting its name. It takes a file (or a buffer of bytes) and a compiled magic database, and returns a human-readable description such as the type or MIME type. The file command is the thin front end; the library lets other programs do the same identification without forking and exec'ing file. One example given is the Python file module, which wraps it.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames it around the idea that command-line systems do not rely on filename extensions and instead inspect the actual contents, which is more reliable but needs some I/O. The README says the library split exists so that 3rd party programs can identify file types without having to fork() and exec() file.
brief.how_it_works: The engine checks the file against a database of 'magic numbers' kept in /etc/magic and a Magdir directory of pieces, parsed by apprentice.c. Tests run in stages: fsmagic.c checks filesystem info first, softmagic.c applies the magic-file rules, and ascmagic.c applies hardwired checks as the last stage. Compressed files can be looked inside via compress.c, though that is compiled out on the Amiga runtimes because they cannot spawn external decompressors.

brief.standout: The database is the interesting part: the README says the maintainer accepts new magic entries in magic(5) format, and the Magdir guidelines are strict, requiring unique matches of at least 32 bits and rejecting matches of 16 bits or fewer. The project also dates to August 1987, when Ian Darwin's first RCS commit was made, after the original Bell Labs file was unavailable in source form.

name: libmonome
desc: Library for easy interaction with monome devices
why: The monome grid is a quirky instrument, and this library opens a door to hardware-driven live music, but it is only a library.

brief.what_it_is: libmonome is a C library for talking to monome devices, the grid, arc and similar USB controllers. It gives programs one API for both the older 40h and the series devices. By default it also includes a third backend that speaks OSC to a running monomeserial process, so a program can pick at runtime between a physical device and the OSC bridge. The README describes it as something that makes monome devices easy to use from C and Python, with FFI wrappers for other languages. The monome.org homepage is the hardware company's storefront and does not describe libmonome itself, so this entry relies on the GitHub README.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says it was developed to make monome devices easy to use with programming languages like C and Python, and that adding wrappers for other languages through a suitable FFI is straightforward.
brief.how_it_works: Programs call a unified libmonome API. At runtime they choose either a direct connection to the physical 40h or series device, or the OSC backend, which talks to a running monomeserial instance and presents the same API as a device.

Compiles the library and installs it system-wide; the install step needs sudo.

Using a physical device requires monome hardware, which the library does not supply.

name: libnpupnp
desc: C++ base UPnP library, derived from Portable UPnP, a.k.a libupnp
why: Opens the door to UPnP, the discovery protocol quietly running on nearly every home router and device.

brief.what_it_is: libnpupnp is a C++ library that implements the base UPnP protocol, derived from the older Portable UPnP library (pupnp, also called libupnp). It is the UPnP layer beneath the libupnpp C++ wrapper, which the upmpdcli and upplay applications use. The homepage describes it as a rewrite that keeps the UPnP-specific parts of the old code and swaps out its XML, HTTP server, and HTTP client components. The page does not spell out a full input and output contract, so the details of the API are not in these notes.
brief.why_it_exists: The author says the old libupnp had suffered for years from indifferent maintenance, with buggy releases shipped by Linux distributions. After contributing fixes and shipping a patched older release for several years, he concluded at the start of 2020 that the situation was unsalvageable and created libnpupnp (new pupnp) from the best parts of the old code.
brief.how_it_works: The custom ixml XML library is dropped in favour of expat, which parses XML when needed. The HTTP server and client are replaced by libmicrohttpd and libcurl. The retained code is converted to C++, with STL containers replacing the old hand-rolled lists and similar structures. The author reports that this cut the UPnP portion from about 24,000 lines of C to about 13,000 lines of C++.
brief.install_notes: The homepage gives no build or install commands. It says the upmpdcli and upplay packages can still be built against libupnpp 0.17.x and libupnp, while the default is now libupnpp 0.18.x with libnpupnp. Source is available as a tar archive on the upmpdcli downloads page and as a git repository, but the page does not give those URLs. No hardware, accounts, or runtime setup is mentioned on this page.
brief.standout: Rather than patching the old library again, the author rewrote it around well-maintained dependencies: expat for XML, libmicrohttpd for serving, and libcurl for client requests. The page reports a large reduction in code size, and the libupnpp layer lets applications switch underneath without changes.
brief.status: Quiet as far as these notes show. The homepage was last updated 2022-09-24. The page shows no release version, last commit date, or changelog, so current maintenance could not be confirmed from this page alone.
brief.caveats: The author says there is no chance the new library is free of bugs. There is no pure C interface yet; the author says one would be easy to add if someone wanted it, because the C++ interface comes from STL containers used at a few entry points. The page does not name a license. It also gives no install instructions and no usage examples, and the docs and git repository were not fetched, so the notes do not cover the API surface.
quotes: libnpupnp : replacing the venerable pupnp/libupnp

I came to the conclusion that the situation was unsalvageable, and, at the beginning of 2020, I created a new library, named libnpupnp (new pupnp), based of the best and most specific parts of the old code.
Of course there is no chance that the new library is free of bugs, but I think that they will be easier to find and fix than previously.

judge.reason: UPnP is worth exploring, but this is a conventional protocol library rewrite, with no distinctive user-facing capability or unusual implementation idea to stand out.

name: libnl
desc: Netlink Library Suite
why: A library for Linux netlink, the kernel's internal messaging channel for networking, a real door into protocols most people never see.

brief.what_it_is: libnl is a suite of C libraries that give programs access to Linux netlink, the kernel's messaging interface used mainly for networking configuration and monitoring. The suite is split into small libraries: libnl (core socket handling, message construction, parsing, send and receive), libnl-route (network interfaces, routes, addresses, neighbours, traffic control), libnl-genl (generic netlink), and libnl-nf (netfilter conntrack, log, and queue). The repository file listing also shows libnl-xfrm, libnl-idiag, and libnl-cli, plus a python directory. Programs call its APIs and get kernel networking state back or change it.
brief.why_it_exists: The docs describe netlink as a more flexible successor to ioctl for networking-related kernel configuration and monitoring. The docs also say the interfaces are split into several small libraries so applications do not have to link against one bloated library.
brief.how_it_works: Applications open netlink sockets, build messages, and send them to kernel subsystems, then parse the replies. Each protocol family (route, generic netlink, netfilter) gets its own library on top of the core. The docs call netlink an IPC mechanism primarily between the kernel and user space processes.
brief.install_notes: The docs recommend installing from your Linux distribution's packages first and list package names per distro, for example libnl-3-dev on Debian and Ubuntu, libnl3-devel on Fedora and openSUSE, and libnl-devel on CentOS. The repo tree includes autogen.sh and configure.ac, which suggests a standard autotools build from source, but I did not see build commands in any page I read. The stated requirement is Linux, since netlink is a Linux kernel interface.
brief.standout: It is a plain C library that talks directly to kernel networking subsystems over netlink, which most people never touch. Its split-by-protocol design lets an application link only the family it needs.
brief.status: unknown. The GitHub page shows 2,213 commits, 491 stars, and a .github/workflows directory, but I did not see a last-commit or release date. The docs site names 3.2.25, released Jul 16, 2014, as the latest stable release, which suggests the release line may be quiet, though the git repo may still see commits.
brief.caveats: The GitHub homepage fetch returned the LGPL-2.1 license text instead of a README, so I have no README content and no README commands. Most of the description comes from the external docs site at infradead.org. The license is LGPL-2.1. The docs site lists 3.2.25 from 2014 as latest stable. Its Known Bugs section says releases 3.2.18 and 3.2.19 shipped with an incorrect SONAME, and that 3.2.18 and 3.2.19 binaries need relinking against 3.2.20 and later. The 1.1.x series has limited support and the docs say not to develop new applications on libnl1.

It was designed to be a more flexible successor to ioctl to provide mainly networking related kernel configuration and monitoring interfaces.
The interfaces are split into several small libraries to not force applications to link against a single, bloated library.

name: libnova
desc: Celestial mechanics, astrometry and astrodynamics library

brief.what_it_is: libnova is a general-purpose, double-precision C/C++ library for celestial mechanics, astrometry and astrodynamics. You call its functions with dates, times and orbital or coordinate inputs, and it returns computed values such as positions, apparent places, sidereal time, rise/set/transit times, magnitudes, semidiameters and orbit velocities. The page lists solar, planetary, lunar, asteroid and comet calculations, plus elliptic, parabolic and hyperbolic motion. It is the calculation engine behind the Nova project. The homepage does not describe a command-line tool beyond the libnovaconfig executable named in the Homebrew metadata, which the page does not mention.
brief.why_it_exists: The page says the intended audience is C/C++ programmers, astronomers, and anyone interested in calculating positions of astronomical objects or celestial mechanics, and that it is free software. Its algorithms come largely from Jean Meeus's Astronomical Algorithms, with the ELP 2000-82B lunar solution and the VSOP87 planetary solution credited.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage does not explain the internal mechanism beyond naming the published algorithms and series it implements (Meeus, ELP82 for the Moon, VSOP87 for the planets). It is a C library, so you link it into your own program and call its functions.
brief.install_notes: The homepage gives no build or install steps and no runtime or configuration requirements. It offers a source download, a git repository, and an offline API documentation tarball. The Homebrew metadata lists an executable called libnovaconfig, which is presumably a pkg-config style helper for compiler flags, but the page does not say so and I did not see its usage.
brief.standout: It is a long-lived, double-precision C library that puts classic published astronomy algorithms (Meeus, ELP82, VSOP87) behind one API, covering planets, Moon, asteroids, comets and rise/set times. It is LGPL-licensed, so you can link it from proprietary code.

name: libpano
desc: Build panoramic images from a set of overlapping images
why: Stitches overlapping photos into panoramas; a real image-geometry transform, though the library is quite plumbing-like.

brief.what_it_is: libpano13 (the Panorama Tools library, called pano13 in the README) is a backend C library for stitching overlapping photographs into panoramas. Its input is a set of overlapping source images plus control-point and projection data. Its output is a stitched panoramic image. The page says it is the backend used by many applications, and it ships with command-line tools: PToptimizer for optimising control points, panoinfo for querying the library version, PTmender as a replacement for PTStitcher, PTblender for colour and brightness correction, PTtiff2psd for converting TIFFs to a PSD, and PTuncrop for converting cropped TIFFs to normal TIFFs.
brief.why_it_exists: The page frames Panorama Tools as the shared engine behind a family of panorama front ends (Hugin, PTGui, PTMac and others), so that the stitching maths lives in one library. The page is a legacy project page, with its last update dated 13 May 2013.
brief.how_it_works: The README gives no algorithm detail. It says most front ends call the PTStitcher tool to do the actual stitching, and that PTmender is a replacement for PTStitcher. It also says the library is the backend that front ends and tools call into.

commands_seen.context: Fetches the libpano13 development source code from the Mercurial repository on SourceForge. The page gives this as the basic instruction for downloading the pano13 library source.

brief.install_notes: Most users do not need to build it: the page says Hugin usually ships with a recent version of the library and command-line tools, so downloading Hugin is the easy route. A Windows installer with the library, command-line tools and Photoshop plugins is available from Jim Watters' site, and an OS X bundle is linked from the page. For the latest code you must compile from source, which needs Mercurial (Windows users must install a Mercurial client first). The page says compiling instructions are in the source and may be out of date for your platform. No runtime or account is mentioned.
brief.standout: It is the shared engine underneath many panorama tools, and it has a deliberate, documented limit: the source caps fisheye input at fields of view of 160 degrees or less, because of possible US patents on fisheye stitching. The page also notes that the PTStitcher tool most front ends use has no available source code, which is why the open replacements PTmender and Hugin's nona exist.
brief.status: Quiet. The latest release listed is libpano13-2.9.18 (2 May 2011). The most recent news item is 13 May 2013, about SourceForge moving repositories. Nothing on the page dates later than that. The page is a legacy SourceForge site, and the README points to the Launchpad bug tracker and the PanoTools wiki for ongoing work.
brief.caveats: Several things on the page are dated: development moved from SVN to Mercurial in 2011, and the 2013 note says some repositories moved. The fisheye field-of-view cap of 160 degrees is built into the source. The README says the compile instructions may be out of date for some platforms. The library is low-level, with no GUI of its own. The page points to a separate Hugin GUI and to front ends. Licensing: the page says all files on the site are under the GNU General Public License. The Brew caveats field was empty, and the scout notes describe it as plumbing-like.
quotes: pano13 is the name of the library (like lotus123 or XFree86) not the version (which is currently 2.9.18).
Most front ends for Panorama Tools use the PTStitcher tool to do the actual stitching, this has no available source-code
All files available on this site are licensed under the GNU General Public License.
