name: libpst
desc: Utilities for the PST file format
why: Utilities for decoding Outlook PST files let you dig into a proprietary, obscure file format.

brief.what_it_is: libpst is a set of command-line utilities for reading Microsoft Outlook Personal Folders (.pst) files. It takes a PST file as input and produces mbox or MH mailbox folders (readpst), a listing of the file's contents (lspst), contacts as LDIF for LDAP import (pst2ldif), and email messages as DII load files for CT Summation products (pst2dii). The homepage also mentions contacts converting to a simple list or vCard. The homepage lists nick2ldif as an installed executable but does not describe it. The homepage advertises version 0.6.76.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says the project exists to convert Outlook PST files, which the page describes as covering both 32-bit files from before Outlook 2003 and 64-bit Outlook 2003 files, into formats other tools can read. The README's framing is 'Utilities for the PST file format'. The homepage points to libpff for documentation of the format.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage does not explain the internals. It names a shared library with developer documentation at /libpst/devel/, so the utilities are built on that library. The page does not describe the parsing approach.
brief.install_notes: The homepage points to source and binary packages at http://www.five-ten-sg.com/libpst/packages/ and a Mercurial source repository at http://hg.five-ten-sg.com/libpst/. The brew formula's executables are lspst, nick2ldif, pst2ldif and readpst. No commands or setup steps appeared on the homepage, and I could not load the readpst documentation page.
brief.standout: It is a long-running, narrow tool for a proprietary, obscure file format, and it covers both old 32-bit and Outlook 2003 64-bit PST files. It also writes DII load files, which suggests a legal-discovery or e-discovery audience.
brief.status: Maintained, as far as the homepage shows: it advertises version 0.6.76 and links to packages and a Mercurial repository. The page shows no release or commit dates, so I could not confirm how recent the release is.
brief.caveats: The homepage only states support for 32-bit files from before Outlook 2003 and 64-bit Outlook 2003 files. It says nothing about newer Outlook PST versions, so check that before relying on it. The documentation page for readpst returned 404 under the two URLs I guessed. No license or platform information appeared on the homepage. The homepage was reachable, so these gaps come from the page content, not from a failed fetch.

name: libslax
desc: Implementation of the SLAX language (an XSLT alternative)
why: An obscure SLAX language implementation offering an XSLT alternative, a strange corner of the language world.

brief.what_it_is: libslax is an open-source C library and command-line toolset that implements SLAX, an alternative syntax for XSLT that follows the look of C and Perl. It takes SLAX source files (.slax) and runs or converts them, and it can emit XML, JSON, or YAML. The installed executables are slaxproc (the SLAX processor), gt (a git-style helper that appears to be the project's own development workflow tool), and slax-config. It is built on top of libxml2 and libxslt.
brief.why_it_exists: The wiki pitches SLAX for readability: 'If you like: if ($this == that) { expr the/other; } else { expr "neither"; } more than: <xsl:choose>... please consider using SLAX.' The README credits libxml2 and libxslt as the foundation the library builds on.
brief.how_it_works: SLAX is parsed into the same model XSLT uses, so libslax leans on libxslt for execution. The release notes show a formatter (--width, line wrapping), a profiler (--profile, --profile-mode), and a --dump-tree option that prints a script's hierarchy. Scripts can also be converted to and from XML with xutil:slax-to-xml() and xutil:xml-to-slax(). The README itself says little about internals, so this is taken from the release notes.

name: libtatsu
desc: Library handling the communication with Apple's Tatsu Signing Server (TSS)
why: A door into Apple's signing server protocol used in firmware restore flows, though it is a library rather than a tool to explore.

brief.what_it_is: libtatsu is a C library from the libimobiledevice project that talks to Apple's Tatsu Signing Server (TSS). According to its README, its main purpose is to build TSS request payloads, send them to Apple's server, and retrieve and process the response. It is a library, not a command-line tool: it ships no executables, and callers link against its headers. The Homebrew entry lists no executables and no caveats.
brief.why_it_exists: The code was originally part of idevicerestore and was split out into its own library, while idevicerestore remains its main consumer. The README gives no broader framing beyond that split.
brief.how_it_works: The library builds TSS request payloads, posts them to Apple's TSS endpoint over libcurl, and parses the response. The README uses plist as its data format through libplist. The README says usage is through the header files, and that documentation 'might be added later'.

name: libupnp
desc: Portable UPnP development kit
why: A portable UPnP stack that opens the door to SSDP discovery and the device control protocols running on almost every home router.

brief.what_it_is: libupnp, the Portable SDK for UPnP Devices, is a C library and development kit for building UPnP device and control point applications, and bridges between them. Per its README it consists of the core UPnP protocols, a UPnP-specific XML parser supporting the DOM Level 2 API, and an optional integrated mini web server for serving UPnP-related documents. Developers call its API from their own code; the build produces libupnp.so and installs public headers (upnp/inc and ixml/inc). It targets UPnP Device Architecture version 1.0 and runs on Linux, *BSD, Solaris and others.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says the project was forked in 2006 as a '100% compatible fork' of Intel's original Linux SDK, after years of stagnation, so that community patches would not be lost and the library could be available 'for all important platforms to become a standard for UPnP'.
brief.how_it_works: The README describes a library-level SDK rather than a runnable tool: an application links against libupnp and uses its API to discover, advertise and control UPnP devices over TCP/IP, HTTP and XML. Multicast discovery needs a route for the 239.0.0.0/8 range on the chosen interface, as the README notes. The optional mini web server serves device description documents.

name: libupnpp
desc: C++ wrapper for libnpupnp
why: A C++ wrapper over UPnP discovery; the door to UPnP is interesting, but this is a wrapper rather than the key itself.

brief.what_it_is: Libupnpp is a C++ library that wraps the UPnP stack (libupnp, or its successor libnpupnp) with a higher-level API. A C++ program uses it to discover UPnP devices on the network, read their parsed descriptions, and send commands to and receive status from their services. It ships predefined classes for UPnP AV RenderingControl and AVTransport and for many OpenHome audio services, and it has a generic string-based interface for any other service. Inputs are network discovery and SOAP/HTTP traffic; outputs are C++ objects and return values.
brief.why_it_exists: The author's framing is that libupnpp gives C++ programs a usable interface to UPnP audio devices, so they do not have to deal with the raw libupnp layer directly. It is the control-point side of the upmpdcli project's tooling.
brief.how_it_works: A global device directory (UPnPDeviceDirectory) runs discovery and keeps a list of active devices; you look a device up by friendly name with getDevByFName(). Each device's description XML is parsed into a UPnPDeviceDesc, which you pass to a Device or Service constructor. Service classes marshal arguments into SOAP, make synchronous calls, and parse the reply. Event reporting works by having the control point run an internal HTTP server that services report to after you subscribe via installReporter(); callbacks run on a separate thread.
brief.install_notes: No install steps, package names, or build instructions were visible on the reference page or the GitLab project page. The library needs a multithreaded build because the underlying library uses threads. Optional libupnp debug logging depends on whether UPNP_HAVE_DEBUG is enabled in upnpconfig.h. Consult the framagit repository for build details, which were not read.
brief.standout: The 'Pythonic quacks like a duck' approach is unusual: device classes do not verify device type, and callers build an a-la-carte object from whatever services exist. It also offers a string-based TypedService interface that works from the device's own service description, so you can call actions that have no hand-written wrapper.
brief.status: Unknown, leaning quiet. The reference page says 'Last updated 2021-01-12', and the GitLab page shows a creation date of March 09, 2020 but no recent release or commit date. The project's own README-like text points at a libnpupnp successor, which implies later activity elsewhere that was not checked.
brief.caveats: The old libupnp base supports only one IP interface; libnpupnp supports multiple IPv4 interfaces but only a single IPv6 interface. Most methods are blocking, so parallelism needs your own threads. Event callbacks come from a separate thread and need synchronization. Embedded devices are described by the author as poorly supported by common control points. The license is GNU LGPLv2.1. The reference doc is the only documentation read; it has no install or usage walkthrough.
quotes: Libupnpp is a C++ wrapper for libupnp a.k.a Portable UPnP (up to branch 0.17), or its C++ descendant, libnpupnp (versions 0.18 and later).
In general, the service is the interesting entity, and the wise approach is the Pythonic 'quacks like a duck' one: if a device has the service you need, you can use it.
Most libupnpp methods are blocking. Multithreading will be needed to achieve parallelism in your program

name: libuvc
desc: Cross-platform library for USB video devices
why: A USB Video Class library lets you talk directly to webcams and microscopes, a real door into how USB devices expose streams.

brief.what_it_is: libuvc is a cross-platform C library for USB video devices, built on top of libusb. It talks to any device that exposes the standard USB Video Class (UVC) interface, giving fine-grained control over it. Developers can use it to write drivers for devices that aren't supported yet, or to access UVC devices in a generic way. name: libyojimbo
desc: Secure client/server network protocol library for multiplayer games
why: A secure client/server protocol library from game networking, a door into reliable UDP and encrypted transport worth a look.

brief.what_it_is: yojimbo is a network library for client/server games, written in C++. It gives a game a secure connection layer over UDP: clients authenticate with connect tokens, and packets are encrypted and signed. On top of that it offers unreliable-unordered messages for time-sensitive data, reliable-ordered messages, and per-connection stats (latency, jitter, packet loss, bandwidth). The README frames it as a library you link into a C++ game engine, not a standalone program.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says it is "designed around the networking requirements of competitive multiplayer games like first person shooters" and that "if you have a game engine written in C++ and you want to network your game, yojimbo is a really good choice."
brief.how_it_works: Authentication uses connect tokens based on the netcode standard, and packets are encrypted and signed before being sent over UDP. Large payloads are split by packet fragmentation and reassembled on receipt. Reliable-ordered messages are resent aggressively until acknowledged, while unreliable-unordered messages are sent without that guarantee. The README also mentions a bitpacker and serialization system but does not explain its internals.

commands_seen.context: Source checkout command given in the README's Source Code section; the README points to releases as an alternative to cloning.

brief.install_notes: No build or install commands appear in the README. It refers to CONTRIBUTING.md for how to build and test, which I did not fetch. Installation is by cloning the repository or downloading a release archive from GitHub. Using it requires that the client and server share the same ClientServerConfig, channels and message factory, and that all yojimbo calls run on one thread.
brief.standout: It is built on a small family of open libraries from the same author (netcode for the connection and token layer, reliable for reliable messaging, serialize for serialization), and the README asks that product credits name all four together. Its design is explicit about its limits, aimed at games with 100 players or fewer.

The reference page warns that the input format is not the C API: calls such as make_lp are wrong input here.

name: luau
desc: Fast, safe, gradually typed embeddable scripting language derived from Lua
why: A sandboxed, gradually typed Lua derivative from Roblox, interesting as an embeddable language with a distinct design lineage.

brief.what_it_is: Luau is a small, fast, embeddable scripting language derived from Lua, with an optional gradual type system and a type inference engine. Its README says it is backwards compatible with Lua 5.1 and largely reimplemented from scratch, with a heavily modified 5.1 runtime and a rewritten interpreter. It takes Luau source, compiles it to bytecode, and runs it in a VM, or type-checks and lints it with luau-analyze. The project also ships luau, a sandboxed REPL that runs files. It was open-sourced by Roblox, which uses it for game scripting and parts of its own applications and editor.
brief.why_it_exists: Roblox open-sourced Luau to foster collaboration in the Roblox community and to let other companies and communities benefit from its language and runtime innovation. The homepage frames it as aiming for performance, safety, accessibility, and embeddability, with a sandbox that lets embedders run untrusted code.
brief.how_it_works: Source is compiled to bytecode by a separate compiler, and the VM loads that bytecode, so a deployed VM does not need the compiler. The embedder compiles source with luau_compile and loads it with luau_load, and the README says the sandbox limits the exposed API surface by default. The type checker and linter (luau-analyze) read types from annotations and from .luaurc or --! comments, and the homepage says its inference aims to rule out errors and provide autocomplete with minimal annotations.

brief.install_notes: Precompiled binaries come from the GitHub releases page. The luau and luau-analyze binaries must be put on PATH or copied to a directory such as /usr/local/bin on Linux and macOS. Packaged versions exist for Homebrew, Arch, Alpine, and Gentoo, but the README says the Luau team does not maintain these. After install, the README says to validate with the test case at luau.org/getting-started. Building from source needs CMake (or make on Linux and macOS) and a C++ compiler: the runtime needs C++11, and the compiler and analysis need C++17, with MSVC 2017 or later, gcc-7 or clang-7 or later. The library components have no external dependencies beyond the STL and CRT. The REPL uses isocline and the tests use doctest. Embedders should call luaL_sandbox on the global state and luaL_sandboxthread for each script thread to get the performance benefits of the safeenv feature. The C API differs from Lua 5.x: compile source separately, and use lua_newuserdatadtor instead of __gc.
brief.standout: It takes Lua 5.1 compatibility and a familiar embedding API and adds gradual typing with aggressive type inference, plus sandboxing designed in from the start for running untrusted code. The README also describes a tooling suite that goes beyond the language, including an analyzer, linter, and a community language server (luau-lsp).
brief.status: Maintained. The GitHub releases page showed a steady weekly cadence: 0.740 on 25 Sep, 0.741 on 2 Oct, 0.742 on 10 Oct, and 0.743 on 16 Oct marked Latest, with the year not shown in the fetched text. The repository has CI and codecov badges. The releases page fetch was truncated, so the list of releases below 0.740 was not seen.
brief.caveats: Several features are still experimental or flag-gated in the release notes: exact tables by default (RFC 11), if-local expressions, and user-defined classes that need DebugLuauUserDefinedClasses flags. The README says Luau is not a full superset of later Lua versions and does not always follow Lua's design decisions. Lua __gc is not supported, so embedders must use lua_newuserdatadtor. The REPL is sandboxed and cannot access the filesystem except through require. Packaged distributions are not maintained by the Luau team. The build needs a C++17 toolchain. The README documents the Roblox origin, but the homepage does not mention a standalone package manager, which it lists as a planned tool. name: lwtools
desc: Cross-development tools for Motorola 6809 and Hitachi 6309
why: Assembler and linker for the Motorola 6809 and Hitachi 6309 CPUs; a retro toolchain with a real hook, though deprecated.

brief.what_it_is: LWTOOLS is a set of cross-development tools for the Motorola 6809 and Hitachi 6309 microprocessors. The main piece is lwasm, an assembler that takes 6809/6309 assembly source and writes raw binaries, CoCo LOADM binaries, or a proprietary object file format for later linking. lwlink combines those object files, and the package also includes lwar (an archiver), lwcc-cpp, and lwobjdump. The homepage says the assembler supports macros and file inclusion, among other things.
brief.why_it_exists: The author, William Astle, started it in 2006 because none of the cross-assemblers available at the time supported all the features he wanted to use.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage gives no internals beyond the output targets. Source goes through lwasm, which emits raw, CoCo LOADM, or its own object format. Object files are then combined by lwlink. The homepage does not describe the object format or the linker's internals.

name: mac-robber
desc: Digital investigation tool
why: A forensic tool that builds MAC-time timelines from filesystems, a window into how investigators reconstruct what happened on a disk.

brief.what_it_is: mac-robber is a digital investigation tool that collects metadata from allocated files in a mounted file system. Its output feeds the mactime tool in The Sleuth Kit, which builds a timeline of file activity. It is written in C and is based on the Perl grave-robber tool from TCT. The homepage describes it as a basic tool that should compile on any UNIX system.
brief.why_it_exists: It is meant for incident response, either on a live system or on a dead system analysed in a lab. The author says it is useful for file systems that The Sleuth Kit does not support, such as an obscure UNIX file system mounted read-only on a trusted machine.
brief.how_it_works: It reads file metadata through the operating system, so the file system must already be mounted, unlike Sleuth Kit tools that parse the file system directly. Because of this, it cannot see deleted files or files hidden by rootkits. The homepage says it will modify access times on directories mounted with write permissions. Its output goes to mactime to produce the timeline.

brief.standout: It works by reading the mounted file system through the OS rather than parsing it, which lets it handle file systems Sleuth Kit cannot read. It is small enough that the author suggests it can run on a trusted machine against a suspect, read-only mounted disk.
brief.status: quiet. The only dated item on the homepage is the 1.02 release on Feb 12, 2010, which also switched to the new mactime body format. The homepage shows no later release or update, and I did not check the repository or commit history.
brief.caveats: It cannot recover deleted files or see rootkit-hidden files, because it relies on the mounted file system view. Running it on a writable mount changes directory access times, so mount read-only when evidence matters. The homepage shows only a source tarball, not a binary, and the last release is from 2010. name: mac
desc: Monkey's Audio lossless codec
why: Monkey's Audio lossless codec, a rarer audio format with a clever compression design worth reading into, though the CLI is modest.

brief.what_it_is: Monkey's Audio is a free lossless audio compressor that turns WAV, AIFF, W64, SND/AU, CAF and RF64 files into its own APE format, and can decompress APE files back to the exact original bytes. The homepage says it is also supported by players and rippers such as foobar2000, Winamp and Windows Media Player. The Windows GUI is described in the Help page, and the Homebrew package installs a command-line executable named mac, which the Help page's pipe examples use. Output is a smaller APE file that can be verified with per-file CRCs.
brief.why_it_exists: The author argues that lossy formats like mp3, ogg and wma permanently discard quality to save space, while Monkey's Audio makes bit-for-bit copies that still shrink, so you can always recreate the original CD. The homepage calls it 'a beefed-up Winzip for your music'.
brief.how_it_works: The Theory page describes the standard lossless pipeline: convert left/right to mid/side (X and Y), pass the samples through an adaptive predictor that subtracts an estimate and keeps a weight m that adjusts up or down as prediction helps, then entropy-code the residuals. It explains Rice coding as the baseline and says Monkey's Audio uses a 'slightly more advanced entropy coder'. The page is a primer and says it is 'by no means complete', so it does not give Monkey's Audio's exact predictor or coder details. Verification works by checking the whole-file CRC stored in modern APE files.

name: melody
desc: Language that compiles to regular expressions
why: A language that compiles down to regular expressions, a genuinely odd transform of ideas.

brief.what_it_is: Melody is a small domain-specific language that compiles to regular expressions. You write statements such as 16 of "na"; or some of <digit>; and the compiler emits a plain regex, for example (?:na){16} or \d+. The README says the output targets ECMAScript regex syntax. The melody_cli tool reads a file or stdin and prints the compiled regex, and can also test it against a string (-t) or a file (-f), or open a REPL (-r). The compiler also ships as WASM bindings, an npm package, a Deno module, and a Babel plugin.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says Melody 'is a language that compiles to regular expressions and aims to be more easily readable and maintainable'. The README wording is 'while aiming to be more readable and maintainable'.
brief.how_it_works: The compiler is written in Rust and is split into crates, with melody_compiler as the core and melody_cli as a wrapper. Each Melody construct maps to a regex construct: 'some of' becomes +, 'any of' becomes *, 'option of' becomes ?, 'match' becomes (?:...), and 'capture' becomes (...). The README performance section, measured on v0.20.0 on an M1 Pro with criterion, reports about 4.4 microseconds for 8 lines and about 470 milliseconds for 1M lines.

name: mednafen
desc: Multi-system emulator
why: A multi-system emulator that doubles as a window into many old console architectures and their quirks.

brief.what_it_is: Mednafen is a portable, command-line-driven multi-system emulator built on OpenGL and SDL. It runs game images for many old consoles and handlers, including Apple II, Atari Lynx, Neo Geo Pocket, WonderSwan, Game Boy, GBA, NES, SNES, Virtual Boy, PC Engine/TurboGrafx-16 CD, SuperGrafx, PC-FX, Game Gear, Genesis/Mega Drive, Master System, Saturn (64-bit builds only), and PlayStation. Input is a ROM or disc image and the output is emulated video and audio on screen. It can also write PNG screenshots and QuickTime movies with lossless codecs. Hotkeys and virtual inputs can be remapped to a keyboard, a joystick, or both.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage gives no explicit mission statement. It presents Mednafen as a portable, accuracy-minded emulator that covers many systems in one program, configured from the command line and config files.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage says emulation runs in a threaded model on top of SDL and OpenGL, and that this threading is why a joystick is preferred over a keyboard for lower input latency. Save states and real-time rewinding are supported. Per-module and per-game override configuration files exist, as the 1.32.0 notes describe.
brief.install_notes: The homepage lists a source tarball (mednafen-1.32.1.tar.xz) and Windows zip builds for win64 and win32, each with a SHA-256 hash. The 1.27.0 notes mention a Windows 98-compatible build that is not provided every release. The 1.27.1 notes say the configure script errors out when iconv is missing. The 1.27.0 notes say the library dependency on libsndfile was dropped in favour of libFLAC. The page does not show a first-run walkthrough or any BIOS requirements, and the brew formula notes contain no extra caveats.
brief.standout: Mednafen is a single emulator that bundles many systems, and it has a long tail of accuracy work recorded in its changelogs, such as SNES VRAM write blocking and Saturn SCSP timing fixes. Its per-game fixes are listed by title in each release, so it reads partly as a record of how specific commercial games misbehaved on real hardware.
brief.status: Maintained as of the homepage. The newest entry is version 1.32.1, dated April 5, 2024, and the page footer says copyright 2005-2024. No later release or news item appears on the homepage. I did not check the GitHub or source repository for recent commits, so this rests on the homepage alone.
brief.caveats: Saturn emulation is 64-bit only. The minimum Windows 98-compatible build targets i686 with MMX, and PS1 MDEC emulation needs SSE2. Keyboard input has more latency than a joystick because of the threaded design. The 1.32.0 notes say the Windows 2000 build was restored for people who enjoy airgaps, firewalls, and insecurities. ST-V support is described as experimental. Licensing is GPLv2. The homepage footer notes that Mednafen is not an official Nintendo product.
quotes: Mednafen is a portable, utilizing OpenGL and SDL, argument(command-line)-driven multi-system emulator.
Mednafen is distributed under the terms of the GNU GPLv2.

Due to the threaded model of emulation used in Mednafen, and limitations of SDL, a joystick is preferred over a keyboard to play games, as the joystick will have slightly less latency, although the latency differences may not be perceptible to most people.

Input is a tracker module file; output is audio sent to whichever sound driver the build uses. The homepage also says it was originally an MS-DOS player and has been ported to Unix, Macintosh, BeOS, and Java.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents it as a portable way to play the module music of the DOS-era tracker scene across platforms. The scout note calls it a piece of old-school sound culture worth hearing. The homepage gives no separate mission statement.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage does not explain the internals. The changelogs describe per-format loaders (for example IT, XM, S3M, STM, AMF, GDM, MED, UNI, 669, FAR) and depackers for compressed modules, plus pluggable output drivers (ALSA, PulseAudio, SDL, OpenAL, WASAPI, CoreAudio, WinMM, OSS, and others). The library also exposes a reader/writer interface, which the changelog says custom implementations must respect.

name: mit-scheme
desc: MIT/GNU Scheme development tools and runtime library
why: A full Scheme environment from MIT with an old-school REPL, SICP heritage and a real runtime to explore for hours.

brief.what_it_is: MIT/GNU Scheme is an implementation of the Scheme programming language from the GNU Project. Per its homepage it provides an interpreter, a compiler, a source-code debugger, an integrated Emacs-like editor, and a large runtime library. It takes Scheme source and REPL input and runs programs on x86-64 or aarch64 Unix-like systems. The homepage says it is best suited to programming large applications with a rapid development cycle.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames it as a full, free-software Scheme environment for building large applications quickly, rather than only a bare interpreter. It is a GNU project, distributed under the GPL.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage says the native-code compiler generates machine code that needs both write and execute memory permissions, which is why it cannot yet run native-compiled on Apple silicon. For those machines and any 64-bit Unix, a portable SVM1 binary is provided instead, which is slower but works. Source builds need a working MIT/GNU Scheme compiler to bootstrap, except the portable C source, which needs only a C compiler.

commands_seen.context: Homepage prose: after running make, run this to generate a macOS mit-scheme.app from the normal distribution, since macOS app bundles are no longer distributed.
Homepage prose: the standard install step that the macOS app route replaces; instead you move the generated mit-scheme.app into /Applications/.

brief.install_notes: Binaries exist for x86-64 and aarch64le Unix, plus a Portable SVM build for any 64-bit Unix including Apple silicon. Check the download against the published MD5 checksum before reporting bugs. Source tarball is for Unix and uses linefeeds. Building from source requires an existing MIT/GNU Scheme compiler unless you use the portable C source, which needs only a C compiler. On macOS, generate the app with make then make macosx-app and move mit-scheme.app to /Applications/. The homepage gives no other first-run or configuration steps.

No native-code compilation on Apple silicon because of W^X restrictions, so SVM1 binaries are used there and run slower. Building from source needs an existing MIT/GNU Scheme compiler except for the portable C source. The macOS app is no longer distributed prebuilt. The homepage describes the project as mostly R7RS small conformant, not fully.

name: modsurfer
desc: Validate, audit and investigate WebAssembly binaries
why: Inspects and audits WebAssembly binaries, a useful way to take modules apart, though it leans toward commercial tooling.

brief.what_it_is: Modsurfer is a set of tools for inspecting and checking WebAssembly modules and components. Its CLI takes a compiled .wasm binary plus an optional YAML "checkfile" that declares requirements such as allowed imports and exports, maximum size, and cyclomatic complexity risk, then reports which properties pass or fail. Output is a table by default, or JSON with --output-format json. The CLI also acts as an HTTP client to a Modsurfer service, either the desktop app or an Enterprise deployment. A free desktop application provides a GUI for browsing module details such as code size, imports/exports, function names, and strings.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says Modsurfer gives ops and dev teams "a system of record + diagnostics application to search, browse, and investigate modules", so teams can see what WebAssembly code runs in their systems. The four listed use cases are at-a-glance insights, searching module details, auditing and tracking WebAssembly code, and debugging issues that are hard to pinpoint in the opaque binary format.
brief.how_it_works: You generate a checkfile with modsurfer generate, then run modsurfer validate against a binary and the checkfile. Validation compares the module's imports, exports, size, and complexity against the declared expectations and classifies each failure (for example ABI Compatibility, Security, or Resource Limit) with a severity. The checkfile can also be a remote URL, so requirements can be tracked centrally.

commands_seen.context: Creates a checkfile (mod.yaml) from an existing module; the README warns the result is very restrictive and should be edited.
Validates a .wasm binary against a checkfile and reports any unmet expectations.

brief.install_notes: The CLI is available as a GitHub Release binary (the README links to the latest release) or as a Docker image at ghcr.io/dylibso/modsurfer. The brew formula installs the modsurfer executable. No accounts or runtimes are mentioned for the CLI's local validation. Using it as an HTTP client needs either the free desktop app (downloaded from dylibso.com/downloads/modsurfer) or an Enterprise deployment. Enterprise self-managed deployment requires contacting support@dylibso.com. The GitHub Action (modsurfer-validate-action) can run validation in CI with no purchase needed.
brief.standout: The checkfile is a declarative YAML policy for WebAssembly binaries. brief.what_it_is: Moscow ML is a lightweight implementation of Standard ML (SML), a strict functional language. It provides an interactive top-level system and a batch compiler, and it reads SML source files and produces bytecode, or compact stand-alone executables. It implements the full language as revised in 1997, including modules, and large parts of the SML Basis Library. The distribution also includes lex and yacc style tools (mosmllex, mosmlyac) and a bytecode runtime (camlrunm).
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage describes it as a light-weight implementation of Standard ML used in teaching and research. The README says it is written to be backwards compatible with versions before 2.00 and to match the 1997 SML revision.
brief.how_it_works: The README says the bytecode generator and runtime system come from the Caml Light implementation by Xavier Leroy and Damien Doligez. It supports separate compilation and can produce compact stand-alone executables in the style of Caml Light. It also supports dynamic linking of external functions on several platforms, and quotations and antiquotations for metaprogramming.

Official routes are: build from source (GitHub releases or the zipball), an Ubuntu PPA, a Mac OS X 10.9 .pkg installer that installs to /usr/local, or a Windows installer made by Sebastian Paaske Tørholm (Eckankar). Installation instructions are in install.txt in the source tree.
brief.standout: It is a small, old Standard ML system with a Caml Light runtime heritage, shipping separate compilation, stand-alone executables and quotation/antiquotation support. That makes it an unusual place to meet SML outside the usual SML/NJ or MLton ecosystems.

brief.what_it_is: mpegdemux is a command-line demultiplexer for MPEG-1 and MPEG-2 system streams (program streams and the packetised container format). It takes an MPEG system stream file as input and can list its contents, report the first packet of each elementary stream, extract elementary streams into separate output files, or write a new MPEG system stream with selected elementary streams removed. The page describes it as a tool for getting an overview of what is inside an MPEG file.
brief.why_it_exists: The page says it can be used to list the contents of an MPEG system stream and to extract elementary streams. It does not give a longer motivation.
brief.how_it_works: It runs in one of four modes: scan reports the first packet of each elementary stream; list prints the contents textually; demux dissolves the system stream packet structure and typically writes each extracted stream to its own file; remux keeps the MPEG system stream structure intact so the output is still a system stream with the unwanted elementary streams removed. Streams are selected by ID values such as 0xe0 (video) and 0xc0-0xdf (audio), with options like -s all and -p all.

Each hash entry has a regex and a summary, and the default view also shows John the Ripper and HashCat mode information. The README says hashes are defined in name_that_hash/hashes.py and that each one is tested for both false and true positives.

name: neko

why: A dynamically typed language with its own VM from the Haxe lineage, an unusual corner of language design worth a look.

brief.what_it_is: Neko is a high-level, dynamically typed programming language with its own bytecode virtual machine. Its compiler turns a .neko source file into a bytecode .n file, which the VM then runs. It can also be embedded as a scripting language inside other applications, and its C foreign function interface lets it call C libraries. The homepage says the compiler can be used as a standalone command-line tool or as a library for compile-and-run in interactive languages.

brief.how_it_works: Source is compiled by the Neko compiler, which the homepage says is written in Neko itself, into bytecode in a .n file. The lightweight, optimized VM runs that bytecode and can be embedded in applications. Libraries are reached through the C foreign function interface, and other languages can have generators that target Neko.

name: never
desc: Statically typed, embedded functional programming language
why: A statically typed functional language designed for embedding, an obscure and interesting language to explore.

brief.what_it_is: Never is a small statically typed, strongly typed, call-by-value functional programming language with an interpreter/VM. You write functions (with int, float, string, char, arrays, records, enums, closures and modules) and the program runs from a main function, which must return an int or float. Input is Never source, either as a file run with the nev binary or as a string compiled from a C host program. Output is printed text (print, printf, prints) plus a final return value from main. The docs describe it as a language meant to be embedded in Unix shell scripts and C code.
brief.why_it_exists: The docs frame it as a demonstration of how functions can be compiled, invoked, and passed as parameters or results. The stated aim is a simple language that is useful for calculating expressions, with basic data types, assignment, control flow, arrays and first-order functions.
brief.how_it_works: Source is compiled (nev_compile_str in the C API) into a program object, then run on a VM created with vm_new and a memory and stack size. A host can pick an entry function with nev_prepare, set parameters, and call nev_execute to get the result back. Control flow such as if, while, do-while and for are expressions, and recursion is the main looping tool; tail recursion is noted as an optimisation. Functions can be nested, passed as arguments, and returned from other functions.

commands_seen.context: Shebang line to put at the top of a Never script so it runs directly without naming the interpreter; the script must also be marked executable.
Runs an executable Never script with two command-line arguments that become main's int parameters; the docs show its output as 'result is 31'.
Sets the NEVER_PATH environment variable, which is the list of directories searched in order for Never modules; the first match is used.

brief.install_notes: The homepage does not describe installation. The brew caveats are empty. The docs show a shell-run form that uses the nev binary (for example '#!/usr/bin/nev' and 'nev -e' with a program), while the brew metadata lists the executable as 'never', so the names do not line up in the text I read. The C embedding example needs nev.h and links against the Never library; the FFI section loads libraries such as libm.so.6 and libc.so.6, so it assumes a Linux-style system. Modules need NEVER_PATH set if you want to use them.
brief.standout: Its selling point is embedding: the same language runs as a Unix shell script via a shebang, as a C library through a small compile/prepare/execute API, and it can call functions in shared libraries directly with extern declarations. Its syntax is unusual for a small language, with conformant arrays (arrays passed with their dimensions), list comprehensions that yield closures, enumerated records, and exceptions attached to functions as catch blocks.

name: nfdump
desc: Tools to collect and process netflow data on the command-line
why: Netflow collection and analysis opens a door into how routers report traffic, though the tooling is conventional.

brief.what_it_is: nfdump is a command-line suite for collecting, storing, filtering and analysing network flow records. The collectors nfcapd and sfcapd receive NetFlow (v1, v5/v7, v9, IPFIX) or sFlow streams from routers and other exporters and write them to nfdump binary files on disk, rotated about every 5 minutes. The nfdump tool then reads those files, applies a tcpdump-like filter, aggregates or lists the flows, and prints text, CSV, JSON or a user-defined format. Companion tools add geolocation (geolookup), Tor exit-node lookup (torlookup), anonymisation (nfanon), expiry and replay. An optional nfpcapd can turn live interface or pcap traffic into flow records.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a tool to collect and analyse NetFlow, IPFIX and sFlow data from network devices, with a focus on efficiency, flexibility and extensibility. It also states a design choice: all collected data is stored to disk before analysis, which separates collection from processing.
brief.how_it_works: Exporters send flow records over UDP to an nfcapd or sfcapd process, which writes them into time-stamped files (nfcapd.YYYYMMDDhhmm) in a per-source directory. nfdump then reads one file or several concatenated files, filters them with an expression syntax similar to tcpdump's, and aggregates or lists the results. Enrichment with geo, AS or Tor data happens at analysis time using databases built by updateGeoDB.sh and updateTorDB.sh.

brief.install_notes: Beyond brew install: a source build needs GNU autotools 2.71 (autoconf 2.71 per the README). Default configure builds nfcapd, sfcapd, nfdump, nfanon, nfexpire, nfreplay, geolookup and torlookup. Optional builds need flags: --enable-nfpcapd, --enable-ja4, --enable-jnat, --enable-readpcap, --enable-ftconv, --enable-nfprofile. Compression libraries ZSTD and bzip2 are auto-detected if present, and LZO and LZ4 are embedded. Older Linux may need libbsd and libbsd-dev. The README gives distro-specific steps for CentOS 7.x (devtoolset-8 via scl) and Ubuntu 18.04 (clang-10). There is a Docker option in extra/docker/README.md. Geo and Tor lookups need databases fetched with updateGeoDB.sh and updateTorDB.sh before use. Running as root is not needed unless binding to ports below 1024.
brief.standout: The most distinctive part is the design split: collection writes time-rotated binary files and analysis happens later, with a tcpdump-style filter language aimed at flow records. Unusual extras include CryptoPAn-based IP anonymisation in nfanon, Tor exit-node enrichment, and NSEL/NAT event logging support. On the surface it is a conventional collector-plus-query setup, as the scout notes suggest.
brief.status: The README says it is actively maintained and calls 1.7.x (codename unicorn) the current release series. It also has a tester call for the 1.8.x beta branch, described as nearing release. I did not see a release date or last-commit date on the page, so recency is only as current as the README's own claims.
brief.caveats: The README is Linux and BSD oriented; it says nothing about macOS, and the Ubuntu and CentOS steps are for old releases. nfprofile and nftrack are legacy binaries for NfSen and may move to a separate archive. NetFlow v5 and v7 use 32-bit counters, so busy routers can overflow them unless the flow-cache timeout is lowered. nfcapd has no built-in access control, so host firewalling is needed. name: nng
desc: Nanomsg-next-generation -- light-weight brokerless messaging
why: Brokerless messaging with scalability protocols is a doorway into messaging patterns, though it reads as a generic library.

brief.what_it_is: NNG is a lightweight C library for brokerless messaging. Applications link against it and use its API to send and receive messages over sockets that implement common messaging patterns such as publish/subscribe, RPC-style request/reply, and service discovery. It handles connection management, retries, and similar plumbing so the application code can focus on its own logic. The page does not describe a command-line tool beyond the executable name nngcat, which the brew metadata lists.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents NNG as the successor to nanomsg, and to some extent ZeroMQ, that keeps a simple API for recurring messaging problems and takes the design further. It also says the project offers wire and API compatibility with nanomsg, so existing nanomsg and mangos applications can interoperate with NNG applications.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage says NNG scales out across cores with a bespoke asynchronous I/O framework that uses thread pools. It avoids tying itself to file descriptors and avoids interlocking state machines, which it credits for making new protocols and transports easier to add; the TLS and ZeroTier transports are given as examples. Optional separation of protocol context and state from sockets is offered for concurrent applications.

name: oak
desc: Expressive, simple, dynamic programming language
why: A small dynamic language of uncertain maturity; a possible curiosity worth a look despite thin evidence of depth.

brief.what_it_is: Oak is a small, dynamically typed, general-purpose programming language with a single-executable toolchain. The oak binary ships an interpreter and a REPL, plus a standard library, a code formatter (oak fmt), a bundler and Oak-to-JavaScript compiler (oak build), a test runner, and a documentation tool for source files. Oak source files ending in .oak are the input, and the output is either run results, a single-file bundle of Oak source, or a JavaScript bundle when built with --web. The homepage includes a sample HTTP server using http.Server and a FizzBuzz example.
brief.why_it_exists: The author built it as a sequel to their earlier toy language Ink, to correct early mistakes and be easier to read and use, and says it is for their own hobby projects. Since late 2021 it has been their main language for simple scripts, side projects, and personal knowledge tools.
brief.how_it_works: Oak is an expression-based imperative language that borrows syntax from Lua and JavaScript and leans on functional idioms, with lists, objects, atoms, and first-class functions. Its if expression works like a pattern-matching switch on deeply compared shapes of data, and the := and <- operators bind names, with <- assigning to an existing variable in an enclosing scope. Iteration is done through recursion with optimized tail calls and standard-library functions such as range, map, each, filter, and reduce, since the language has no for or while loops. The homepage also describes a with expression that places a trailing callback argument after the call, and says the bundler and compiler were built on the author's earlier Ink toolchain, September.

name: objc-run
desc: Use Objective-C files for shell script-like tasks
why: Running Objective-C as shell scripts is a strange, delightful idea, though it is tiny and niche.

brief.what_it_is: objc-run is a shell script that compiles and runs a single Objective-C source file. You give it a .m file plus any parameters. It compiles the file into an application named after the file, launches it, passes the remaining parameters to it, and deletes the built app when it exits. It can also pull CocoaPods dependencies from a podfile written inside a C comment in the source file. The README's example use case is small tasks such as manipulating plist files.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says it is for small programming tasks you want to handle in Objective-C that don't justify setting up a complete Xcode project. It describes itself as "Think of it as CodeRunner without an user interface."
brief.how_it_works: objc-run compiles the .m file into an application named after the file, runs it if compilation succeeds, and passes along the remaining command-line arguments. Once the program finishes, the built application is removed. With a #!/usr/bin/env objc-run first line, the .m file can be launched directly as a script. CocoaPods modules are enabled by placing podfile contents between podfile-start and podfile-end inside a /* */ comment.

brief.how_it_works: Code is compiled either to bytecode or to native machine code, and a garbage collector handles memory. Packages are installed through opam, which the install page says installs both the compiler and additional packages into isolated environments called switches. The homepage says the type system infers types, as the top-level session shows the inferred signature val square : int -> int.

name: ol
desc: Purely functional dialect of Lisp

brief.what_it_is: Ol (Otus Lisp) is a purely functional dialect of Lisp that implements an extended subset of R7RS Scheme plus some SRFIs. It runs as a REPL, takes Lisp source from a file or stdin, and prints results or compiles source to a binary bytecode form with the -c option. The interpreter/VM is described as tiny (about 64KB) and embeddable, and it can call native shared-library functions through a built-in FFI. The README says it also runs in WebAssembly in browsers.
brief.why_it_exists: The README presents it as a small, embeddable, cross-platform Lisp that provides a portable high-level interface for calling code written in other languages (C, Python, Lua, etc.). It descends from Owl Lisp, which the author credits as the project that gave birth to it.
brief.how_it_works: Source is compiled to Ol bytecode and run by olvm, the Ol virtual machine (C source in src/olvm.c). Compiled binaries need only the VM, so the README says they run without the compiler (about 450KB). The FFI, in extensions/ffi.c, loads shared libraries and declares foreign function prototypes that can be called from Lisp, with callbacks back into Lisp.

brief.what_it_is: openRTSP is a command-line program that opens, streams, receives, and optionally records media streams identified by an rtsp:// URL. It sends RTSP DESCRIBE to get the session's SDP description, then SETUPs and PLAYs each audio/video subsession whose RTP payload format it understands. Received data goes to files named by MIME type (for example audio-MPA-1 and video-MPV-2), to stdout with -a, -v, or -L, or to QuickTime .mov, MP4, or AVI output. A sibling program, playSIP, does the same job for SIP sessions.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents it as a standalone tool for pulling RTSP streams from network cameras and servers into files or pipes, built on the LIVE555 streaming media library. Its own source notes say it was designed as a standalone application rather than as example code.

Digest authentication is handled with -u, and -R can wait for a REGISTER command to learn the stream URL. Output is written per subsession as RTP packets arrive, and the program stops after the SDP duration, a -d limit, or an inter-packet gap set with -D.

name: orbiton
desc: Fast and config-free text editor and IDE limited by VT100
why: An editor and IDE deliberately limited to VT100 with no config, an odd design constraint with personality.

brief.what_it_is: Orbiton is a terminal text editor with a simple IDE built in, written in Go. It is limited to VT100 terminal features and has no configuration file; the only exception the README names is the optional O_THEME environment variable for themes. It takes a filename (or a line number after it) and opens it for editing, with syntax highlighting, build and format keys (ctrl-b, ctrl-w), a debugger for C and C++ via gdb, and LSP tab-completion for many languages. It ships as a single self-contained executable.
brief.why_it_exists: The author writes that he 'spent too much time configuring text editors, IDEs and plugins, so I could just as well create a new one', and wanted something 'simple, but capable'. The stated principles are minimal annoyance within VT100 limits, no configuration to help users stay focused (apart from themes), and rapid edit-format-compile-run cycles.
brief.how_it_works: Because it targets VT100, it draws and reads input through plain terminal escape sequences rather than a GUI toolkit, so it runs over SSH and on live images. Build and format keys map to per-language external tools: the README has a table pairing each language with a build command (for example gcc, go build, cargo build, zig build-exe) and a format command (for example clang-format, rustfmt, ruff format). For Go, Rust, C, C++, Python, Zig, Odin, Haskell, Gleam, Lua, Ruby and Bash it can also talk to a language server for tab completion.

name: osmfilter
desc: Command-line tool to filter OpenStreetMap files for specific tags
why: A quirky, fast filter that reads OpenStreetMap's binary PBF format and slices the world by tag, a door into map data internals.

brief.what_it_is: osmfilter is a command-line tool for filtering OpenStreetMap data files by tag. It reads .osm or .o5m files; the wiki says other formats such as PBF should first be converted to .o5m with osmconvert. It writes filtered .osm or .o5m output to a file or stdout. Filters can keep or drop whole nodes, ways and relations by tag expression, and by default keep the nodes, ways or members that kept objects depend on. It can also filter or modify individual tags and print tag statistics.
brief.why_it_exists: The wiki gives no separate motivation; it describes the tool as a way to filter OpenStreetMap data files for specific tags. It recommends o5m input for fast processing.
brief.how_it_works: Object filters decide for each node, way or relation whether it stays, using expressions with =, !=, <, >, <=, >=, wildcards, and and/or. Unless --ignore-dependencies is set, objects used by a kept object (nodes of a kept way, members of a kept relation) are kept too. Tag filters never remove whole objects; they keep, drop or rewrite individual tags.

Reads the filter options from a parameter file instead of a long command line.

No accounts or runtime needed beyond a C compiler for the source build. For large planet files the wiki benchmarks used 16GB RAM and a 7200rpm disk or SSD.
brief.standout: A single small C program that filters planet-scale OSM data with dependency-aware keep rules: keeping ways automatically keeps their nodes, and keeping relations keeps their members. It also has built-in tag statistics (--out-count, --out-key) so you can explore a file's tags before writing a filter.

name: ovh-ttyrec
desc: Enhanced (but compatible) version of the classic ttyrec
why: Terminal session recorder compatible with classic ttyrec, a neat way to capture and replay programs as they ran.

brief.what_it_is: ovh-ttyrec is a terminal session recorder written in C. Running `ttyrec` launches your shell (or a command you give it) and records the session to a ttyrec file until it exits. `ttyplay` replays a recorded file in the terminal. A third binary, `ttytime`, is also installed, but the README does not describe it. The input is the live terminal session; the output is a ttyrec recording file, optionally zstd-compressed. It is a drop-in replacement for the original ttyrec and adds features such as session locking and termination after keyboard inactivity.
brief.why_it_exists: The README presents it as an enhanced but fully compatible version of the classic ttyrec, which is based on the `script` program. The goal is a drop-in replacement that adds features without breaking existing ttyrec use.
brief.how_it_works: The README says it uses pseudoterminals (via openpty() or grantpt()/unlockpt()) to capture the session, and falls back to pipes in a no-tty mode that still records stdout and stderr. It detects which to use automatically, and this can be overridden on the command line. Compression is applied on the fly with zstd, and output files can be rotated without interrupting the session. The README does not give further internal detail.

Replays a previously recorded session file.

The README does not mention a Homebrew formula, accounts, or runtime configuration.

name: pari-elldata
desc: J.E. Cremona elliptic curve data for PARI/GP
why: Cremona's elliptic curve database for PARI/GP; real number theory data, though it is only a data package.

brief.what_it_is: elldata is an optional data package for PARI/GP, the number theory system. It is the PARI/GP-format version of J. E. Cremona's table of elliptic curve data. The package is a compressed archive (elldata.tgz, about 54.8 MB) that adds a data folder to a PARI/GP installation. Once installed, PARI/GP can look up curves by their Cremona labels, and the ellsearch and ellidentify functions use it. The package contains data only, with no executables. The source for this entry is the PARI group's shared packages page, which lists about seven optional packages, so this brief covers only the elldata entry.
brief.why_it_exists: The PARI group distributes these packages separately because they take up a nonnegligible amount of disk space and would be useless to most users. The page says they are 'distributed separately and maintained independently'.
brief.how_it_works: The archive is unpacked into a 'data' folder, and the elldata folder inside it is placed where PARI/GP expects architecture-independent files (the directory reported by default(datadir)), or next to gp.exe on Windows, or in the PARI source top directory before ./Configure for source builds. PARI/GP then reads the curve data from that folder when a function such as ellinit is given a Cremona label. The page says the package requires PARI/GP 2.2.11 or later.

(B) From a source distribution, extract the archive in the top-level pari directory before running ./Configure, then make install-data, make test-all, and make install. (C) For an existing installation, including the Windows self-extracting binary, run default(datadir) in gp, extract the archive anywhere, and move the elldata folder into the datadir. The archive is about 54.8 MB and has a published sha256 and md5. The package has no Homebrew-specific instructions on the page. The brew formula name is pari-elldata.

Its clever part is that the data is delivered as a plain folder that PARI/GP finds by path, so a single data package can be added to an existing installation without rebuilding anything. The page also gives a neat check, ellinit("11a1"), that tells you whether the package is present.

name: pastel
desc: Command-line tool to generate, analyze, convert and manipulate colors
why: Colour manipulation in pipes with colour-space and chemistry-style operations, a pleasant small transform to poke at.

brief.what_it_is: pastel is a command-line tool written in Rust for generating, analyzing, converting and manipulating colors. It accepts colors as names (like lightslategray), hex (778899 or '#778899' or 789), rgb or hsl strings, or comma-separated triples, either as arguments or on standard input. name: pcalc
desc: Calculator for those working with multiple bases, sizes, and close to the bits

brief.what_it_is: pcalc is a terminal calculator for programmers that shows binary, hexadecimal and decimal representations of a number at the same time. You type expressions such as 0xff + 0b101101 - 5 or 2+2*3, and it displays the result in all three bases. It also offers bitwise operators (AND, OR, NOR, XOR, NOT, shifts, rotates, two's complement, and byte-order swap) and lets you choose the operand width, from 1 to 64 bits. It is built with ncurses and runs in a terminal.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says the idea came while its author was developing a Nintendo Game Boy emulator, where the online tools they found were clunky and did not allow "nice multitasking". brief.how_it_works: Input is parsed as an inline expression with operator precedence and parentheses, and numbers can be written in decimal, 0x hex, or 0b binary. Arithmetic runs at 64 bits by default, and typing a width such as 16bit or 8bit switches the operand size; the displayed number is unsigned. Single-character operators map to operations, and the interface panels (history, binary, hex, decimal, operation) can be toggled by typing their names or set at launch with command-line flags.

name: pedump
desc: Dump Windows PE files using Ruby
why: Dumping Windows PE headers from the terminal is a friendly way to see inside executables.

brief.what_it_is: pedump is a pure Ruby command-line tool that dumps the internals of Windows executables. You point it at a PE file (and it also handles DOS MZ, win16 NE, and EFI TE files) and it prints the headers, sections, data directories, resources, strings, imports, exports, version info, and packer/compiler guess to the terminal. Output defaults to a table and can be switched to bin, c, dump, hex, inspect, json, or yaml. It can also upload a file to the pedump.me website for an HTML rendering.
brief.why_it_exists: The README gives no separate problem statement. The homepage pitches it as a way to "dump your PE!", and the README describes it as a pure Ruby implementation of a win32 PE binary dumper.
brief.how_it_works: It parses the binary's structures in Ruby and prints them per section, selected with flags such as --pe, --sections, --imports, or --resources. Extraction flags such as --extract resource:VERSION/#1 or --extract section:.text write raw bytes to stdout, so they pipe into hexdump. Conversion flags such as --rva2file and --va2file translate addresses. Packer detection is heuristic, and --deep runs a slower scan.

name: prips

You give it a start and end address, or a CIDR block like 192.168.0.0/24, and it outputs each address in turn. It can also go the other way with -c, turning a start and end address into a single CIDR block. The -i option sets the step between printed addresses, and -e excludes addresses from the output.

name: procmail
desc: Autonomous mail processor
why: An old mail filter driven by its own recipe syntax, a small surviving piece of Unix history.

brief.what_it_is: Procmail is a mail processing program written in C. It reads each incoming message and applies rules from a per-user .procmailrc file to sort it into folders or files, forward it, or start programs on arrival. The package also ships formail, which can generate autoreplies, split mailboxes or digests into single messages, and reformat or extract headers. It also includes lockfile, which makes NFS-safe lock files for shell scripts, and mailstat, an example shell script that summarizes procmail's logs.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a robust local delivery agent and mail filter: it can sort mail into folders when you subscribe to mailing lists, prioritise mail, build mailing lists or mail servers, or act as a drop-in replacement for /bin/mail. Its stated design goal is delivering mail even under the worst conditions, such as a full filesystem, no swap space, or missing executables.
brief.how_it_works: Procmail is event driven: it is invoked when mail arrives, typically through a .forward file in the user's home directory, and it follows the recipes in .procmailrc. The README says it uses standard egrep regular expressions, can make yes/no decisions based on message size, and supports weighted scoring of messages. It delivers to single-file folders, one-file-per-message directories, MH folders, Maildir, or /var/mail-style spools, and it writes a mail log file that records each arrival and where it went.

Edit the Makefile and config.h as needed, then run make install; the build runs an autoconf step that checks the compiler and system, and it obeys the current umask. Per-user installs work without root. Each user who wants procmail needs a .forward file, which must be world readable, and a .procmailrc file, with examples in the examples directory and the procmail(1) man page. MMDF users need a .maildelivery file instead of .forward. On NFS, autoconf runs locking tests on directories you specify. For system-wide use, INSTALL says to consider making procmail suid root and lockfile sgid maildaemon, and to run make recommend for specifics. The brew formula installs the same four executables with no extra caveats.

name: procyon-decompiler
desc: Modern decompiler for Java 5 and beyond
why: A Java decompiler that turns compiled class files back into readable source, a satisfying way to watch bytecode become code.

brief.what_it_is: procyon-decompiler is a standalone command-line front-end for the Java decompiler in Procyon's Compiler Toolset. You pass it class names (dotted or binary form), .class file paths, or whole jar files, and it prints reconstructed Java source to the console. It can also print raw bytecode or a bytecode AST instead of Java. The decompiler itself is a framework that other applications can call through the com.strobel.decompiler.Decompiler helper class.
brief.why_it_exists: The author, Mike Strobel, found the Java decompiler options lacking. Jad is no longer maintained and does not support Java 5+ features, and JD-GUI tends to fail on code emitted by his LINQ/DLR tree compiler. He wrote Procyon's decompiler, inspired by and borrowing heavily from ILSpy and Mono.Cecil.
brief.how_it_works: The decompiler is based on ILSpy and Mono.Cecil, per the wiki. Input can be a type name, which is loaded from the user or bootstrap classpath, a file path, or a jar. Output is written to System.out. The README says the front-end embeds all dependencies in the JAR, so it can be redistributed as a single file.

name: proxytunnel
desc: Create TCP tunnels through HTTPS proxies
why: Tunnels TCP through HTTPS proxies via CONNECT, a neat door into how proxies carry arbitrary traffic.

brief.what_it_is: proxytunnel is a command-line program that connects stdin and stdout to a server on the Internet by sending the traffic through an HTTPS proxy using the HTTP CONNECT method. It takes a destination host and port, plus optional proxy host, port, and credentials, and passes the bytes through as a tunnel. The README is written around using it as an SSH ProxyCommand, so SSH traffic travels through a corporate or other HTTP proxy. It also runs as an inetd service or a standalone daemon, and it supports SSL encryption, NTLM authentication, and chaining through a second proxy. The README says the version is 1.12.1.
brief.why_it_exists: The author wrote it to reach his home machine over SSH from behind a proxy that only allowed HTTPS-style outbound traffic. The README says: "I originally wrote this program to be used as an extension to SSH, to be able to SSH to my box at home."
brief.how_it_works: The client connects to the HTTP proxy and sends a CONNECT request for the destination host:port, optionally with Proxy-Authorization credentials, and then relays stdin and stdout over the resulting connection. With -e or -E, the connection to the proxy or to the destination is wrapped in SSL, which helps when a proxy inspects protocol and rejects non-HTTPS traffic. The README says that in that case you need stunnel4 or a server that understands SSL on the other end.

commands_seen.context: Prints the built-in option list (version 1.12.1 is shown in the output).
Example line for ~/.ssh/config under a Host entry. It sends SSH through the proxy with SSL to the proxy, prompts for the password, and targets port 443 on the home box.
Final step once the ProxyCommand is set up; the README says "execute an 'ssh foobar' and you're in business!"

brief.install_notes: The README links to INSTALL.md for build instructions, which I did not fetch. Credentials can be given with -P on the command line (the password is then prompted for), with the PROXYPASS or PROXYUSER environment variables, with the HTTP_PROXY variable (format http://host:port/), or with a passfile (-F) containing proxy_user, proxy_passwd, remproxy_user, and remproxy_passwd. The server side needs sshd listening on 443 or 563 through an extra Port line in sshd_config, or a firewall redirect, because most HTTPS proxies allow only those ports. The README also mentions an Nginx, Apache, or Caddy setup, described in a linked blog post.
brief.standout: It reuses the ordinary HTTPS proxy CONNECT method as a generic byte pipe, so any TCP service, SSH being the main example, can get through a proxy that was built only for web traffic. The README is also a personal, first-person document from the original author, with a practical, hands-on tone.
brief.status: Status is unclear from the README alone. The version shown is 1.12.1, the copyright line says 2001-2024, and the README has no release date or commit date. The Travis CI badge points to travis-ci.org, which suggests older CI setup, and the README carries a 'maintainers wanted' badge, which suggests the project is looking for maintainers. I did not check the commit history, so this is not confirmed.
brief.caveats: Many corporate proxies filter traffic, so plain CONNECT tunnels may fail without -e or -E and extra server-side setup. The README warns that most HTTPS proxies only allow ports 443 and 563, so SSH has to be moved onto one of those. Self-signed certificates need -z, which turns off certificate verification. NTLM support needs -N, and the domain may need -t if autodetection fails. Build steps are in a separate INSTALL.md that I did not read, and the man page at docs/proxytunnel.1.adoc was not fetched either. The README does not state a license.

name: reliable
desc: Simple packet acknowledgement system for UDP-based protocols
why: A packet acknowledgement scheme for UDP is a neat look at how reliability is built on unreliable transport.

brief.what_it_is: reliable is a C library, from the README a simple packet acknowledgement system for UDP-based protocols. You give it packets you want to send and the raw bytes of packets you receive, and it tells you which of your sent packets the other side acknowledged. It works through callbacks: you supply a transmit function that puts bytes on your own UDP socket and a process function that handles received packets. It also reports RTT, jitter and packet loss estimates, and it handles fragmentation, reassembly and duplicate detection. It does not include a socket layer of its own.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says it is 'useful in situations where you need to know which UDP packets you sent were received by the other side.' It is meant to sit under your own protocol so you can resend messages until a packet carrying them is acked.
brief.how_it_works: Each endpoint assigns a sequence number to every packet it sends and tracks what the peer has received. Acks are collected in an array that you read with reliable_endpoint_get_acks and clear each frame. reliable_endpoint_update is called once per frame to refresh RTT, jitter, packet loss and bandwidth estimates. The README does not describe the ack bitfield encoding or the fragmentation wire format in detail.

commands_seen.context: Fills the config struct with defaults before you override fields such as max_packet_size, fragment_above and the callbacks.
Creates an endpoint from the config; returns NULL on invalid config or failed allocation, so the README says to check the result.

Sends a packet through the endpoint, which goes out via your transmit callback.
Returns a read-only array of acked sequence numbers and sets the count; valid only until the next receive, clear, reset or destroy.
Clears the accumulated acks once you have processed them; the README says to do this every frame.
Returns the sequence number the next sent packet will have, so you can map acks back to message contents before sending.
Called once per frame to keep latency, jitter, packet loss and bandwidth stats current.

brief.install_notes: The README gives no package-manager or build instructions beyond the C API. It says reliable is designed to work with your own socket library, and suggests the author's netcode library if you do not have one. No runtime, accounts or hardware are mentioned. The brew formula has no executables, so this is a library to link against, not a command-line tool.
brief.standout: It is a small, reliability-on-top-of-UDP layer with no socket code of its own, designed to pair with the author's netcode library. The caveats section is unusually careful about callback lifetimes and reentrancy, such as the rule that the transmit callback must not send on the same endpoint it was called from.
brief.status: The README says 'reliable is stable and production ready' and has a CI badge pointing to a GitHub Actions workflow. I did not see a release date or last commit date on the page I fetched, so recency is unknown.
brief.caveats: Endpoints are not thread safe; use one per thread or add your own lock, and the log, printf and assert handlers are process-global. Acks accumulate until cleared, and extra acks are dropped with a logged error when the buffer fills. Callback pointers and the ack array are valid only for the duration of the call or until the next mutating call, so data must be copied to be kept. The transmit callback must not send on its own endpoint. It is not a full messaging layer. Licence is BSD 3-Clause, with a credit request for products that use it.

name: rogcat
desc: Adb logcat wrapper
why: Adb logcat wrapper with some Android device depth, a close call for a hardware-facing door into Android logs.

brief.what_it_is: rogcat is a command-line wrapper around Android's `adb logcat`, written in Rust by Felix Obenhuber. By default it runs `adb logcat` and reads the device's log stream, parses each record, applies optional filters, and writes the result as a colored, column-based view on the terminal or to a file in csv, raw, html, human or json format. It can also read from a custom command's stdout/stderr, one or more files, stdin, a TCP port, or a SocketCAN device on Linux. A `--fx` switch runs Fuchsia's `ffx log` instead of adb. The README calls the painted, reformatted view its main feature.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says `adb logcat` exposes Android's internal log buffers, and that rogcat "tries to give access to those logs in a convenient way including post processing capabilities."
brief.how_it_works: Each run is a pipeline: read records from the chosen source, parse them, apply tag, pid, thread and message filters (RE2 regexes, with a leading '!' to invert), then format the output. With no command given, rogcat runs adb logcat and restarts it when adb exits, so it reconnects after device power cycles or disconnects. Profiles in a TOML file bundle filters and settings under names selected with -p, and a profile can extend others.

Build and install from a source checkout; the README says this requires Rust 2018 edition.

brief.install_notes: adb must be on PATH at runtime; the Homebrew caveat says it can be installed with `brew install --cask android-platform-tools`. Building from source needs Rust (2018 edition) via cargo, and on Debian-based systems the package libudev-dev (and its dependencies) is needed. Binary releases are on the GitHub releases page. Optional config.toml (per-OS path: $HOME/Library/Preferences/rogcat/ on macOS, $HOME/.config/rogcat/ on Linux, %HOME%/AppData/Roaming/rogcat/ on Windows) sets defaults such as restart, buffer and terminal options. Optional profiles.toml sits in the same directory, or at the path in ROGCAT_PROFILES. Fuchsia use needs ffx installed.
brief.standout: It is more than a viewer: input can come from adb, a serial port, a SocketCAN bus, a TCP stream or a file, and the output can be fed back into rogcat, with TOML profiles that can extend each other. The Fuchsia `--fx`/ffx path and SocketCAN support also make it an unusual single tool for reading device logs across ecosystems.

name: rp
desc: Tool to find ROP sequences in PE/Elf/Mach-O x86/x64 binaries
why: Finds ROP gadgets in binaries, a direct window into how exploits chain code fragments together.

brief.what_it_is: rp++ (invoked as rp) is a C++ command-line tool that searches compiled executables for ROP gadgets, which are short instruction sequences ending in a return that exploit chains can reuse. It takes a PE, ELF, or Mach-O binary (or a raw code dump with --raw) and an instruction-count limit given with --rop, and prints the gadgets it finds. It also searches a binary for pointers to specific integer values (--search-int) or byte strings (--search-hexa), which are useful when assembling a ROP chain. The README describes it as supporting x86, x64, ARM, and ARM64 architectures.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a helper for building ROP chains: when constructing one, you often need gadgets and also pointers to integers or strings with specific values. The author describes it as a fast gadget finder.
brief.how_it_works: You point it at a file with --file or -f and set the maximum number of instructions per gadget with --rop or -r. --va sets the module base address (passing 0 gives relative offsets), and --raw analyses raw code dumps instead of parsed executables. The README does not describe the internal scanning algorithm.
