name: wireshark
desc: Network analyzer and capture tool - without graphical user interface
why: Command-line packet capture is a door into every protocol on the wire, though it is a famous default.

brief.what_it_is: Wireshark is a free, open-source network protocol analyzer. It captures live traffic from a computer's network interfaces and lets you browse it interactively, with deep inspection of hundreds of protocols. Its input is live traffic or existing capture files, and its output is decoded packet views, statistics, and exported or converted capture files. This Homebrew formula packages only the command-line side: tshark (terminal Wireshark), dumpcap (capture), capinfos, captype, editcap, mergecap, text2pcap, reordercap, rawshark, randpkt, dftest, idl2wrs, mmdbresolve, and sharkd. The homepage and the User's Guide describe the graphical app, which this formula does not install by default.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage pitches it as 'The world's leading network protocol analyzer' for diagnosing networks and understanding traffic: finding bottlenecks, troubleshooting faster, and seeing what protocols are doing. The formula description frames it as a door into every protocol on the wire.
brief.how_it_works: The User's Guide's table of contents shows a capture layer (live capture with capture filters and capture file modes), a dissection layer that decodes protocols, and statistics and reassembly on top. Capture is done with dumpcap, and tshark gives the same dissection on the terminal. The fetched pages are only a table of contents and homepage copy, so the detailed mechanism is not confirmed here.

On macOS, if the list of capture interfaces is empty (the default), install ChmodBPF with 'brew install --cask wireshark-chmodbpf'. name: wla-dx
desc: Yet another crossassembler package
why: Multi-platform retro CPU crossassembler, an old-school door into 8-bit console programming.

brief.what_it_is: WLA DX is a multi-platform cross-assembler package written in ANSI C. Its wla-ARCH programs assemble assembly source files into object or library files, and wlalink links those objects together. It covers many CPUs, including Z80, GB-Z80, 6502, 65816, 68000, 6809, 8080, HuC6280, SH-2, SPC700 and SuperFX. The package is not tied to one console, since you define your own memory map, which is shared across all object and library files. The Homebrew executables include wla-6502, wla-65816, wla-z80, wla-gb, wlab and wlalink, among others.
brief.why_it_exists: The README presents WLA DX as 'Yet Another ANSI C' cross-assembler package. Its stated design point is that it isn't bound to one system such as the NES or C64; instead you define the memory map yourself.
brief.how_it_works: Each wla-ARCH assembler turns a source file into an object or library file. wlalink then combines those objects using the memory map you define. The README does not go into more detail on the internals. The docs index lists sections on linking, compiling object and library files, and an architectural overview, but I did not fetch those pages.

name: woof-doom
desc: Woof! is a continuation of the Boom/MBF bloodline of Doom source ports
why: A modern Doom source port in the Boom/MBF lineage, an excellent and historically rich way to play classic engine variants.

brief.what_it_is: Woof! is a Doom source port, meaning a re-implementation of the Doom engine that runs the original game data (WAD files) on modern systems. It is based on WinMBF, the Windows port of Lee Killough's MBF engine, and is maintained by Fabian Greffrath. It loads Doom IWADs and PWADs and runs them with modern rendering and input: uncapped frame rate with frame interpolation, widescreen, adjustable FOV, modern gamepad support, and 3D or PC-speaker audio. Its default compatibility level is MBF21, with Vanilla, Boom and MBF also selectable. Output is the game window and audio on screen. The Homebrew formula also installs a woof-setup executable, though the pages I read do not describe it.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says MBF was limited to MS-DOS and that WinMBF was the only way to run it elsewhere. Greffrath wrote that the code only compiled and ran on 32-bit systems and still used outdated SDL-1 libraries, and that this frustration led to the project. The stated goal is to 'fast-forward MBF.EXE from DOS to 21st century and remove all the stumbling blocks on the way.'
brief.how_it_works: It is a C codebase built with CMake on SDL3 and SDL3_net, with optional libraries for audio (openal-soft, libsndfile, fluidsynth, libxmp) and image and JSON support (libspng, yyjson). Music can come from native MIDI, FluidSynth with a bundled soundfont, or a built-in OPL3 emulator. The source also includes a NanoBSP node builder for maps that lack nodes. The README does not describe the internals beyond this.

name: xa
desc: 6502 cross assembler
why: A 6502 cross assembler; a gateway into writing code for classic 8-bit machines like the NES and Apple II.

brief.what_it_is: xa (xa65) is Andre Fachat's open-source, portable 6502 cross assembler, now maintained by Cameron Kaiser. It takes 6502-family assembly source and produces binary output, with a C-like preprocessor, a rich expression syntax, and pseudo-ops. It targets NMOS 6502 variants, CMOS 65C02 and Rockwell R65C02, and the 65816. It can emit plain binary or o65 relocatable objects, and it includes a linker and relocation tools. The package ships several executables: xa, file65, ldo65, printcbm, reloc65 and uncpk. Its companion disassembler dxa is distributed separately as alpha software.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage gives no single mission statement. Andre Fachat's history says he wrote xa to build programs for his self-built CS/A65 computer, and he added o65 objects and a linker in 1996 when he needed to push that homebrew OS further.
brief.how_it_works: xa is described as a two-pass assembler. It reads mnemonics and directives, and it emits machine code for the selected CPU type. Relocatable output goes to o65 objects, which the linker and relocation suite (ldo65, reloc65) can combine later. Relocation mode can leave undefined labels unresolved so they can be linked at a later time.

name: xpipe
desc: Split input and feed it into the given utility
why: Splits input into a utility with a clever pipeline trick, a small but genuine oddity in the Unix toolbox.

brief.what_it_is: xpipe is a Unix command-line utility that reads standard input and splits it into chunks, by a given number of bytes, a given number of lines, or wherever a given pattern matches. It then runs the utility you name once per chunk, feeding each chunk to that utility as its input. The chunks are fed to the command, so a tool that handles only one input at a time can process a multi-item file in one invocation. The page's example pipes a PEM bundle of x509 certificates through openssl x509 and gets subject and validity dates for every certificate.
brief.why_it_exists: The author describes it as a Unix love-child of split(1), tee(1), and xargs(1), built for the case where a tool accepts only one certificate at a time and you would otherwise have to split the file into pieces and loop over them. The page also jokes that you probably have to google how to use sed(1) or awk(1) to pull out blocks between patterns.
brief.how_it_works: xpipe reads stdin and cuts it into chunks at the boundary you specify (-p takes a regular expression pattern for splitting). For each chunk it invokes the trailing command, passing the chunk as input. The page shows only the pattern-split form and does not detail the byte-count and line-count options.

commands_seen.context: Example from the page: reads certs.pem, splits it after each END CERTIFICATE line, and runs openssl x509 -noout -subject -dates on each certificate, printing notBefore, notAfter, and subject for each one.

brief.standout: Most split-and-loop tasks need a shell loop or an awk flip-flop. xpipe folds the split, the repeated invocation, and the per-chunk pattern into one command line, and the example output shows it working on a real multi-certificate file.
brief.status: unknown. The homepage is a single man-page-style web page with no release date, version number, changelog, or commit history. It does have a contact link for the author, but that does not show whether the project is active.
brief.caveats: The page covers only the basic example and points to xpipe(1) for more detail, but no further docs link was visible on the page. The page gives no license, source repository, or install instructions. Homebrew's scout notes and caveats are empty, so nothing extra is known from that side. I did not follow any further links.

And, let's be honest, you probably have to google how to use sed(1) or awk(1) to extract subsequent blocks from a flip-flop pattern.

name: z80asm
desc: Assembler for the Zilog Z80 microprcessor and compatibles
why: A Z80 assembler opens the door to retro 8-bit programming and the machine code that drove a generation of home computers.

brief.what_it_is: z80asm is a free assembler for the Zilog Z80 microprocessor and compatible chips. You feed it Z80 assembly source files and it produces a binary output file. It can also write a label file listing every label in the program, and a listing file that puts the source and the assembled bytes side by side. Source files can include other source files and contain conditional sections. The homepage says it is written in ANSI C and has been tested on GNU/Linux.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames it as a goal of having a free, easy to expand, easy to use assembler, with the GPL license so users can read, modify and redistribute the source. The Savannah page adds that it aims to be portable and complete, and that it was written with the MSX computer in mind as the target, though it works for any system with a Z80.
brief.how_it_works: The README describes the inputs and outputs but not the internals. Source files are assembled with bash-style expressions and can include other files and use conditional blocks. The label file can be included by other source files, which gives linker-like behaviour across separately assembled pieces. Some header files with MSX BIOS, BDOS and system-variable labels are bundled.
brief.install_notes: Nothing beyond a C compiler and the usual source build was mentioned. The homepage says it is ANSI C and should compile on any good platform, but it has only been tested on GNU/Linux. I did not see build steps, a configure line, or a binary download on either page. The brew formula name is z80asm and the executable is z80asm.
brief.standout: The label file can be included by other source files, so separately assembled pieces can link together without a separate linker. It also ships MSX-specific header files of BIOS, BDOS and system-variable labels, which is unusual for a general-purpose assembler.
brief.status: Quiet, not clearly maintained. The Savannah summary lists Development Status as 4 - Beta, registration in November 2003, 20 open bugs out of 31 total, and 1 open patch out of 12. Four members are listed, with Bas Wijnen as group admin. I could not find a last release date or last commit date on either page.
brief.caveats: Only tested on GNU/Linux according to the homepage. Development status is Beta. The homepage's link to the documentation says only "here" and I could not find its URL, so I did not read the full manual. The Savannah page says the project is not part of the GNU Project itself even though it is hosted on Savannah and the homepage is under nongnu.org. The README does not give a version number or changelog.
quotes: The goal of The Z80 assembler project is having a free, easy to expand, easy to use assembler. Free as in free speech, that is.
All official mnemonics are recognized.
Very complex expressions are allowed (bash style).
Beside the binary output file, a label file can be output with a list of all labels in the program.

name: zsdx
desc: Zelda Mystery of Solarus DX
why: A fan-made open Zelda engine port; a fun game but mostly a conventional, well-known style of game.

brief.what_it_is: Zelda: Mystery of Solarus DX is a free, fan-made action-RPG adventure and a direct sequel to The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past, using the same graphics and mechanics. The zsdx package contains only the game's data files, which the Solarus engine loads and runs, so you need Solarus installed to play. It is also an enhanced remake of Mystery of Solarus, a 2002 French-only game made with RPG Maker 2000. The homepage lists version 1.12.3 for Solarus 1.6.x.
brief.why_it_exists: The game was the first made with the Solarus engine, and the homepage says Solarus was primarily designed for it. The DX project was unveiled on April 1st, 2008 to fix the original's flaws, including the battle system, the bosses, and the use of items.
brief.how_it_works: The zsdx repository is a quest data package, not an engine. The solarus_run binary takes a quest path, either a directory with a data subdirectory or a directory containing a data.solarus zip archive. The CMake build packages the data into data.solarus and installs a zsdx launcher script that calls solarus_run with the installed quest path.

commands_seen.context: Runs the quest from the current directory, which must contain a data subdirectory (or data.solarus archive).
Runs the quest with no arguments; works only if Solarus was compiled with the default quest set to '.'.
Build step that generates the data.solarus archive containing all quest data files (the README gives these as two separate commands, cmake . then make).
Installs data.solarus to /usr/local/share/solarus/zsdx/ and a zsdx script to /usr/local/bin/ (assuming /usr/local prefix).
Launches the game after install; equivalent to solarus_run /usr/local/share/solarus/zsdx.
Configures the build to install to a custom prefix, for example without root access; followed by make and make install.

brief.install_notes: The README assumes Solarus is already installed; zsdx is a data package that needs the Solarus engine (the homepage targets Solarus 1.6.x). Building needs cmake and zip, which the README recommends. The default install goes to /usr/local and needs root; a custom prefix is possible via CMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX. Beyond the brew formula, the README describes no accounts or runtime configuration beyond the build and install steps.
brief.standout: It is a full-length, professionally finished fan game built on an open-source engine, and the engine was designed around this game. The scout note calls it an 'engine port', but that is not accurate: it is a fan-made sequel and remake running on the Solarus engine, not a port of a Zelda game.

name: zshdb
desc: Debugger for zsh
why: A step debugger for zsh scripts lets you watch a shell program execute line by line, a useful way into how shells run code.

brief.what_it_is: zshdb is a gdb-like interactive debugger for zsh scripts. You run a zsh script under it and step through execution line by line, setting breakpoints and inspecting state, with gdb-style command syntax. It is a port of the author's bashdb, so many commands match. The documentation index lists version 1.1.3.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says it started as a port of Rocky Bernstein's bash debugger bashdb, so zsh users get the same kind of debugging. The command syntax follows the trepanning debuggers and gdb, so skills carry over to those tools.
brief.install_notes: The README does not give install steps. The documentation index has sections titled 'From a Package' and 'From Source' and 'Invoking the Debugger Initially', but I did not open those pages, so I have no details on them.
brief.standout: It is a shell debugger that follows gdb and trepanning command syntax, so gdb users can use it without learning a new interface. It also has editor and IDE integrations: an Emacs interface through realgud and a Visual Studio Code extension, ZshDebug, by rogalmic.

name: zydis
desc: Fast and lightweight x86/x86_64 disassembler library
why: A fast x86 disassembler library, a real door into how machine code is decoded.

brief.what_it_is: Zydis is an open-source C library for decoding and disassembling x86 and x86-64 (AMD64) machine code. You hand it a memory buffer of raw bytes and it returns decoded instructions with their mnemonics, operands, and per-instruction detail such as accessed registers, flags, and byte offsets of instruction fragments. The README also describes it as a code generation library, so it includes an encoder, shown in the examples as turning a mov into bytes. The package ships two command-line tools, ZydisDisasm and ZydisInfo. The README documents ZydisInfo as a tool for inspecting essentially all the information Zydis provides about an instruction, and shows a screenshot of it. It does not show a ZydisDisasm command line.
brief.why_it_exists: The README presents Zydis as a fast, lightweight, complete x86 and x86-64 disassembler and code generation library, with no third-party dependencies. The homepage pitches it as 'the ultimate X86 & X86-64 disassembler library' and emphasizes correctness, full ISA coverage from Intel and AMD, and small binaries.
brief.how_it_works: The README gives no internal mechanism beyond the claims that it does no dynamic memory allocation, is thread-safe by design, and has no dependencies, not even libc. It says it should compile on any platform with a C11 compiler. The homepage says the library's tables were checked against Intel's XED and LLVM instruction data, with the author acknowledging that correctness is hard to benchmark.

commands_seen.context: Clones the repository with submodules, as the first step of the CMake build.
Configures the CMake build in a build directory.
Compiles Zydis using four parallel jobs after configuration.
Homebrew install command listed in the package manager table.

brief.install_notes: Beyond brew install, the README lists several routes. Build from source with CMake, which needs a recent git clone with submodules and CMake installed; on Windows there is also a manually maintained Visual Studio 2022 project and a way to generate a VS project with CMake. Alternatively, use the amalgamated single-header and single-source distribution from the GitHub release page (zydis-amalgamated.tar.gz), which needs only a C11 compiler. Other packages come from Arch, Debian, Ubuntu, NixOS, vcpkg, and Homebrew. Troubleshooting covers forcing -fPIC when linking a static build into a shared library, via -DCMAKE_POSITION_INDEPENDENT_CODE=ON. No accounts or runtime are required. Official bindings exist for Rust and Python 3.
brief.standout: Zero dependencies, not even libc, and no heap allocation, so it runs in user mode, kernel drivers, and UEFI. It is also very small: the homepage says the full library with all ISA extensions is about 300KB. It is used inside x64dbg, Mozilla Firefox, and WebKit, per the README.
brief.status: Maintained, according to the README and repo structure. Evidence: CI and OSS-Fuzz badges, a master branch for unreleased work, and a maintenance/v4 branch that the README says receives feature updates. v3 receives only security updates until 2025, and v2 is end-of-life. I did not see a last release or commit date, so I cannot give an exact date.
brief.caveats: The homepage is mostly marketing. Its figures (2713 GitHub stars, 1582 instructions, 20792 lines of code) and claims like 'Fast AF' and 'one of the most correct in the industry' are the author's own and unbenchmarked. The homepage's ISA section contains a broken sentence. The README says the library is tested on Windows, macOS, FreeBSD, Linux, and UEFI, but the Windows-specific build paths are secondary. The README gives no license detail beyond MIT. Commercial support is available by contacting the company. The v3 maintenance window ends in 2025, so check the version you pick.
quotes: Fast and lightweight x86/x86-64 disassembler and code generation library.
Absolutely no third party dependencies — not even libc
Should compile on any platform with a working C11 compiler
